div.head: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.
div.p: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.

It takes two to make a betrothal, and both are to blame. No man is ignorant who knows enough to con- ceal what he doesn't know. The man who thinks he can make a success of several things isn't a successful thinker. Dollars are dross--man can take his ashes to the grave, but must leave his "clinkers" behind. A HOMELY TRITTEL—Some people have " speak- ing " countenances—and as plain as words can be. "You seem fascinatedwith cycling ? " "Oh, yes; now I have once got into the habit of it," she rejoined, glancing at her costume. HE ENVIED THEM.—" Scientists say there are microbes in kisses," said Miss Kittish to Mr. Hunker. "Happy microbes!" exclaimed the

young man, ecstatically. WANTED No QuARRELLING.—He (encouragingly) : "I'm sure of one thing, my angel—you and I will never quarrel as that couple are doing." She (with decision) : "Indeed we won't. If you ever speak to me as he did to her, I'll call the police." A WISE PROVISION.—LittIe Ethel (who has been looking at pictures) : "When boys go to heaven, they just take their heads an' put wings on them, an' they fly around that way." Little Johnny: " Wot's that for ? " Little Ethel: "I guess that's

so they can't fight." AN OFF DAY.—Miss Newage : "What was done at the New Woman International Progressive Club to-day?" Bachelor Girl: "Nothing. You see, Mrs. Sweetie happened to come in with her baby, and before we all got through kissing the little
cherub, it was time to adjourii." NOT QUITE FU'LL.—Parker : "I would join the church if it wasn't full of hypocrites." Tucker: "Oh, you are mistaken about that. There's always room for one more."

LITTLE Miss Freckles: "I made ugly faces at your stuck-up sister the other day, but I guess she didn't see me." Little Johnny: "Yes, she did; but she thought they were natural." THE SUPERIORITY OF WOMAN.—Ada: "Men are so slow! It took him nearly two hours to propose to me last night." Helen: " And how lon, did it take you to accept him, dear?" Ada: "Just two seconds ! " DUTY NEGLECTED.—An old song says that Britons never, never will be slaves, And boasts about Britannia, the ruler of the waves; But I've just crossed the stormy sea and I regret to state That if Britannia ruled the waves she didn't rule 'ern straight. Too CLOSE QUARTERS.—Sweet Girl (in photo- graph gallery) : "I wish you wouldn't put that big camera so close to me." Photographer: "Don't you want the picture cabinet size ? ' Sweet Girl: " Yes ; but I don't want the freckles cabinet size." HANDLED WITH CARE.—Customer (who has just purchased a wonderfully cheap set of furniture) : "Do you always pack furniture carefully before delivering it ? ' New Boy: "This kind we do, 'cause the jarring would shake it to pieces." A CERTAINTY.—Things are coming to such a pass that pretty soon when we see a young man who is walking ahead of us carefully lift one coat tail as he crosses the street we may feel morally certain that he is an advanced young woman. ALL'S FAIR IN LOVE.—Miss Million: "So you know Miss Tiptop, the belle of the season ? " Mr. Sharpwit (after Miss Million's heart, hand, and bank account) : "Oh yes; she and I move in—in—ah---- much the same set." Miss Million: "By the way, here comes Miss. Tiptop now. We will meet her face to face. . . . Why, she did not recognize you." Mr. Sharpwit : "She always acts that way when I'm with a prettier girl than she is."— FORGET HIS NAME.—Magistrate why didn't you answer to your name ? " Vagrant: "Beg parding, jedge, but I forgot wot name I gave las' night." Magistrate: "Didn't you give your own name ? " Vagrant: "No, jedge, I'm travellin' incog." DIFFERENT.—Chase (to dentist) : "I won't pay anything extra for gas. Just pull the tooth out even if does hurt a little." Dentist : "I must say you are very plucky. Just let me see the tooth.' Chase: "Oh, I haven't got any toothache. It's Mrs. Chase; she'll be here in a minute." MUCH TO ANSWER FOR.—Nagger: "There goes the wretch who ruined my life." Wagger: " What ? Explain yourself, old man." Nagger: "He was engaged to my wife, and jilted her before I met her." HIS RECOGN'ISED VlB.TUE.—Bootles (the shoe- maker) : "Young Howling swell is dead; he was a mighty wild young man, but he always paid his bills." Tapes (the tailor) : " Yes ; I always gave him credit for that." EXCHANGE OF CIVILITIES.—First Good Fellow: "Have a cigar ? " Second Good Fellow: "Thanks. Try one of mine." Each (to himself, a few moments later) "This miserable weed is even worse than the one I gave him." HORRIBLE. —" Did ye ever hear of dese priests in India," said Reginald de Bumme, " dat sticks needles through dere cheeks an' burns dere skin jes' fur fun ? " " Dat an't nothin'," replied Clarence Fitz Hautbeau. "I knowed a man dat tuck a bath every day 'cause he said he liked it !" NOT SATISFIED.—" And you saw Niagara?" "Yes." "And did you not consider it wonderful ?" "Not so very. The water simply fell over the rocks. If it were the other way, now, and the water climbed them, it would have been quite marvellous. HE (after popping the question) : "Why do you cry, my angel? Did I offend you by my proposal ? " She (still sobbing) : "Oh no, dear, it is not that; I am crying for joy. Mother always said to me, May, she said, you are such an idiot that you would not get even a donkey for a lover,' and now I have got one after all." HANDY DEFINITIONS.—" Pa," asked Johnnie Wilkins, "what is a pathologist?" "He's a man who lays out paths in parks and elsewhere, my boy. Now, don't bother papa any more. He's busy." "Well, I only want to know one more thing, papa," said Johnnie. "Well, what is it ? " "What's a mancipated woman?" "Why don't you reason it out for yourself ? " asked the father. "What does M-A-N spell?" "Man," said Johnnie. "Well, then, a Man-cipated woman is a woman that thinks she's a man. Now, run away." ARISING out of the late stoppage in the coal trade, a capital story is worth repeating concerning Lord Derby and a collier. Wandering on some land belonging to Earl Derby, the collier there chanced to meet the owner of Knowsley face to face. His lordship inquired if the collier knew he was walking on his land. "Thy land? Well, I've got no land Tnysel '," was the reply, "and I'm like to walk on somebody's. Wheer did tha' get it fro' ?" "Oh," explained his lordship, "I got it from my ancestors." "An' wheer did you get it fro' ? " queried the collier. "They got it from their ancestors," was the reply. " And wheer did their ancestors get it fro' ? ' "They fought for it." "Well, begad," said the collier, squaring up to the noble earl, " I'll feight thee for it !"

Monday was the last day for sending in applica- tions for the vacant position of Clerk to the Lon- don County Council. An enormous number of ap- lications has been received, but none of the appli- cants are, it is said, in the very first rank as muni- cipal administrators. The annual salary which the Council offers (X 2,000 did not attract the older men from the larger provincial cities. They receive the same salaries now, accompanied with a pension,and most of the leading men are too old to care for a change. Several London vestry clerks are among the applicants, who also include clerks and chair- men of boards of guardians, bank managers, bar- risters,retired officers,and clerks of county councils. The Council's selection will, it is expected,be made some some time next month.

Here is an interesting piece of information which may throw a light on the connection of city specu- lators with the invasion of the Transvaal. On the evening of the day when Jameson started on his unfortunate expedition a man from the City told a friend" Jameson has crossed into the Transvaal." The friend was not particularly impressed by the information, and did not value its gravity until the official announcement was published. It then ap- peared that the man from the City announced the fact long before it was known at the Colonial Office. How did the City get to know? Did some friendly hand send the information directly Jame- son started, and before the wires were cut, or was it known here that he was to march that day?

It is evident that the omnibus and cab companies in London do not anticipate an early reign for the " horseless ca:riage." A contract has just been entered into with an Am9rican firm to supply 6,000 horses, or more than hall the entire stud of the General Omnibus Company, during the present year for metropolitan purposes. The price is consider- ably under the average paid by the companies, which is sufficient reason for the importation. The life of a bus horse is about five years.

Lord Charles Beresford manages to keep himself before tte public as successfully as the German mperor. He has just invented a plan of naval defence, which is to be capable of being put into operation in 24 hours; but he has not yet informed the public whether it will be proof against Mr. Edison's system of electric water-hose, his airy navies, and his 24-mile carrying guns, if gun is to be the name of this new mythical apparatus. Lord Charles seems to be set free now from Chatham Dockyard, and is voyaging to the Mediterranean for the purpose of visiting Gibraltar, Malta, Con- stantinople, and Egypt, in order to enlarge or test his schemes. The tour will freshen public interest in him, and give him a new status as a naval autho- rity in the military clubs, as well as secure the ear of the House of Commons when he obtains the stat there for which he is aspiring. He will not leave the public long in ignorance of his novel panacea, and he has already submitted it, in its inchoate state, to the Admiralty, who have very probably had something of the kind under consideration before. _

The New York "World." in giving a very full account of the meetings of the American Federation of Labour, thus refers to the English delegates, Messrs. Mawdsley and Cowey "They come as the representatives of at least a million English work- ing men,a very respectable army, one differing from other European armies In that it supports itself and does not get beaten." Of the American delegates present the" World" says: "They looked prosper- I ous. Men accustomed to bodies of European work- ing men would have taken these men for lawyers or merchants. The average of intelligence, judged by physiognomy, was not less high than that of a con- vention of lawyers. It was considerably higher than the average of a State political convention. . . Everyone wore an expression more cheerful than the expression commonly worn by Russell Sage, Pierpoint Morgan, or John D. Rockefeller. Every delegate looked much healthier than the majority of men of great wealth." The " World " goes on to say that concrete plans for social improvement were listened to with far greater interest than the "worn-out catch phrases of professional agitation."

A reprint just issued at Cambridge of the "Weekly Flying Post" of January 4, 1746, has in addition to a great deal of quaint and interesting matter, some evidence of the tranquil courage with which Great Britain had faced a particularly peril- ous situation in the preceding year. The parallel is full of interest at the present moment. In 1745 there appeared to be a formidable Continental com- bination against England. The Young Pretender's forces were in possession of a portion of the ceuntry, a considerable ma.s of opinion was dis- affected to the Government of the day and favour- able to the Pretender's cause, and therefore to those Powers which championed it. In such circumstances it would not have been surprising if language approaching that of panic had been employed by the majority who supported the Hanoverian dynasty, The reverse, however, was the case. A courageous determination to grapple with and overthrow the peril to the realm was steadfastly but calmly manifested. Witness this extract: "It is said the Spaniards intend to make an embarkation at Ferrol, whilst the French invade us from their ports in the Channel ; hut no doubt if these schemes should be put in execution 200,000 Englishmen will immediately appear in arms (as ready as their glorious ancestors) to defend their lives and the best Constitution in the world."

Great is the glory of the god of fashion! A private letter from Sydney, New Smith Wales,doted Dec. B,and received this week says :—"Lord Hamp- den, our new Govenor, has settled down. I think he will be popular. His daughters are great bicy- clists,and consequently the wheel is now de rigueur here. The craze is tremendous and terrible, and all the ladies" bikes 'in Sydney have been sold out." And this with the theremometer at 95deg. and up- wards in the shade ! Until the advent of the Misses Brand there does not seem to have been so much cycling in the N.S.W., capital as in some places.

A new and a useful departure in the training of our London volunteers was made on Tuesday even- ing, when Lieut.. Sutton, of the Coldstream Guards, delivered the first of a course of lectures on minor tactics to an audience composed of officers and non-commissioned officers of the North London Bri- gade, to the staff of which Lieut. Sutton is attached as brigade-major. The lecture waq given at the drill-hall of the 19th Middlesex in Chenieg-street, Bloomsbury, Lord Falmouth, who commands the brigade, presiding. The subject was " Outposts," and the questions put to the lecturer at the end both officers and serßeants howed the attention and interest with which the lecture was followed.

We are only now beginning to realise the xtent of the commercial crisis from which the United States now seems happily to be emerging. For in- stance,the railway foreclosure sales of 1895 eclipsed those of any previous year. Fifty-three railways, comprising 13.129 miles of line, were sold, and they represented 775,000,000:dols.in'hondA and stock. That is more that the capital of all our Scottish railways. Tn 1894, forty-two lines were sold, representing 319,000,000 dols.of capital. The railway insol- vencies of 1895 concerned thirty-one railways and 369,000.000 dots. of capital.

The fact is much commented on among politi- cians.and financiers that, while our Australian colonies have sent to the British Government e combined message, conve3ing an assurance of sympathy and support in the present crisis, no similar note of goodwill has been received from Canada. In the first place, the expression of kindly feeling on the part of the Australians has given widespread satisfaction,and is heartily reciprocated by Australian residents in London, who are toler- ably numerous at present, and with some of whom I come into contact every day. Australia is already capable of providing a very considerable amount of f.elf-defence against any foe; and it is believed to be probable that the present danger, or series of dangers, to which the British Empire has been ex- posed, will lead to an effective enlargement of the present colonial power of resisting. attack. Neither Canada nor Australia was in the slightest danger from the misunderstanding from Germany ; hut in case of a quarrel with America the dancer of both would be very great. American Alabamas, despite the greatest vigilance of the British fleet, would find their way to Australian harbours ; and the in- vasion of Canada is a foregone certainty. .Perh..n. The most expensive drug is physostigmine, two ounces of which would cost nearly four hundred thousand pounds. It is prepared from the calabar bean, and is used in diseases of the eye. The late Sir Andrew Clark used to declare that, while China tea was wholesome enough, Indian tea was so powerful that a cup in the morning was sufficient to disorder the nerves for the whole day. Mme places of amusement are now open in New York than are to be found in London or „Paris. It takes four million pounds capital to run them, and they give em- ployment to twenty thousand persons. According to Sir Benjamin Richardson, the normal period of human life is about 110 years,and seven out of ten average people,if they took proper care of themselves ought to attain that age. Bunches of dried sea-weed, window corks, crackers, tobacco, and similar fibre substances indicate the ap- proach of rain, because their fibres become soft by ab- sorbing the moisture of the air when the atmosphere is approaching the point of saturation. The most stubborn cases of neuralgia are apt to yield to a hot-water treatment. Wherever the pain is located there a hot-water bag should be applied. The suffering part should be wrapped in a blanket, and the unfor- tunate patient should be put to bed and covered with more blankets, and induced to drink at least three cups of water as hot as the palate can stand. This treatment may seem severe, but it is sure to bring relief.
Feminine Feet

A Paris saleswoman says that the Madrid ladies have the smallest feet she knows of, Peruvians and Chilians coming next. American ladies from the United States aro also remarkable for their small feet. The Russians have heavy splay feet. It is impossible to classify those of Vienna, there are so many varieties there. The Em- press of Austria requires a long, narrow shoe. She haf no flesh on her foot, and her instep is high. The best- shaped feet in Northern Europe are in Sweden. German ladies coming from Germany are generally neatly shod. English ladies coming from England have awkwardly made boots and shoes. The Belgian ladies are better off in their shoemakers, but they have large feet. Jewish ladies—in Paris, at any rate—have small feet, and are particular about their shoes and stockings. It appears that Lady Ermyntrude Malet has a phenomenally small foot. Dona Bertha (de Bohan), wife of Don Carlos, shows Breton descent in her feet. Her -number is 5 or a " small 6." The Empress Eugenie's white satin shoes used to be sent to the orphanage she patronised to be worn by "first communicants," aged 11 to 12.
A Woman Pastor.

_ The town of Littleton, N.H., has a woman pastor,Mrs. Frost. She first came to that town as the wife of the pastor of the Congregational Church, Rev. George B. Frost. Owing to ill-health he was obliged to go abroad, and the church invited Mrs. Frost to supply the pulpit during his absence. This she did for a year, when an ecclesiastical council was called.and after a rigid exam- ination, the rite ,f ordination was administered, and Mrs. Frost was thus fitted for all the functions of a minister. In pulpit, parish work, at funerals, marriage ceremonies, and all other services she was equally ac- ceptable,and when the pastor was forced,from continued ill health,to ask a dismissal, it was granted on condition that Mrs. Frost should be installed as the pastor. Eieh step leading to this arrangement pas been taken by the people. In no instance has Mrs. Frost put herself for- ward. She is a modest, retiring woman of marked ability.

Example not Precept. A number of ladies in the neighbourhood of Godalm- ing and Guildford have commenced a crusade against the wearing of any aigrettes or feathers, the obtaining of which leads to the destruction of rare or beautiful birds. In an appeal which is made by two ladies of Charterhouse. Goda'ming, it is pointed out that when it was remembered that 60,000 dozen aigrettes were sup- plied to one dealer in London alone, and that an Ameri- can lady was seen wearing a coat made of the breasts of humming bird', it is evident that no species can long withstand such a drain, and that the white heron, the bird of paradise, and many other beautiful birds must become extinct unless the demand deases. Over one hundred ladies in the neighbourhood have pledged themselves nat to wear any aigrettes or feathers except those of the ostrich, domesticated birds, or birds killed for food.

A Shoe-Mending Case. A convenient trifle is a shoe-mending case. It is made from half a yard or two inch ribbon. Fold the ribbon in the middle and slip into it a large spool of black twist of linen thread. Hold the spool so that it cannot slip out, and on each side of it mark a line. Feather stitch this line across the ribbon, and you have the first pocket made. Directly above and across the ribbon slip a paper of needles and cat-stitch a line across for the second pocket. Next above it is a pocket tor scissors. To keep them from slipping, put a loop on the inside of the poc- ket and divide it from the space above by feather-stitch- ing. The ends of all the pockets are open at the sides. The space above the pocket for sc!ssors is overcast on each side, as that is to be the pocket for shoe buttons. Turn the ands of the ribbon in to form a narrow frill, 'and through the casing run a bay ribbon, ending in a full bow on each side. Finish with a ribbon tacked to either end, so that the case can be hung if one chooses. Make the bags of ribbon that will match the colours of the rooms where they are likely to go.

THE OUTLAW'S RENDEZVOUS. "Our plots fall short like darts which rash hand throw With an ill aim, and have too far to go ; Nor can we long discoveries prevent; God is too much about the innocent! —SIR ROBERT HOWARD. "The Old Road Inn," described in the dying deposition of poor Nancy Grewell, was situated some miles from Hurricane Hall, by the side of a forsaken turnpike in the midst of a thickly-wooded, long, and narrow valley, shut in by two lofty ranges of mountains. Once this turnpike was lively with travel, and this inn gay with custom; hut, for the last twenty- five years, since the highway had been turned off in another direction, both road and tavern had been abandoned, and suffered to fall to ruin. The road was washed and furrowed into deep and dangerous gullies, and obstructed by fallen timber; the house was disfigured by mouldering walls, broken chim- neys and patched windows. Had any traveller lost himself, and chanced to have passed that way, he might have seen a little, old, dried-up woman, sitting knitting at one of the winelows. She was known by those who were old enough to remember her and her home, as Granny Raven, the daughter of the last proprietor of the inn. She was reputed to be dumb, but none could speak with certainty of the fact. In truth, for as far back as the memory of the "oldest inhabitant" could reach, she had been feared, disliked, and avoided, as one of malign reputation; indeed, the Ignorant and superstitious believed her to possess the "evil eye," and to be gifted with "second sight." But of late years as the old road and the old inn were quite forsaken, so the old beldame was quita forgotten. It was one evening, a few weeks after Ca.pitola's fearful adventure in the forest, that this old woman carefully closed up every door and window in the front of the house, stopping every crevice through which a ray of light might gleam and warn that Impossible phenomenon—a chance traveller, on the old road, ot life within the habitation. Having, so to speak, hermetically sealed the front of the house, she betook herself to a large back kitchen. This kitchen was strangely and rudely furnished —having an extra broad fire-place with the recesses on each side of the chimney filled with oaken shelves, laden with strong pewter plates, dishes and mugs; all along the walls were arranged rude, oaken benches; down the length of the room, was left, always standing, a long deal table, capable of accommodating from fifteen to twenty guests. On entering this kitchen Granny Raven struck a light, kindled a fire, and began to prepare a large supper. Nor did this old beldame look unlike the ill- omened bird whose name she bore, in her close clinging black gown, and flapping black cape and hood, and with her sharp eyes, hooked nose and protruding chin. Having put a large surloin of beef before the fire, she took down a pile of pewter plates and arranged them along on the sides of the table; then to every plate she placed a pewter mug. A huge wheaten loaf of bread, a great roll of butter and several plates of pickles were next put upon the board, and when all was ready the old woman sat down to the patient turning of the spit. She had not been thus occupied more than twenty minutes when a hasty, scuffling step was heard at the back of the house, accompanied by a peculiar whistle, immediately under the window. "That's Headlong Hal,' for a penny! He never can learn the cat's tread 1" thought the crone, as she arose and withdrew the bolt of the back door. A little, dark-skinned, black-eyed, black-haired, thin and wiry man came hurrying in, exclaiming: "How now, old girl—supper ready?" She shook her head, poiated to the roasting beef, lifted up boths hands with the ten fingers spread out twice, and then made a rotary motion with one arm. "Oh—you mean it will be done in twenty turns; but hang me if I understand your dumb show half the time.—Have none of the men come yet?" She put her fingers together, flung her hands wildly apart in all directions, brought them slowly together again, and pointed to the supper table. "Urn l—that is to say they are dispersed about their business, but will all be here to-night?" She nodded. "Where's the cap'n ?" She pointed over her left shoulder upwards— placed her two hands out broad from her temples— then made a motion as of lifting and carrying a basket, and displaying goods. " Humph ! humph! gone to Tip-Top to sell goods disguised as a peddler I " She nodded. And before he could put another question, a low, soft mew was heard at the door. "There's Stealthy Steve l'—he might walk with hob-nailed high-lows over a gravelly road, and you would never hear his footfall," said the man, as the door noiselessly opened and shut, and a soft-footed, low-voiced, subtle looking mulatto entered the kitchen, and gave good evening to its occupants. "Ha! I'm devilish glad you've come, Steve, for hang me if I'm not tired to death trying to talk to this crone, who, to the charms of old age and ugliness, adds that of dumbness. Seen the (Lapin 7 " "No, he's gone out to hear the people talk, and find out what they think of him." Hal burst into a loud and scornful laugh, saying —"I should think it would not require much seek- ing to discover that!" Here the old woman came forward, and, by signs, managed to inquired whether he had brought her "the tea." Steve drew a packet from his pocket, saying softly: "Yes, mother, when I was in Spicer's store I saw this lying with the other things on the counter, and remembering you, quietly put it into my pocket." The old crone's eyes danced; she seized the packet, patted the excellent thief on the shoulder, wagged her head deridingly at the delinquent one, and hobbled off to prepare her favourite beverage. While she was thus occupied the whistle was once more heard at the door, followed by the entrance of a man decidedly the most repulsive looking of the whole party—a man one having a full pocket would scarcely like to meet on a lonely road in a dark night. In form he was of Dutch proportions, short but stout; with a large, round bead, covered with stiff, sandy hair; broad, flat face; coarse features; pale, half-closed eyes, and an expression of countenance strangely made up of elements as opposite as they were forbidding— a mixture of stupidity and subtility, cowardice and ferocity, caution and cruelty. His name in the gang was Demon Dick, a sobriquet of which he was eminently deserving and characteristically proud. He came in sulkily, neither saluting the company ncr returning their salutations. He pulled a chair to the fire, threw himself into it, and ordered the old woman to draw him a mug of ale. "Dick's in a bad humour to-night," murmured Steve, softly. "When was he ever in a good one 7 " roughly broke forth Hal. "H—sh I " said Steve, glancing at Dick, who with a hideous expression, was listening to the conversation. "There's the cap'n I " exclaimed Hal, as a ringing footstep sounded outside, followed by the abrupt opening of the door and entrance of the leader. Setting down a large basket, and throwing off a broad-brimmed Quaker hat amo, broad skirted over- coat, Black Donald stood roaring with laughter. Black Donald, from his great stature might have been a giant walked out of the age of fable into the middle of the nineteenth century. From his atature alone he might have been chosen leader of this band of desperadoes. He stood six feet eight inches in his boots, and was stout and muscular in proportion. He had a well-formed, stately head, fine aquiline features, dark complexion, strong, steady, dark eyes, and an abundance of long, curl- ing black hair and beard that would have driven to despair a Broadway beau, broken the heart of a Washington belle, or made his own fortune in any city of America as a French count or a German baron 1 He had decidedly "the air noble and distinguished." While he threw his broad brim in one direction and his broad coat in another and gave way to peals of laughter, Headlong Hal said: " Cap'n, I don't know what you think of it; but I think it just as churlish to laugh alone as to get drunk in solitude." "Oh, you shall laugh Wait until I tell you! But. first, answer me: Does not my broad-skirted grey coat and broad-brimmed grey hat make me ;ook about twelve inches shorter and broader?" "That's so, Cap'n 1" "And when I bury my black beard and chin deep down in this drab neckcloth, and pull the broad brim low over my black hair and eyes, I look as mild and respectable as William Penn."

div.head: REMARKABLE ESSAY IN ENGLISH
div.p: A REMARKABLE ESSAY IN ENGLISH

The "Times of India" prints the subjoined remark- ably worded petition from an ex-member of the Silledar Mounted Police. The simple request which the writer wished to convey was that he might be furnished with a formal certificate of his service in the police force : "The humble petition of —, late Silledar Mounted Police, most humbly sheweth : That, pity my grievances, my trumbling steps have dragged me before your Honour's most greeted chairs, my days are dwind- ling to the shortest span, blessed Lord give ma relief and heaven will bless your Honour's stores. That owing to my adverse fates, which had then frowned my wife and my sister to retire out from their public lives, leaving my father and sister in bed of hopeless healths. My father exposed out his perishable dispositions. There is not a soul into my family elder or younger thar me, to attend on the sickness as above, which then compelled me by nolens volens, to tender resignation of my former post by my own, leaving me no time to apply your honour for certificee. By the blessing of God and your honour, my father and my sister restored to their former health, but the money so saved for future expenses, when necessary for, has been exhausted on medicining them. When I found quite involved in poverty, that we endured severe fastings from the flummery floor even, I came in Bombay in search of my prey, presented my circumstauces to the Commissioner of Police who asked me for a certificate of my former post without which lam refused by my bread. My humble services extended over two years under your honour's most auspicious orders, during which I toiled impatiently by my acsiduity and attention with a view to start with my further aivancement in life honestly. Under the stern cravings of hunger, I crave your leniency will be graciously pleased to stretch forth your honour's chant. ful hand to fill up my wallet spread for a certificate for the time being under your honour's august orders, only to relieve our lives from the panic clutches of starvation. Pray let me teat the gold of my fortune in the alembic of success, but let not my ardent hopes be refused by rejec- tion, because your honour's one word would supply my law wants. Pray do not blast out my fervent hopes without which I am not to be taken in any kind of ser- vice. For which boon of your honour's merciful philan- thropy and equity in charity, I shall jointly invoke heavenly choicest blessings to dwell with your honour's Long life in years and advancing chair."

div.head: 1 LADIES' LETTER.
div.p: 1 LADIES' LETTER.

bfr -bIIAREST NELLIE, Children's party dresses are prettier than evet this year, and pretty blendings of colour are seen everywhere. Elder girls---I mean those about 15 or 16—at children's parties usually wear simple gowns which cannot suffer seriously from the ani- mated actions of the little ones. Glacti silks, faintly flowered, are useful for this purpose, being strong enough to resist pulls, and with sufficienb substance to stand the sponging process consequent upon receiving stains from contact with sweet- isnairched fingers. Thin materials are ill-adapted for such hard wear. A very pretty dress for an occasion of this sort is known as the Louis XVI. The bodice and skirt are in flowered glace. silk, the blossoms running downwards in narrow stripes, as is the fancy at the present moment. The waistcoat is white satin, and the underskirt white muslin, bordered with a flounce of lace over one of muslin, put on with the heading characteristic of the period of the unhappy Marie Antoinette. The basque of the bodice is very full at the back, and is cut out all round the edge in deep vandykes. The gimp trimming on the waistcoat ends in two fringed ornaments, and was copied from an illustration in the British Museum. The revers of lace form a berthe of the old style all round the shoulders, and the sleeves have none of the exaggerated size of our owu day. Them is hardly an evening gown of any note which does not boast lavish embroideries, and these for the most part are worked on the garment itself. Graduated panels picked out with sequins and con- verging at the bottom of the skirt make an exceed- ingly popular design, the same idea appearing on the bodice in a modified degree. Embroideries again are preferred to passementerie for caps and cloaks, while milliners are using this decoration in lavish quantities. One of the prettiest models is of satin ntery (which may be of any colour).

The front is lull, and the décolletage is decked with a scarf of satin, which is drawn through a diamond buckle and falls with pleated ends on either side; over the shoulders of this are silk-edged loops of chiffon, and the sleeves are set into two puffs. Oita podrida seems, perhaps, the best way ol describing the present shapes in hats and bonnets. To say they are varied is a mild expression. I may tell you, however, that black seems much in vogue, nlivened with white, either aigrette, choux, or marabout. A Rembrandt hat that .1 saw quite lately was black felt lined with velvet, with a bunch of black feathers on the left side, and a large velvet bow with a paste ornament. A large tuft of white chrysanthemums, with aigrette of pointed velvet bows, enhances a pretty little toque of two shades of violet. Another toque without strings was of violet chenille and silk straw plaited, with aigrette of the same straw, and on the brim tufts of large velvet violets and leaves, and chou of glycine velvet. One of the most becoming and picturesque shapes, however, is a at with a wide and perfectly level brim all round

of felt, with a wide crown in black velvet, arranged in folds and surrounded by a band of scarlet satin ribbon with a bow of the same at one side. This hat, worn well forward in the present custom, throws the eyes into shadow and adds to their expressiveness and charm. A splendid coat for travelling is made in Lovat tweed. It is voluminous and completely covers the entire dress. It is lined with brocaded satin, and has four seams at the back, the material being entirely, waterproof. The great novelty is in the sleeves. These are made like a skirt for a doll's dress, joined underneath the arm, full, and forming a complete protection for the arm without at all confining the dress sleeves. The hand is slipped through in a moment, and it is comfortable and admirably cut. It has a velvet collar, and the sleeves are rendered additionally firm by being lined with fibre chamois. I want to tell you of an awfully smart tailor- made costume I saw just the other day. It was

in fashionable shades of shrunk Venetian coating, and the jacket, 'which had the large fashionable sleeves, had revers of faced habit cloth to match (they might also be made to contrast). There were the usual large medallion buttons.
Your loving JENNIE.

"Yes, verily, friend Donald," said Hal. "Well, in this meek guise I went peddling to- day." "Aye, Cap'n, we knew it; and you'll go once too often." _
" I have gone just once too often.." "I knew it."
" We said so."

" D—n 1" were some of the ejaculations as the members of the band sprang to their feet and handled secret arms. " Pshaw I put up your knives and pistols! There Is no danger; I was not traced; our rendezvous is still a secret for which the government would pay a thousand dollars 1" "How, then, do you say that you went once too often, Cap 7" "It was accurate. I should have said that I had gone for the last time, for that it would not be safe to venture again. Come—l must tell you the whole story ;-IDttt in the meantime let us have supper. Mother Raven, dish the beef. Dick, draw the ale. Hal, cut the bread. Steve, carve. Bestir your- selves, burn you! or you shall have no story 1" ex- claimed the captain, flinging himself into a chair at the head of the table. _ _
When his orders had been obeyed, and the men were gathered around the table, and the first draught of ale had been quaffed by all, Black Douala asked:
_ "Where do you think I went peddling to-day 7" - -

"Devil knows," said Hal. - "That's a secret between the Demon and Black Donald," said Dick. " Hush 1 he's about to tell us," murmured Steve. "Wooden heads! you'd never guess, I went—l went to—Do you give it up? I went right straight Into the lion's jaws—not only into the very clutches, but into the very teeth, and down the very throat of the lion! and have come out as safe as Jonas from the whale's belly I—in a word, I have been up to the county seat where the court is now in session, and sold cigar-cases, snuff-boxes and smoking caps to the grand and petit jury, and a pair of gold spectacles to the learned judge himseli 1" "No!" "No ! !" "No! 11" exclaimed Hal, Steve and Dick in a breath.

"YES! and moreover, I offered a pair of patent steel spring handcuffs to the sheriff, John Keepe, in person, and pressed him to purchase them, as- suring him that he would have occasion for their use if ever be caught that grand rascal, Black Donald 1" " Ah 1 the atrocious villain, if I theught I should ever have the satisfaction of springing them upon his wrists, I'd buy them at my own proper cost l' said the sheriff, taking them in his hands, and ex- amining them curiously. " • Alai he's a man of Belial, that same Black Donald I—ithee'd better buy the handcuffs, John,' said I. "'Nay, friend, I don't know; and as for Black Donald, we have some hopes of taking the wretch at last!' said the simple gentleman. " Ah, verily, John, that's a good hearing for peaceful travellers like myself,' said I. " ' Excellent excellent! for when that fell marauder once swings from a gallows--' " ' His ner:k will be broken John l' "'Yes, friend; yes, probably; after which honest men may travel in safety! Ah 1 never have I ad- justed a hempen cravat about the throat of any aspirant for such an honour, with less pain than I shall officiate it the last toilet of Black Donald l', " ' If thee catch him 7' _ _ _

"Exactly friend, if I catch him; but the addi- tional reward offered by Major Warfield, together with the report that he often frequents our towns and villages in disguise, will stimulate people to renewed efforts to discover and capture him,' said the sheriff. " Ah 1 that will be a great day for Alleghany. And when Black Donald is hanged, I shall make an effort to be present at the solemnity myself!' "'Do, friend,' said the sheriff, 'and I will see to getting you a good place for witnessing the pro- ceedings.' " I have no doubt thee will, John—a very good place! and I assure thee, that there will not be one present more interested in those proceodings than myself,' said I. "'Of course that is very natural; for there is no one more in danger from these marauders than men of your itinerant calling. Good heavens I it was but three years age a peddler was robbed and murdered in the woods around the Hidden House.' "'Just so, John,' said I; "and it's my opinion that often when I've been travelling along the road at night Black Donald hasn't been tar of! But teil me, John, so that I may have a chance of earn- ing that thousand dollars—what disguises does this son of Moloch take 7' "Why, friend, it is said that he appears as a Methodist missionary, going about selling tracts; and sometimes as a knife-grinder, and sometimes simulates your calling as a peddler l' said the un- suspicious sheriff. "I thought, however, it was time to be off, so I said, "thee had better let me sell thee those hand- culls, John. Allow me I I will show thee their beautiful machinery I Hold out thy wrists, if thee pleases, John.' "The unsuspicious officer, with a face brimful of interest, held out his wrists for experiment. "I snapped the ornaments on them in a little less than no time, and took up my pack and disappeared before the sheriff had collected his faculties and found out his position." "Ha, ha, ha! haw, haw, haw I ho, ho, ho I" laughed the outlaws, in every kly of laughter— "and so our captain, instead of being pinioned by the sheriff, turned the tables and actually manacled Ms honour! Hip, hip, hurrah 1 three times three for the merry captain, that manacled the sheriff 1" "flush, burn you! there's some one coming 1" exclaimed the captain, rising and listening. "It is Le Noir, who was to meet me here to-night on important business."

div.head: CHAPTER XXI.
div.p: CHAPTER XXI.
GABRIEL LE NOIR, " Naught's had ! all's spent! When our desires are gained without content."
-SIIAKESPEABIL

"The colonel !" exclaimed the three men in a breath, as the door opened and a tall, handsome and distinguished-looking gentleman, wrapped in a black military coat, and having his black beaver pulled low over his brow, strode into the room. All arose upon their feet to greet him ats thou& Le had been a prince.

With a haughty wave of his hand, he bade them resume their seats, and beckoning their leader, said: "Donald, I would have a word with you." "At your command, Colonel," said the outlaw, rising and taking a candle and leading the way into the adjoining room, the same in which fourteen years before old Granny Grewell and the child had been detained. Setting the candle upon the mantlepieee, Black Donald stood waiting for the visitor to onen the conversation; a thing that the latter seemed in no hurry to do, for he began walking up and down the room in stern silence. "You seem disturbed, Colonel," at length said the outlaw. "I am disturbed--more than disturbed! lam suffering I" " Svffering, Colonel!" " A)e I—suffering !—from what, think you I—the pangs of remore 1" "Remorse! ha-ha-ha-ha-ha 1" laughed the outlaw till all the rafters rang. "Aye, man, you may laugh! but I repeat that I am tortured with remorse !—and for what do you suppose I—for those acts of self-preservation that fanatics and fools would stigmatise as crimes? No, my good fellow; but for one unacted crime l'" "1 told your honour so 1" cried the outlaw, triumphantly. "Donald, when I go to church, as I do con- stantly, I hear the preacher prating of repentance; t,. man, I never knew the meaning of the word until recently I" " And I can almost guess what it is that has enlightened your honour," said the outlaw. " Yes! it is that miserable old woman and babe! Doaaid, in every vein of my soul, I repent not having silenced them both forever while they were yet in my power!" "Just so, Colonel; the dead never come back; o:, if they do, are not recognised as property-holders this world! I wish your honour had taken my advice, and sent that woman and child on a longer :ourney." " Donald—l was yonnger then than now. I— shrank. from bloodshed," said the man, in a husky voice. "Bah I superstition. Bloodshed I—blood is shed eery day! We kill to live,' say the butchers. So do we! Every creature preys upon some other creature weaker than himself—the big beasts eat up the little ones; artful men live on the simple- so be it ! the world was made for the strong and cunning; let the weak and foolish look to them- selves !" said the outlaw, with a loud laugh. While he spoke, the visitor resumed his rapid, restless striding up and down the room. Presently he came again to the side of the robber, and whis-
pered : Donald. that grid has returned to the neighbour-

hood, brikkht back by ofd Warfielcl. My on met her in the woods a month ago, fell into conversation with her—heard her history, or as much of it as she herself knows. Her name is Capitola! she is the living image of her mother. How she came under the notice of old Warfield—to what extent he bit acquainted with her birth and rights—what proofs may be in his possession, I know not. All that I have discoveted, after the strictest inquiry that I was enabled to make, is this: that the old beggar- woman that died and was buried at Major War- field's expense, was no other than Nancy Grewell, returned—that the night before she died she sent for Major Warf eld, and had a long talk with him, and that shortly afterwards the old scoundrel travelled to the North and brought home this girl." "Humph 1 it is an ugly business, your honour, especially with your honour's little prejudice against—" "Donald! this is no time for weakness! I have gone too far to stop—Capitola must die." "That's so, Colonel; the pity is that it wasn't found out fourteen years ago. It is so much easier to pinch a baby's nose until it falls asleep, than to stifle a young girl's shrieks and cries! Then the baby would not have been missed; but the young girl will sure to be inquired after." "I know that there will be additional risk; but there shall be the larger compensation, larger than your most sanguine hopes would suggest. Donald, listen 1" said the colonel, stooping, and whispering low—" the day that you brine me undeniable proof that Capitola La Noir is dead you finger one thou- sand dollars!"

_ "Ha-ha-ha 1" laughed the outlaw, in angry scorn —" Capitola Le Noir is the sole heiress of a fortune —in land, negroes, coal-mines, iron-foundries, rail- way shares and bank stock, of half a million of dollars—and you ask me to get her out of your way for a thousand dollars 1 I'll do it! you know I will! ha-ha-ha 1"

"Why, the government doesn't value your whole carcass at more than I offer you for the temporary use of your hands, you villain !" frowned the colonel. "No ill names, your honour Between us they are like kicking guns—apt to recoil 1" "You forget that your are in my power." "I remember that your honour is in mine! Ha- ha-ha I The day Black Donald stands at the bar, the honourable Colonel Le Noir will probably be beside him." "Enough of this! Confound you, do you take me for one of your pals I" "No, your wor-hip ! my pale are too poor to hire their work done; but then they are brave enough to do it themselves." "Enough of this, I say! Name the price of this new service 1" "Ten thousand dollars—five thousand in advance —the remainder when the deed is accomplished." "Extortioner I—shameless, ruthless extortioner 1"

" Your honour wi/Z fall into that vulgar habit of calling ill names I—it isn't worth while; it doesn't pay. If your honour doesn't like my terms you needn't employ me; what is certain is, that I can- not work for less." _ _

“You take advantage of my necessities.” "Not at all; but the truth is, Colonel, that I am tired of this sort of life, and wish to retire from active business. Besides, every man has his ambi- tion, and I have mine. I wish to emigrate to the glorious West, settle, marry, turn my attention to politics, he elected to Congress, then to the Senate, then to the Cabinet, then to the White House; for success in which career, I flatter myself nature and education have especially fitted me. Ten thousand dollars will give me a fair start. Many a successful politician, your honour knows, has started on less character and less capital!" To this impudent slander the colonel made no answer; with his arms folded, and his head bowed upon his chest, he walked moodily up and down the length of the apartment; then muttering, "Why should I hesitate l" he came to the side of the out- law, and said: "I agree to your terms; accomplish the work, and the sum shall be yours. Meet me here on to-morrow evening to receive the earnest money. In the meantime, in order to make sure of the girl's identity, it will be necessary for you to get sight of her beforehand at her home, if possible; find out her habits and her haunts—where she walks, or rides—when she is most likely to be alone, and so on. Be very careful I A mistake might be fatal."

"Your honour may trust me." "And now good-bye; remember, to-morrow evening," said the colonel, as, wrapping himself closely in his dark cloak, and pulling his hat lovt over his eyes, he passed out by the back passage- door, and left the house. "Ha 1 ha-ha Why does that man think it needful to look so villainous ? If / were to go about in such a bandit-like dress as that, every child I met would take me for—what I am." laughed Black Donald, returning to his comrades. During the next hour other members of the band dropped in, until some twenty men were collected together in the large kitchen around the long table, where the remainder of the night Was spent in revelry.
(To be continued).

JEW TOO SHARP FOR THE PROFESSOE.—A good story is told of the celebrated surgeon Professor Billrotte of Vienna. He was asked a short time ago to perform an operation upon a Roman Jew, and he agreed to do the same for a fee of 250 guineas. On making the journey to the small town in which his patient lived he was informed that the Jew had suddenly died. However, in order that he should not suffer loss by the transaction, the professor was asked whether he would treat five hospital patients for a fee of 60 guineas each. Ho accepted the offer and did the work, and just as he was starting homewards he ascertained that one of the five patients upon whom he had operated was the Jew who was reported to have been dead—so at least the story runs.

div.head: DEATH'S DOOR.
div.p: DEATH'S DOOR.
A VILLAGE TRAGEDY AVERTED . SENSATIONAL INTERVIEW.

When a person at death's door, whose family and friends have taken a last farewell, is miraculously restored to health, there is little wonder that the case should excite interest and give rise to reports, in a small village. Such a case is brought under notice by a local correspondent, who has made a point of ascertaining the facts. This is what he learnt from personal inquiries. Miss Bessie Portlock, a young woman of eighteen,lives with her parents at Parsonage Cottage, Frilsha.m, Berk- shire. Her father, a type of the geod-old-fashioned Eng- lish agriculturist, has lived on the Marlstone Estate for over thirty years, his present employer being Mr. George Palmer, of Messrs. Huntley and Palmer," where the biscuits come from."

The mother is a strong hard-working woman, whose character can best be read in her scrupulously clean and comfortable cottage. When I first saw Bessie, writes the the reporter, she was walking down the garden to fetch some coal from the wood-house. She certainly did not look mach of an invalid. She wears glasses, but has a pleasant manner, and speaks with an intelligence far above the ordinary style of the country girl. She told her story simply and plainly.

"I was out in service," she said, " but being taken ill in June, 1894, I was obliged to leave my place and come home. My mother took me to a doctor,who said it was a case for the hospital. At Newbury Hospital, the doc- tors said I had a tendency to consumption of the bowels. I stayed there seven weeks, and was a little better when I came out. But I got worse in a short time. The pain was something dreadful. Our doctor said he could do nothing for me, and advised mother to send me to the Reading Hospital. I was there for ten weeks, and seemed a little relieved when I came out. But soon after I was taken much worse, and mother again went to our doctor, who, however, said he could do nothing for me. I had wasted away to a skeleton, and could not walk up and down stairs. The neighbours used te say I was dying. I couldn't eat anything; and I was in dreadful pain, and had given up all hope my- self. Mother one day read in the •‘ Newbury News " what wonderful cures were being made by Dr. Williams' Pink Pills tor Pale People. I said, 'Oh, do get some, mother,' and she sent into Newbury for a box. I began taking them according to the directions, and felt better the second or third day. Before the box was empty I was able to get up and about. I continued to take them, and gradually got better." • "And you feel better and stronger ?"

"Oh, yes," she replied ; "I am able to assir my mother in the house work,and last Monday walked three miles. The neighbours could scarcely believe their eyes when they saw me,and the doctor said, What have you been doing to make yourself so much better ? ' I told him I had been taking Dr. Williams' Pink Pills.

The mother was equally emphatic: "It's the Pills,and nothing but the Pills," she said. " Our doctor said to me in his surgeory, lam afraid I can do nothing for your daughter; it's consumption of the bowels, and we cannot save her.' At Whitsuntide all her brothers and sisters came home to see her for the last time; they never expected to see her again. lam so thankful we tried the Pills." Dr. Williams' Pink Pills directly enrich the blood, and hence are famous for the cure of anaamia, influenza, rheumatism, scrofula, chronic erysipelas, and to restore pale and sallow complexions to the glow of health. They are also a splendid nerve and spinal tonic, and thus have 'lured many cases of paralysis, locomotor ataxy, neuralgia. St. Vitus' dance, and nervous head- ache. They are sold by chemists, and Dr. Williams* Medicine Company, 46, Holborn Viaduct, London, at 2s. 9d., but are genuine only with full name, Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People. A specific for all ladies' troubles, and in men cure all the ills arising from worry, fatigue, and excess, whether of work or otherwise.

div.head: GERMANS IN ENGLAND.
div.p: GERMANS IN ENGLAND.

A correspondent of the " Times" gives a variety of particulars concerning the Germans who are living in England and the employments in which they earn their bread. "According to the census Of 1891 the number of Germans in the United Kingdom was," he says, "53,591, of whom all but 3,000 were living in England and Wales. These figures only refer to subjects of the German Emperor born in Germany. They do not in- clude either Germans who have become neutralised or the children of German parents born in Easland. If the latter be added the total will not be less than 100,000 since there are absut 16,000 German families settled in England, and an average of three children for each family would be a moderate estimate." "The Germans are distributed in nearly every part of England:but they chiefly affect large towns. London takes rather more than 50 per cent ,and the Home coun- ties (that is, Greater London) another i 0 per cent.,Lan- lcashire 10 per cent., Yorkshire 7 per cent., Northumber- land and Durham 5 per cent., Wales 2 per cent.,the Mid lands 3 per cent, while the rest are scattered about in every county except the extreme West, which appears to enjoy immunity. Their distribution is equally wide with respect to occupations. Out of 30,000 male Ger- mans, nearly all adults in England,only 332 are returned as "living an their own means" without occupation— that is to say 99 per cent, earn their own living in com- petition with the native population. They are occupied in no fewer than 300 different callings, and serve their adopted country in such unexpected capacities as those of policemen, farmers, and even agricultural labourers. The twelve occupations in which they are most exten- sively engaged, including males and females, are as fol- lows :—Servants (demestic and hotel), 5,358 ; sailors, 2,833 ; tailors, 2,489; bakers. 2,340; teachers. 1,981; clerks, 1,986; butchers, 1,309: musicians, 1,198 ; hair- dressers, 961 ; watchmalcers, 889 ; cabinetmakers, 794 ; merchants, 671. After th.se comes shoemakers, cooks (other than domestic), brokers and agents, furriers,and commercial travellers. It will be observed that contr- ary to general belief, the industrial far exceeds the com- mercial section." Comparing the increase or diminution in the various occupations from decade to decade, the writer finds that "the greatest increase has taken place among female domestics, who have more than doubled in numbers during twenty years. In 1871 there were 1,522, in 1881 they had risen to 2,553, and in 1891 to 3,312. German governesses and school mistresses, on the other hand, have actually diminished since 1881. Next to servants the most striking increase has taken place among bakers, who have grown since 1871 from 1,310 to 2.340. The multiplication of German hairdressers is astonishing. In 1871 they numbered 169; to-day they are 1,000. Tailors, and still more tailoresses, have also increased considerably in the last decade, although they diminished between 1871 and 1881. Some are employed in high- class houses, but the great majority work on the cheap. est kinds of goods. These three trades—tailoring, hair- dressing, and baking—are pre-eminently those to which the incompetent have recourse, because, they are the most easily attempted without previous skill and the most quickly learnt. The other skilled trades much affected by Germans—namely, watchmaking, cabinet- making, shoemaking, and far-cutting—all require more apprenticeship, and the last-mentioned needs a very special skill, in which the Germans are unrivalled." Turning to the non-industrial classes, the correspon- dent says :—" The merchants have steadily diminished in number, while the clerks have increased. Twenty years ago the two were almost equal, now the clerks are thrice as numerous. The diminution of merchants is probably due to their migration to newer and more pro- mising fields in the United States or the colonies,whither they have taken the business knowledge and connections acquired in England. The employment of German clerks is rather a sore point,particularly in London, where they are most numerous,though less so than is commonly sup- posed. Some years ago an attempt was made in the London Chamber of Commerce to get rid of them, but it failed. They have made themselves indispensable in many offices. They are better linguists, more careful, and more interested in mastering the business than Eng- lish clerks In short, they work harder, not necessarily during office hours, but in general, and they are always ready to work overtime. But their merits have this de- fect in the eyes of an employer, that he only enjoys the benefit temporarily, and that the very qualities which he prizes are eventually turned against him; for the diligent clerk presently becomes a competitor, so soon as he has thoroughly mastered the business. This is, indeed, the real secret of his diligence. Perhaps for this reason and also because English lads are now more systematically Prepared for the career,the demand for Germans, though still maintained,does not advance so fast as it did ten or whom fifteen years ago." With respect to British subjects living in Germanv,the correspondent says that in 1891 these numbered 15,748, g m two thirds were females. div.head: WAR SCARE.
div.p: THE WAR SCARE.
BY MR. 11. Christmas eve. After a week of intense _excite-

ment the war scare seems to be cooling down a little To the press belongs all the credit for stir- ring up the war feeling. 'The Jingo, of whatever nationality, rarely stops to consider. In the present . . _
_ dispute he has, I am afraid, allowed his patriotism to get the better of his discretion. Now, what has all this noise and smoke been about? I venture to _ .

say that not 10 per cent, of the peop:e of the Bri- tish Isles know the first word in the dispute—a dispute in which an unwise issue would lauueh the two foremost nations of the earth in a fratricidal war, in a war that would be to all intents and pur- poses a civil war, the end of which no man could tell. These two nations stand first among nations for missionary enterprise. They boast loudest of their liberty and civilizing influence, and yet with all these latter end of the 19th century ideas they are unable to decide about a bit of a paltry bound- ary line for an insignificant South American republic. This boundary line question is not a new develop- ment in itself. It seems to have been a nice little bone of contention that has been transmitted from Government to Government, seemingly for no other object than to find an hour or two's work each day for officialism, and to keep our ,diplomats in exer- cise. These sort of things come in bandy for our rulers at times when the people are becoming res- tive, or when some new political move is contem- plated. They always act like good red herrings and when thrown among the people surely draw them away on a „false scent. Now,whether the message sent by President Cleve- land to Congress was a political move or not I am unable to say, but I am inclined to think it was partly so. Since his election, se,veral small matters have arisen that have given his opponents the op- portunity to throw the Anglopholia stone at him. These coupled with the Democratic opposition to high protection have altogether brought the Demo- cratic party into the same position the Liberal party are in England, so it would almost seem as if the President had determined to do something desper- ate to retrieve his popularity—hence this war- breathing massage. But this explanation does not explain how it comes about that from the Atlantic to the Pacific popular opinion is on the side of the President. Irrespective of political party, or of re- ligious views, the people are almost a unit in their determination to maintain the integrity of the Western Hemisphere against the encroachments of England or any European power, and I must say them's my views." Generally speaking, I have not much of the jingo about me, andl rarely give out any of the blood and thunder rot, but on this question I go with the deep underlying sentiment of true liberty put forth in the President's Message, and I say to you Britishers "Stand off." As an Englishman born I have been often pained at reading much of the rubbish and downright lies that are circulated among the American people touching their English cousins. It is undoubtedly true that there is a strong feeling against Englishmen who are making this country their home. In the one case it may be a mere matter of jealousy; on the other that we represent a laud-grabbing nation, and that we do not as a whole, make good citizens; that is, we do not as a rule, throw off with the same joyous alacrity the old love to take on with the new. One has but to walk through the streets of any Ameri- can city and note the names over the saloon doors to be convinced of the nationality of the people who are to-day the drag on all progress social or political. I see the Irish are, from cities all over the States sending in petitions begging for the right to form regiments to defend the country they hope to see the Pope the ruler of sooner or later. Of course there is plenty of talk on the platform and in the Press as to what would be done in the event of war being declared. Canada and British commerce would vanish quite suddenly. Russia would settle the Armenian question and would alter the politi- cal aspect of India on short order, while Ireland would at once seize the opportunity for arming a few home bred native samples of the Ameri- can boss, and the dear old mother country would be sat on, trampled on, and bombarded out of all shape. You Britishers, of course, would see Iwhat you could do with your mighty fleet of iron- ' clads. New York, Boston and all other sea ports on the Atlantic or Pacific would be your targets,and I, even I, would have to take to the sandhills, be- cause my home might possibly obstruct your cannon balls. This all seems like joking, but it is all sad, sober fact, so far as public opinion has ex- pressed itself, should the Monroe Dochine not be accepted and America be forced to defend it as an lAmerican political principle,and outside altogether lof international law. The Venezuela boundary question may, or not involve the M.D. A commis- sion is now being appointed to determine that, singularly enough, moot point, but there can be no doubt that the future peace of America depends, largely upon its acceptance. Its meaning is that no European power shall have the opportunity of harrasing or breaking up any of the petty re- publics of America; that no outside power shall have the right 60 introduce on the American Con- tinent the military system that so criminally pre- vails elsewhere. What Europe already has on this continent she must be satisfied with. Lord Salisbury has refused arbitration, for very insufficient reasons. Where there is a dispute there are two opinions, and where there are two opinions there is always just cause for arbitration. The commission appointed by the President may not be acepted in England but it is the outcome of Salis- bury's refusal to arbitrate. Under wiser leadership it would have been a court of arbitration. Its decision will be accepted by the America people, and, unless Salisbury finds another way out of his difficulty,should be accepted by the English people. No benefit can possibly accrue to English commerce by antagonizing the South American republics. Already Brazil has taken the initiative to draw them all into a strong commercial bond for the purpose of boycotting English produce. The American Congress has also taken what its majority thinks are vigorous steps, to raise money, that is they are raising the tariff on imported goods. How that will be done when the commerce is destroyed, I don't know. Of course the protection party are out in England also, and the farmer will make the workingman pay his landlord a higher rent. The cry of the people in both nations should now be " arbitrate.'

div.head: NEGRO "CONVERSIONS."
div.p: NEGRO "CONVERSIONS."
SENSATIONAL REPORT.

- The New York Correspondent of the "Daily Chronicle' says :—Protessor Cook, the ropresentative ot tie New York State Colonisation Society in Liberia, has just seat home a sensational report which will excite the indigna- tion of all who profess an interest in the negro problem. Be affirms that in their eagerness to prove their useful- ness many missionaries are making negro converts by the easy process of buying them at three dollars a head, and then forcing or persuading them to join the Chris- tian Church. "If only the good work goes far enough," says Professor Coek, " we shall have regulation slave raids, towns burned, people slaughtered, and children carried away," to satisfy the demand for negro con- verts.

div.head: FINANCIAL AND MINING NEWS.
div.p: FINANCIAL AND MINING NEWS.
ACHILLES GOLD.

We have frequently called the attention of investors to the low price 2s. 3d. per share at which the fully paid shares of the Achilles Goldfields, Limited, could be purchased on the London Stock Exchange,and the prob- ability that a sharp advanded upon this low price would take place shortly after the receipt of the next crushing. The Company's property is entirely situated in New Zealand, and includes the well-known Phcenix Mine,said to be the best gold mine in that colony. The cablegram announcing the crushing was received on January 13,,h, 1896. as follows :—" Have cleaned up after crushing 720 tons of quartz; grossyleld, 725 ounces (gold) ; a most excellent return." Those in quest of a good specu- lative investment, and having cash in hand to spare, should at once purchase as many of these shares as they can afford to take up and pay for, before the advance takes place which is certain to occur, now that favour- able crushings have commenced and good dividends may be expected in the near future.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: SHIP CANAL.
LAST WEEK'S TRAFFIC.

The traffic upon the Ship Canal last week was fully up to tho average,and considerable activity was mani- fested not only at the Manchester end of the waterway, but also at Runcorn, Saltport,and Ellesmere Port. Dur- ing the seven days ended January 10th, 147 sea-going vessels, with an aggregate net registered tonnage of 40,438 tons, arrived and sailed, against 136 vessels of 38,515 tons in the previous week. Coastwise traffic in- creased by 17 ships and 5,485 tons, while foreign trade fell off by six ships of 3,562 tons. Twelve tugs, ten hoppers, and 113 cargo barges passed inwards through Eastbam locks, and 12 tugs, 11 hoppers, and 114 barges left the canal. Amongst the carges imported were 18 of china clay, 16 of general merchandise, 14 of stone and slate, five of pig iron, three of wood pulp, and one each of iron ore, bone ash, soda ash,rock salt, fustic, and log- wood. Three steamers arrived with 11,892 bales of American and Egyptian co tton ; consignments of green fruit were received from Jaffa, Messina, and Seville ; flour from Fiume,and grain from New Orleans. Twenty- one general cargoes were exported, four of coal, two of salt, and one of purple ore.

div.head: PRESENTATION TO THE LATE CHIEF CONSTABLE OF WARRINGTON.
div.p: PRESENTATION TO THE LATE CHIEF CONSTABLE OF WARRINGTON.

The presentation to Mr. Hunt, the ex-chief constable, which has been raised by public subscriptions, took place at the Council Chamber of the Town Hall,on Tues- day. The Mayor (Councillor J.Fairclough) occupied the ' chair, and there were also present Councillors Shaw Green Alfred Woods, Wilkinson, Bennett, and Evans; and Messrs. Thomas Morris, F.G.S., Arthur Browne, H. Toit, George F. F. White (deputy magistrates' clerk), John Fairhurst (borough treasurer), H. Milling, George Powlson, Thomas Birtles, S.Wilson (deputy town clerk), H. Taylor (Police Court missionary) Luke Talbot (the present chief constable), Hesketh, Peter Crimes, and Mather. Mr. Hunt occupied a seat on the right of the Mayor, while Mr. Morris sat on his left. There were also present Inspectors James, Spinks, Cox and Taylor. The MAYOR having expressed the pleasure it gave him to be present, Councillor Woods read the adaress which had been prepared. It read as follows :—" Presented to Samuel Hunt, Esq.. late chief constable of the borough of Warrington, in the county of Lancaster. To Simnel Hunt, Esq. Dear Sir,-1 our retirement from the posi- tion of Chief Constable of the town and borough of Warrington, after some 30 years of arduous and active service, affords us, the subscribers, who are manufac- turers, tradesmen, and residents, a welcome opportunity of giving some expression to our appreciation of the uniform urbanity and gentlemanly bearing which has always characterized your attitude in all matters coming within the scope of your official capacity, for it is pleasing for us to say we have observed that, while a high sense of public duty seems ever to have been your paramount rule, you have invariably so happily blended it with such a delicate sympathy and consideration for the private feelings of all persons concerned as to disrobe justice of much of its sternness. While a matter of much congratu- lation to the whole borough the fact is well worth re- cording, and will doubtless be a very pleasant feature in the recollection of your past career, that although at its commencement, in the year 1866, when the popula- tion of the borough of Warrington was below 25,000,vet now at the close of your public life in the year :1895, when with its increased prosperity and widely extended boundaries and a population exceeding 57,000 inhabit- ants there does not appear to have occurred within your experience the single instance of a crime which has cul- minated in capital punishment to the offender. We, therefore, bespeak your kind acceptance of a silver cigar case a silver match box, a silver cake basket, together withla purse of gold (£150) in order somewhat to em- phasize alike our appreciation of your public services and our cordial esteem and regard for yourself. We are, yours faithfully." Then follow the names of 250 sub- scribers and Mr. Morris (chairman ot the committee),and Messrs. A. Woods ond H. Toft (secs.) Mr. MORRIS, in making the presentation, said that a feeling of pride crept over him when the committee chose him to make the presentation. That day the in- habitants of Warrington were, through a few of them, doing such an honour to their late Chief Constable that perhaps so far as the extent of it went, and in propor- tion to the population of the town,had not been equalled in Great Britain before. That Mr. Hunt during his many years of official service had proved himself worthy of the high esteem in which he was :now held, was for- cibly testified by the tangible tokens before them. The duties of his late office were conducted in a thoughtful,
, _ - unpresuming manner, never in haste, never coveting favour from the rich, or from the profession he daily

came in contact with, or realising fear from the poor,or the:prisoner who might be brAught before him to report upon. It was never in his nature to do by design a dis- honourable act, or behave in a discourteous manner to those above or beneath him. Mr. Hunt must at times have erred during his official life. Of that he knew no- thing ; but he did say that if he had deviated, it had been on the side of kindness and not that of severity. His successor on the day of his succeeding him might have been purtraying his (Mr. fludt's) character and disposition all through his official life in Warrington when he was giving his likes of the conduct of a police officer. What he said in words Mr. Hunt had acted in deeds, and words were not in the reckoning by the side of actions. It was those actions that endeared the hearts of the people towards him. (Applause.) It waslhis square conduct in everyday life that had caused this magnifi- cent result which lay before them and it gave him one of the greatest pleasures of his life to hand to Mr. Hunt on behalf of the committee in particular and of Warrington and its people in general. (Applause.) Mr. PowLsoN was asked to say a few words, and he said that he could not refuse to do so. He would like to join in the chorus of congratulation and compliments to their esteemed friend, Mr. Hunt. He had rendered great services to the town. Mr. Powlson then went on to give details of various events which had happened during Mr. Hunt's term of office, all of which, he said, Mr. Hunt had come out a credit. He also gave an illustration of Mr. Hunt as an adviser as well as a chief constable. Mr.Hesketh and Mr. MILLING also spoke a few compli- mentary words of Mr. Hunt's connection with the town. Mr. HUNT in reply said that he was no speaker. He had had a lot to do with criminals,but with ameeting like that.he bad not had much to do.He asked them to allow him first, on behalf of Mrs. Haat, to thank the members of the Testimonial Committee for their kindly remarks and also for the time and trouble they had been put to in connection with their desire to recognise in a substan- tial manner his long services to his fellow townsmen. He was pleased that his services as chief constable to the borough, for upwards of 28 years had been so magnific- ently appreciated by all classes. He also thanked the subscribers. the Watch Committee, the Town Council, the magistrates, and his Masonic brethren and members of the public at large for their efforts on his behalf which had resulted in such a handsome pre- sent. He was glad to notice besides the large sums eon- tributed by subscribers, such a large number of sums under 103. from anonymous subscribers. Mr. Hunt also paid a compliment to the members of the police force, and again thanking the subscribers, he wished all a happy new year. (Applause.) Councillor SHAW GREEN proposed a vote of thanks to the Mayor for presiding, as he said that that gave an official recognition to the proceedings. Mr. ARTHUR BROWNE seconded the vote of thanks, and said that his duties of honorary treasurer had not been very onerous, as nearly every subscriber had given in their money very willingly. The vote was carried, and the Mayor thanked them and said that he had as first magistrate of the borough, never had the slightest hitch with Mr. Hunt. He was very pleased to be present on that occasion. The proceedings then terminated.
A heavy fall of snow took place early on Wed nesday morning in the central and western districts of Perth- shire. There has also been a considerable snowstorm in D u m friegshi re.
John Dobson, foreman porter at Oxenhoime Station, was killed on Wednesday morning by an express train.

THE BALANCE SHEET.

The 21st annual ordinarygeneral meeting of this Com- pany will be held at the Cannon-st. Hotel, London, on Thursday next. The balance sheet issued by the direc- tors is as follows :—"The Directors in submitting to the shareholders the balance sheet of the Bank at 31st of December, 1895, certified by the auditors, have to report that the position and prospect of the business continue to be in every way satisfactory. Including £34,609 3s. sd. brought forward at 30th June, 1895. the net balance of profits, after providing amply for all bad and doubtful debts, and rebating the current bills at 5 per cent., is £136,046 lea. 9d. From this sum the directors recommend the payment of a Dividend at the rate ot 19 per cent. per annum, free of income tax, for the quar- ter ended 31st December, 1895, to be payable on the Ist February, 1896, £47,500 ; dividend at the same rats for the quarter ending 31st March, 1896, to be payable on Ist May, 1896, to the shareholders whose names shall be on the register on 16th April, £47,500 ; to reserve fund, £10,000—£105,000; leeving balance to be carried to next account, £31,046 las. 9d. A Branch of the Bank has been opened at Crewe, and it has been decided to open a Sub-Branch at Alsager. The Hon. St. John Brodrick, M.P.,has,in consequence of his duties as Under-Secretary, for War, resigned his seat at the Board, and the Direc- tors much regret to lose his services. The Directors who retire at this time by rotation are Sir Thomas G. Frost, Mr. Peter Stubbs, Colonel David Gamble, C. 8., Mr. John Dun, Mr. E. W. Nix, and Mr. E. Banbury, all of whom areeligible, and are recommended for re-election. The Auditors, Messrs. Turquand,Youngs.Bishop and Clarke, London, also retire,and offer themselves for re-election."

On Monday morning a- young man, named John Stockton, aged 18 years, living in Howley-lane,was admitted to the Infirmary suffering from severe in- juries to the head. It appears that the injured youth was working on the roof of the joinery mills in Messrs. R. A. Naylor's timber works when be overbalanced himself and fell a distance of thirty or forty feet.
