div.head: REPAIR OF THE ARPLEY NEW
div.p: THE REPAIR OF THE ARPLEY NEW
ROAD.

SHIP CANAL. COMPANY v. HIGHWAY BOARD. At the Warrington County Petty Sessions on Wednes- day, before Mr. James Tinsley (chairman), Mr. John Crosfield and Mr. John White, Mr. E. A. White applied on behalf of the Warrington and District Highway Board for an order on the Manchester Ship Canal Company to put the Arpley New-road in repair, under the provisions of the Ship Canal Act, 1885. Mr. Byrne, barrister, and Mr. Kershaw, solicitor (Manchester), appeared for the Ship Canal Co. Mr. White, who stated his case a great length, said the road was numbered work 23 of section 28 in the Ship Canal Act. They. the Highway Board only had to do with the Lancashire portion, from the centre of the river at one end to the centre of the river at the other. The Canal Company by cutting through the Chester road were bound to make a road over the Canal. For their own purposes the company fixed a bridge at the Stag Inn, and they were bound to find the approaches. Una er the circumstances the company were bound to provide a new passage in lieu of the one stopped up. Under section 46, even if that stood alone, the company were bound to maintain the pas9age. Section 46 said that "such bridge and immediate approaches, and all other necessary works connected therewith, shall be executed and at all times thereinafter maintained at the expense of the company." Obviously this road was an approach to the bridge. If the company made, clearly they must maintain. Mr. White read several lengthy judgments in support of his contention,and said the road was a new passage over the canal in lieu of the Chester highroad stopped up. For eighteen months nothing had been done to the road. Its condition was,indeed, a cry- ing evil. rhe public were complaining about it, and if the Bench made an order, he trusted that the time they would fix within which the work was to be completed would be a short one. It was a matter that did not admit of further delay. Mr. Jo%n Thompson, surveyor to the Board, said the road was an entirely new one and the whole of the Lancashire portio, was in the borough. After detailing the condition of the road no said that if proper exertions were. used it could be repaired in a fortnight. It WM 1,253 yards in length. Mr. Byrne said the only liability of the Ship Canal was expressed in section 46, if section 46 applied, where it said that the Canal Company should keep in repair the bridge over the canal and all the immediate approaches to the bridge. Section 46 failed in two particulars. The road was nut a turnpike road carried over the canal, and .not an immediate approach to the bridge, and he ven- tured to submit that the section did not apply in this case and failed on those grounds. Continuing, he said that the Canal Company had a double option, they might make and they might maintain, they might make and they might not maintain. They were empowered to make a number of locks, basins, ard branch railways, but they were not bound to maintain them. All the six roads they had made, and of which this was one, were not required to be repaired by the Company. His last contention was that this 1,253 yards of road could not possibly be an approach or other work within the mean- ing of the section referred to. He therefore submitted that the cage should be dismissed. The Bench then retired from the court to consider their decision, and on their return The Chairman said: The unanimous opinion of the Bench is that an order be granted to the Highway Board, and that the work be completed within a month. Mr. Byrne: I ask that you will grant me a case. The Chairman said the Bench saw no objection to do- ing so. Mr. White applied for costs and was granted two guineas.

div.head: WARRINGTON HIGHWAY BOARD.
div.p: WARRINGTON HIGHWAY BOARD.

A meeting of the Highway Board was held at the Bewsey Chambers on Wednesday afternoon, the chair being occupied by Captain S. Ellames Withington. There were also present Messrs. Royston. Houghton, Kerfoot, Clare, Millington, Matthews, Warburton, H. Bate, Ormrod, P. J. Bate, E. A. White (deputy clerk), and Thompson (surveyor). THE REPAIR. OF THE NEW ROAD AT ARPLEY. The CLERK said that application had been duly made to the magistrates for an order upon the Ship Canal Co., to put the road in Arpley in repair, and the Canal Co. were represented by Mr. Byrne and Mr. Kershaw. It was ordered that the Canal Company put the road into repair within a calendar month. They were also ordered to pay two guineas for the costs in connection with the matter. The Company asked for a case, as it was anti- cipated they would, on the legal questions involved, and this was granted, and assuming that they would go on with the matter,it would be argued out in a higher court. —Mr. MATTHEWS said that he thought that it was likely that the Canal Company were likely to fight the matter out to the bitter end, in order to delay the matter until Nov. Ist, when the Corporation would have to repair the road. In the meantime, he thought that they ought to appoint a small committee to put the matter before the Company to see if they would give the surveyor a little money to put the road into something like suitable order. He thought it was absurd that both sides should spend so much money in legal expenses. He thought the Company were reasonable and it would be well to meet them in the matter.—The CLERK said that the Canal Company would be liable, assuming that they lost the appeal, to a penalty of £5 a day over a month, if the road was not repaired within the time ordered. He thought that it would be as well to leave the matter in the hands of the committee who had the case in hand. It was not certain as yet that the appeal could be proceed,,d with. It would he known within six days whether the company intended to proceed.—Mr. MILLINGTON did not know why they should spend money in legal expenses, when the road was not under their authority. He thought that the inhabitants of the Cheshire parishes who de- rived all the benefit from the road, oueht to take the matter up.—The CLERK said that the Board, or two in- -I,abitants of the township of Little Sankey, were the only persons competent to proceed with the matter. It was in the interests of the public that the matter was pushed forward.—After some further discussion, it was decided that the matter be left in the hands of the com- mittee, which would meet on Wednesday at 2.30, by which time it was expected that it would be known whether the Canal Company would decide whether to appeal or not.

div.head: HALTON'S BRIDGE.
div.p: HALTON'S BRIDGE.

The CLEalt reported that in reply to the proposal of the Board that the County Council should borrow money for the purpose of repairing Halton's bridge, Penketh, that the Main Roads Committee had met but had passed no resolution upon the subject.—Mr. MILLINGTON : That means that the thing is shelved for an indefinite period. —The CHAIRMAN : They ought to do it.—The CLERK said that it would be an improper thing for a Board which would so son come to an end to borrow such a large sum as £1,300. It would be well if someone would be killed there. (Laughter.) The matter would be then brought to the fore.—The CHAIRMAN (to Mr. Millington) If you would like to 131 the one Mr. Millington you would do a service. (Renewed laughter.)—Mr. MAT- TITRWS : We can't afford to lose him.— Mr. MILLINGTON said that it was a matter of great inconvenience to the inhabitants of Penketh and the road ought to be re- paired.—lt was finally decided on the advice of the Clerk that the Penketh Parish Council,which was chiefly interested in the matter,should press the question on the County Council.

div.head: BALANCE IN HAND.
div.p: BALANCE IN HAND.

The CLERIC reported that the balance in hand was £383 2s. 64. The November calls were still unpaid by the townspeople of Cuerdley, Culcheth, Little Sankey, Southworth-with-Crnft, and Winwick. K.nyon was the only township which had paid the January calls.

William James Morgan, a hawker, was sentenced to death at the Central Criminal Court on Wednesday for the murder of his wife. A solicitor's clerk named Charles Ernest Wallace was sentenced at the Old Bailey on Wednesday to five years' penal servitude for forging and uttering cheques to the am ount of £770.

div.head: SUDDEN DEATH.
div.p: SUDDEN DEATH.

The death took place very suddenly on Tuesday, of Charles Beesley, who resided with his brother at 107, Lovely-lane. The deceased was employed in the electro-plating room at the Lubricate Com- pany's Works, Bunk Quay, and he went to his work in his usual health at seven o'clock on the morning in question. At about 8,45 on a fellow-workman entering the room be found deceased lying on his back insensible. Dr. Joseph was at once called in, but on his arrival he found life extinct. SILVBR-BT. ENGLISH NEWS "MADE IN FRANCE,'

An amusing blague is told in the French papers con- cerning the musical proclivities of members of the Royal Family. According to "L 9 Menestrel," not only did the Princess Christian recently sing at Slough in "The Messiah," which is true,but also that " the Royal Family of England are about to give g. series of concerts in aid of a fund to provide new wind instruments for the num- erous German bands which infest London and other towns ot the United Kingdom." Perhaps this is supposed in Paris to have something to do with the general adop- tion of the Continental musical pitch; but the Royal family will be even more astonished to learn, according to the same authority, that "the Prince of Wales has followed the example of his nephew, the composer of the Hymn to Egir," and has written a cantata for soloists, chorus, amd orchestra, which will shortly be performed in a London concert-room. His son, the Duke of York, I will give a pianoforte recital, and his daughter-in-law, the Duchess May of York, will be heard on the banje,att instrument used by the American negroes, which has become, very popular in the drawing-rooms of the grand monde Anglais." This sort of thing seems to be firmly believed in France by people wno cannot drive it out o their head that the Lor' Maire is president of the nous of Lords, and that the Queen resides at the Tower if Landon.

div.head: CLASS.
div.p: CLASS.

The annual tea meeting in connection with the above class was held in Bewsey-road Wesleyan Chapel on Monday evening when abont 100 people , sat down to a substantial tea. The room bad been decorated very tastefully by members of the society classes. A meeting was afterwards held presided over by Mr. John Bennett, of Bewsey Hall, who made a very racy speech. Mrs. Watkins in the absence of Mrs. Shaw Green distributed the prizes to members of the class. A programme, vocal and instrumental was submitted by the choir,and Messrs. W. H. Wallington and B. Corlett, and during the , course of the evening, speeches were delivered by the Rev. W. 3. Triggs and Councillor Shaw Green. PRIZE SUNDAY AT BANE QUAY MISSION. After the lapse of several years, it was decided to again give prizes to scholars who were regular in their attendance at the Sunday school which is held in connection with the Workingmen's Mis- sion, Bank Quay, and the result has been very i gratifying to those n authority. The distribution of prizes took place on Sunday when the school was crowded with the children and their parents, and a most enjoyable meeting was held. The proceed- ings were opened by Mr. Thomas Dale, and the subsequent portion. of the meeting was in the hands of the supermtendent.Mr.Joseph Monks,jun., and Mr. James Woolley. A solo was given by Mr. Hassell, and recitations by Mrs. Edwards, Miss Barton, and Miss E. Lawton. In the absence of Mr. John Crosfield, J.P., who unfortunately could not be present, the prizes, 80 in number, were given to the scholars by Mr. Joseph Monks.

div.head: SOME OF THE " HEROES " OF
div.p: SOME OF THE " HEROES " OF
JOHANNESBURG.

A correspondent of the "Daily Telegraph." who reached Johannesburg in the midst of the political fer- ment, gives a graphic description of the scene vhich met his view. He says :—" Most of the shops were closed and their windows barricaded. The greater part of the gold mines were deserted and shut down. At the railway static n an excited, frantic crowd were fighting for places and throwing off from the carriage doors those trying ,o escape. In the streets of the town larger or smaller thrones were gathering, .end parading espe- cially thick round the Goldfields offisce,where they were denaanding information. Being told that up to Thurs- Iday night Jameson was reported safe,they became gene- rally enraged, and wanted to set fire to the offices, and I threatened to hang their leaders who had not started to his assistance. The spectacle on all sides was in many respects excruciatingly comic, if it had not been so tragical. Amid all this uproar the Johannesburgers were to be seen drilling in the public squares, forming up into fours with badges and ribbons and most of para- phernalia of war. But among them one could plainly see many clerks, shopmen, and people of every white nationality, who were supplying by panic and agitation the real spirit of the belligerents. Many among them were holding their rifles as if they had been umbrellas or walking sticks, their captains and lieutenants vainly shouting to the chaos in the hope of reducing it to order. I suppose there might have been picked out of the mob of noisy insurgents some thousand good men and true, of real colonial grit ; but the rest were the merest riff raff. The National Committee had lied to them and to the world about the arms in its possession. I do not believe they had more than 3,000 serviceable rifles, car- ried for the most part by a set of rowdies, described by a Cape politician as 'having a half.crown cigar in their mouths, a quart of champagne in their stomachs, and their brains in their pockets.' against this un- wieldy mass was silently ranged 8,000 Boers closing round the town, and so strong is the spirit of gambling in the place that bookmakers were betting on the event and laying a hundred to one that Dr. 'Jim' would come through safely. Great nervousness, however, prevailed among some of these heroes. A noted financier got away by bribing a Boer guard to let him through the ladies' lavatory on payment of £25 sterling. Another evaded the troops by dressing up as a black woman." With regard to the Boers, the correspondent says they had spies everywhere watching everybodv,and it is clear that they were well prepared beforehand for emergen- cies. In every outlying household mobilisation had been well prepared for, and every detachment was well warned, well armed,and well mounted. The Boer com- mandos were everywhere hidden behind hills, with patrols scouring the country, and they really held Johannesburg like a trap full of rats.

div.head: pEDE§TRIAN JOURNEY ROUND THE
div.p: pEDE§TRIAN JOURNEY ROUND THE
WORLD.

The " Times " Teheran correspondent sends some detaiis as to a curious journey round the world. Messrs. Kogel and Thoerner, two pedestrians, started from San Francisco on June 10, 1894, and crossed the States to New York, whence steamer was taken to Southampton. They went on foot to London,thence by boat to Lisbon, and on foot through Portugal,Spain,the South of France, Switzerland, and Germany. They were joined by M. Stupp at Munich on July 31,1895, and proceeded on foot through Austro-Hungary, Servia, and Roumania to Con- stantinople,which was reached on October 31. Thoerner fell ill at Bucharest, and was left behind. Owing to the Armenian difficulties, they were not allowed to travel through Turkey-in-Asia, consequently boat was taken to Batoum, whence they travelled on foot through the Caucasus to Baku, and reached Meshed on November 22, 1895. The two travellers appeared to be in good health and spirits, and not suffering from fatigue. It was decided to proceed thence via Kerman (East Persia), through Beluchistan, and they left Meshed on November 29. Their intention was to make for Bombay, cross India to Calcutta, go up the Brahmaputra valley, and proceed through Siam and South China to Shang- hai, cross to the nearest port of Japan, walk to Yoko- hama, and afterwards take steamer for San Francisco, where Kogel would complete his trip. The conditions of the journcy are that Kogel and Thoerner each pay 3,000d015. if the journey is not completed within two years ; if they succeed, they receive from an athletic club in an Francisca 5,000d015. each. They must cover a distance of 26,000 kilometres (18,000 miles). M.Stupp is an amateur long-distance walker. He contemplated doing the round of the world in twenty months. During their travels the pedestrians state that they have met with every kindness and courtesy. The most exciting scene was the Armenian massacres at Trebizond, of which Kogel and Stupp were eye-witnesses. Kogel and Thoerner, by the terms of their wager, are not allowed any money to cover expenses, but must find means as they go along.

though the outlook here too seems to be distinctly more hopeful. It has been announced that all the evidence upon which the British claim rests will be made public at as early a date as possible, and this announcemeat seems to have given con- siderable satisfaction in the United States. As time goes on the mere thought of a war with the United States gets to be more re- pellent to the people of this country. Mr. BALFOUR undoubtedly spoke the national sentiment when in his speech at Manchester on Tuesday he declared that" the idea of war with the United States of America carried with it something of the unnat- ural horror of civil war." Mr. BALFOUR seems to be cf the opinion that the people of the United States are not so averse to a conflict as we are in this country. Bazing his judgment upon the newspaper reports, he says large sections of the Americans" seem to regard a war with this coun- try as a thing to be lightly indulged in, an exhilar- ating exercise, a gentle national stimulus." If this is a correct interpretation of the American newspapers, it is devoutly to be hoped that the newspapers do not faithfully repro sent the people on this particular subject.

THE speech which Mr. BALFOUR Mr. Balfour at made at Manchester on Wednes- day was for the most part mono- polised by such all-absorbing subjects as the Transvaal and Venezuelan questions, but certain minor topics were not altogether neglected. With regard to the treatment of voluntary schools he intimated that the Government would "not fall be- hind those expressions of intention which we gave to the public when we were asking them for their support." But as he made the same declaration with regard to the cotton duties, the friends of the vpluntary schools may not feel thoroughly re- assured. Mr. BALFOUR declined to enter into any details as to the way the Government intended to deal with the schools. He did not say whether additional assistance would be given from the 1 rates or from the imperial funds, nor did 'he say whether any attempt would be made to 1 cripple the Board schools. As to the Indian cotton duties Mr. BALFOUR was just a trifle mis- understood by his audience. A Manchester audience had no difficulty in calling to mind the promises that were made in this part of the country by Tories at the last election, and when Mr. BALFOUR declared that the Government would "not fall behind those promises," the natural conclusion was that the duties were to be repealed. The enthusiasm was, therefore, of the warmest order, and Sir W. H. HOULDSWORT3, assured Mr. BALFOUR that his statement would "send a thrill of satisfaction throughout the whole of Lancashire and many other manu- facturing parts of England." But Mr. BALFOUR had not meant what he said after all, or at least he had not meant what the audience understood him to say. In respond- ing to the vote of thanks he chilled the hopes that had been prematurely raised, by announcing that the cotton duties were not to be " totally " abolished. The Indian Government must have revenue and it could not do without these duties. The duties would, however, be re-arranged so that they would not act as protection to the Indian manufacturers as against Lancashire. That is all, and as a matter of, fact Mr. BALFOUR said neither more for less than has been said all along by those who supported the imposition of these duties. The central fact remains that these duties are still to be imposed, and that the Lancashire people have been deluded and betrayed by the Tory politicians they returned to Parliament. Alr.Beuouß's references to the Armenian question were decidedly depressing and discouraging. Tory diplomacy has certainly done nothing to telieve ! the dreadful sufferings of the Armenians, nor is any hope held out in this speech that it will be able:to do anything. The A.rmenians are, evid- ently, so far as this Government is concerned, to . be left to the tender mercies of the Turks.

THERE has been during the past The Foreign week a very considerable improve- -0 utlook. ment in the foreign outlook. The difficulties in South Africa which at one time threatened to bring about some serious complica- tions have, so far, been smoothed over with a sue- ces that is, taking all the circumstances into account, really extraordinary. For this success two men are in a pre-eminent degree entitled to praise; namely, Mr. CHAMBERLAIN in this country; and President KRUGE R in South Africa. There can now be no question that upon the first intima- tion of JAMESON'S raid, Mr. CHAMBERLAIN thorouglkly realised the situation and all that it involved. In some very influential quarters there was undoubtedly a disposition to await the result of the filibustering expedition before taking any decided action with regard to it. Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN did not give any countenance to this un- worthy and, indeed, ignoble view of imperial responsibilities. His repudiation and eondemna- tion of JAMEsON's lawless act was immediate and complete, and he promptly and vigorously used all the powers he possessed as Colonial Secretary to secure the withdrawal of that expedition. He did not succeed in pre- venting bloodshed, but he certainly saved the honour of this country from an ugly stain. While, however, it is only fair to say this for Mr. CHAM- BERLAIN personally,there is still ono matter which seriously affects the colonial administration of the present Government to be considered. The ques- tion has been asked, how it came about that this large and thoroughly equipped expeditionary force was mobilised on the Transvaal frontier without thecolonial authorities knowing anything about it or about the objects for which it was to be used. There has not yet been any answer to that ques- tion, but an answer will have to be given. It may be taken for granted that,when Parliament meets, this will be one of the points upon which the Liberals will ask for very complete information. As to President KRUGER'S share in bringing about an amicable arrangement, there can now be no dispute. "Own Paul," as he is familarily called in South Africa, has once again displayed the po9session of those statesmanlike qualities with which, it is said, he has been credited by no less an authority than PRINCE BISMARCK him- self. He has throughout this crisis played the part of a vigilant protector of his own country, and at the same time of a true friend of South Africa in general. He has evidently thoroughly realised the fact that if South Africa is to prosper there must be peace, or at least friendly rivalry, between the two domin- ant races, the British and the Dutch. It is to be hoped that, acting in the same conciliatory spirit which induced him to hand over JAMF.SON and his followers to the Imperial Government, he will be- fore long concede the reforms which are demanded by the " Outlanders in the Transvaal. These reforms cannot be withheld for many years, and at the present time they would be received as a particularly graceful concession. So far as the dispute with the United States is concerned there is no progress to be reported,

div.head: PORTRAIT PHOTOGRAPHY BY GAS-
div.p: PORTRAIT PHOTOGRAPHY BY GAS-
LIGHT.

Mr. Birtles, the well-known photographer, of Sankey-st., Warrington, has just brought the equip- ment of his establishment up to date by the addi- tion of an appliance by which the operator and the sitter are alike rendered independent of daylight and the many annoyances which arise from its un- certainty in the English climate. By an ingenious use of the now familiar incandescent gaslight, the studil is illuminated in the evening hours and upon dull and dark days with a sunlike effulgence,whica is not only pleasant in itself to the sitter,but which in actually working, throws an attractive glamour over the interior of the studio and its accustomed and often too prosaic paraphernalia. By the aid of Mr. Birtles' special device " exposures " can be made in a period of time very little, if anything, exceeding what is necessary for daylight photo- graphy, and on Tuesday evening when we had the opportunity ef witnessing a demonstration of the photography by gaslight, some charming negotia- tions were obtained, of which prints are now on view in the windows of Mr. Birtles' establishment. For readiness of manipulation and certainty of results, the new light would seem to leave little to be desired. The source of illumination being of large superficial area, there is a total absence of anything like harsh shadows. Indeed the ease with which the apparatus can be adjusted so as to secure the most delicate gradations of tone as well as the strong " Rembrandt " contrasts affords the strongest argument in favour of its usefulness and ultimate popularity. And when it is remembered that the device is sufficiently portable to make it an easy matter for the photographer to practise his art in one's own parlour or sitting-room, the suc- cess of the new method of photography seems assured, and it is seen that an immense step in advance has been made. Mr. Birtles is to be con- gratulated on his most recent achievement, the possibilities of which we have little doubt will be taken full advantage of by his numerous patrons.

div.head: AUSTRALIAN LOYALTY TO THE
div.p: AUSTRALIAN LOYALTY TO THE
EMPIRE.

The Hon. G. H. Reid, Premier of New South Wales, despatched from Sydney the following cable message to Lord Salisbury "From the Prime Minister of New South Wales.—The Government of Australia and Tasmania view with satis- faction the prompt and fearless measures adopted by i her Majesty's Gbvernment n defence of the integrity of the Empire. We desire to convey our united assurances of loyal support. The people of Australia are in full sympathy with the determination of the mother country to resent foreign interference in matters of British and colonial concern.—Signed,on behalf of and at the request of the Governments of New South Wales, Victoria,Scuth Australia,Queensland, Tasmania, and Western Australia, G. H. BID." The following reply has been addressed by Lord Salis- bury to the telegram Her Majesty 's Government heartily thank you, and, through you, the Governments of Australia and Tas- mania, for your patriotic assurance of sympathy and support. Nothing can give to us greater confidence in maintaining the rights of our country than the know- ledge that we have the full approval and goodwill of our fellow subjects in thegreat colonies of the Empire.--. SALISBURY."

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, JANUARY 18, 1896.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, JANUARY 18, 1896.
RUNCORN AND WIDNES.

Mennszns' Csuncii IldissroN. Another of the series of concerts was given in this mission on Monday evening. An organ voluntary was played by Mr. Gardiner, and songs were rendered by Mimes C. Williamson, Foster, M. and A. Hill, Temple, and Lunt, and Messrs. W. Lunt and Bazley. There were also recitations by Mr. W. Hunter, Mr. W. Page, Miss B. Rawlinson, and a sketch by Mr. J. Williamson. Mr. Gardiner was the accompanist, and the chair was taken by Mr. J. Sweetman before a very good audience.

div.head: SINKING OF A VI IDNES FLAT.
div.p: SINKING OF A VI IDNES FLAT.

_ During the prevalence of the gale on Wednesday, the flat William, belonging to Mr. Cooper, of Widnes, was wink in the Mersey, between Garston and Speke. Four Widnes men composed the crew, the captain being Mr. Holden. Unfortunately the small boat on board became filled and went down, which made it impossible for the men to escape by it. They, therefore, climbed into the rigging and their perilous position being noticed by the captain of a passing steamer, named the Alice Capper,of Northwich, he immediately went to their rescue. The barge the steamer was towing was drawn alongside the sunken vessel, and the men safely got on board.

HOT-POT SUPPER. On Wednesday evening a hot-pot supper was given in the L. and N.-W. Hotel, the result of a billiard match between sides chosen by two well-known cueists. There was a splendid spread, and much credit is due to Mrs. Jones. A concert was afterwards held at which Mr. W. H. Mundy presided, and made a humorous speech. Songs were rendered by Messrs. Carry, Shingler,Sergeant Walker, P. Radley, Fox and Banks. Messrs. Parry and Shingler were repeatedly encored. Mr. H. Grounds was the accompanist. A pleasant evening concluded with a vote of thanks to the host and hostess, and chairman, and suitable replies were given. THE NEW INDUSTRIES FOR RUNCORN. It is now said that a commencement will be made with the construction of the new chemical works at Weston, for the Castner-Kellner Alkali Company in the course of a few weeks. During the past few days exca- vations have been made to ascertain the subsoil on the site. When building operations have been commenced the work is to be pushed forward with the utmost ex- pedition. Progress is being made in the erection of the brick plant for the new industry of converting "blue billy" into blocks at the Old Quay works ot the United Alkali Company. PLEASANT SATURDAY EVENINGS. The Pleasant Evening entertainment in the Guild Hall, on Saturday, promoted by the Runcorn Women's Tem- perance Association, was a success. The Rev. W. George was in the chair. The programme, which was highly appreciated, was as follows :—Song, Miss With- iligton ; song, "The Diver," Mr. Shingler ; song, Alicia Pritchard; recitation, Mr. George Page; song, Miss Wilson; reading, " Tennyson's Emmie," Miss Hallding ; song, Mr. Charles Leath wood ;song, "The Old Sexton," Mr. Shingler ; duet, "'rho Sol-fa Duet," Miss Simkin and Mr. Morris; and recitation, Jack Harrop. Coffee and , buns were dispensed as usual.

AN UNHAPPY MARRIAGE AT_RUNCORN.

On Saturday-m-o-r-ning,at Runcorn Police Court,before Messrs. F. J. Norman and E. Imison, Peter Knight, ship carpenter,was charged under a warrant with neglecting to fulfil the conditions of an order made on October 9th, by which he had to contribata 15s. a week towards the maintainance of his wife and children. It was stated that he was £9 15s. in arreers,and the prisoner acknow- ledged the debt,but contended that he had had DO wark. —Annie Knight,his wife,stated that he would not follow his employment. He was content to be kept by his mother,who found him in food, clothes, tobacco, &. The Chairman characterised the case as a painful one. There was no earthly reason why they should not be in a happier position. He would have to go to gaol for two months, and afterwards find the money. JIIVENILE INCHABITES TEA MINTING.

The annual tea meeting in connection with the " On- ward " tent of Juvenile Rechabites, Runcorn, was held in St. John's Schoolroom, on Wednesday evening. A substantial tea was provided, the wants of the " juveniles " being attended to by Mesdames Sayle, Richardson, Williamson, and Leach. An excellent en- tertainment was afterwards provided, the chair being taken by Mr. Sayle. A number of parents were pre- sent, and an interesting feature of the proceedings was the initiation of several new members, the address being delivered by Bro. Warburton. Songs were well ren- dered by Masters W. Sutton, and Percy Gatley, and recitations were given by Masters W. Sutton, A. Fox, and G. A. Goodier. Brothers Williamson and Richardson also delivered addresses. At the close, fruit was dis- tributed.
" CHARLES DICKENS."

Under the auspices of the Bethesda Literary and Social Class on Tuesday evening, the pastor of the church (Rev. J. Simpson) continued his studies in En- glish literature taking for his subject "Charles Dickens." He said the sad experiences of Dicken's early life never left him and he stamped them undoubtedly in his works. He was probably the most energetic man of letters of the present century. In his literary work he was in- tensely theatrical, there being more of the play writer than the novelist about him. He had singular power in the creating of comic character ; a writer of wonderful force in humous and pathos—a writer too, who more than any of his contemporaries, haa a fund of animal spirits, cheeriness, vivacity, and energy which he was capable of infusing into his works. Pleasure was ex- pressed by the members of the class at the close, at the interesting light in which Dickens had been put before chem. TUB ENDORSBDIBNT OF A RUNCORN PUBLICAN'S LICENSH. At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday morning before Sir Richard Brooke (chairman) and Mr. F. J. Norman, an application was made by Mr. A. Browne, solicitor, Warrington, for the magistrates to fix upon the amount of surety they required from Mr. Smith in appealing against the decision of the magistrates of the previous Monday when they endorsed his license of the Welling- ton Hotel, Percival-lane. The only reason that recogni- , sauces were required was a guarantee that the costs would be paid and that the prosecution would not be given the foolish errand to Knutsford through the appeal not being proceeded with. Mr. Smith was a man of means, and he (Mr. Browne) suggested that Mr. Smith in a surety of £lOO, and another of £5O, would be ample. The magistrates acceded to the application, and Mr. Smith was accordingly bound over in a surety of £lOO, and Mr. Joseph Houghton Smith (Greenall, Whit- ley and Co.) in a surety of £5O. PBRFORMANCI4 BY GREBNWAY-ROLD ScROOL BOARD

CHILDREN. The entertainment at the Seamen's Institute on Wed- nesday evening was chiefly provided by children con- nected with.erreenway-road Board Schools who it will be remembered achieved great success at their annual concert a few weeks ago, when a performance of the operetta "The Pay ot the Pied Piper "was given. Cap- tain Westbrook presided at the entertainment on Wed- nesday,when an exceedingly interesting programme was gone through. The first part consisted of the perform- ance of a number of action songs in character,and other items. 'A number of lads admirably acquitted them- selves in a sword drill, and the same may be said of the performance of the smaller boys representing "John Chinaman." The dairymaids were most appro- priately attired, and their singing of a dairy- maid's song was much appreciated. A still more pleasing item was the musical medley , and , a well deserved encore was demanded. Fifteen youngsters dressed as rats provoked the audience te laughter with their amusing antics. The latter portion of the evening was occupied by a magic lantern exhibi- tion of numerous views in the British Isles including many local ones. A number of comic slides was also shown. Mr. Thomas Bowyer manipulated the lantern, and explanatory remarks were made by Mr. J. F. Moul- ton (headmaster at the Greenway-road Board School) Miss Kilburn (the headmistress) accompanied the chil- dren on the piano in their performances. A vote of thanks for their services was unanimously accorded them on the motion of Mr. Shaw (missionary), secc.nded by Mr. H. Cook. Mr. Moulton responded, and a pleasant evening's entertainment concluded. PARISH CHURCH TEA PARTY.

The Congregational tea party in connection with Run- corn Parish Church was held on Monday evening in the National Infants' school. About 400 persons sat down to tea,trays having been given by the following:—Rev. Canon Wood, Mr. and Mrs. P. Speakman, Mesdames H. White, Whittaker, C. Harrison, Hazlehurst, J. E. Mere- dith, W. Sutton, William Bate, F. Smith, M. Barker, W. Timmins, E. Gregory, J. Johnson, John Littler, A.Buck, J. Leicester, R.Abel,John Davies, Broadhurst,T.Nicholls, G. Shone, J. W. Hamilton, Hampson, A. Jordan,E. Imi- son, J. Ball, H. Briscoe, Joseph Savage, A. Salkeld, E. Newton, W. B. Kay, J. K. Digges, William Anderton,W. Jones, Coward, A, Hough, J. Yates, Messrs. Crosby and Sons, Dr. McLennan, and Mr. and Mrs. Collier. A most interesting programme was afterwards submitted, and the proceedings were presided over by the Rev. Canon Maitland Wood,M.A. (vicar). He was supported by the Revs. W. H. Stables, H. B. Firth, H. C. Moyle, and W. Scholes. Mr. John Littler (churchwarden) in the course of a few appropriate remarks referred to the Vicar's im- pending departure from Runcorn for a short time for the benefit of his health. He was, however, leaving a very fine staff behind him, to carry on the work, and he (Mr. Littler) was sure tnat the lay- men would most willingly support them in their labours. The Vicar briefly addressed the meeting, and thanked the previous speaker for his kind remarks. Three part songs were well sung by the members of the choir, and songs were most efficiently rendered by Miss Nellie Wells (Wavertree), Miss Simkin, Master Lana, Mr. Branch, Mr. Pownall, and Mr. Clare. Miss Wells' singing was greatly appreciated ,and she was awarded an encore. Messrs. Littler and Branch con- tributed a duet "The GQlden Goose." and • "The Star of Bethlehem "was als% sung as a duet by Master Lane and Bauner. Mr. Clifford Le Couteur was the accom- panist. The usual votes of thanks were passed, and a most interesting gathering terminated.

div.head: VESTRY MEETING AT RUNCORN.
div.p: VESTRY MEETING AT RUNCORN.

THE NEW POWERS FOR THE URBAN COUNCIL. A vestry meeting was held in Bethesda schoolroom on Friday evening for ,the purpose of considering a com- munication from the Local Government Board conferr- ing upon the Urban District Council of Runcorn power to appoint, and to revoke the appointment of assistant overseers tor the township, and also for the purpose of considering an application by the Ut ban District Council for the powers of a Parish Council. The Vicar (Rev. Canon Wood) occupied the chair, and amongst those present were the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Messrs. E. Imison, J.P., William Handley, William Hankinson, F. Johnson, J. E. Meredith, F. A. Lake klaw clerk to the Urban Council), and W. Sutton (assistant overseer). The following letter was read by Mr. Sutton (assistant overseer). Local Government Board, Whitehall, S.W. 21st December, 1895. Gentlemen I am directed by the Local Government Board to forward to you the enclosed copy of an application from the Urban District Council of Runcorn Lor an order under section 33 of the Local Government Act, 1894, conferring certain pOwers on the Council. lam directed to state that the Board purpose to issue an order conferring upon the Council the power of appointing overseers for the parish, but before doing so they will be prepared to consider any representations which you may desire to offer on the subject. The Board are desirous of being furnished with the observations of the overseers with reference to the application of the Council for the powers, duties, and liabilities of overseers, which are by section 6 (1) c (1) transferred to Parish Councils, and with the observations of the churchwardens as regards the application for the powers transferred to Parish Councils by section 6 (1) (b). The Board also propose 0 issue an order conferring on the Council the power to appoint, and to revoke the appointment of assistant overseers, but before doing so they will be prepared to consider any observations which the Vestry may desire to make with respect to the proposal. Having regard to the provisions of section 33 (4) of the Act, the Board propose to direct by the order that any existing assist- ant overseer shall hold his office on the same terms as at present. The effect of this wilt be in the case of an assistant overseer appointed by the Vestry and the jus- tices, that his appointment will only be revocable by the Vestry, and that his duties and salary can only be altered by the same body. On the occurrence of a vacancy from any cause toe next and all future appoint- ments will be made by the Council. The Board wish to be furnished with the observations of the Vestry with referenze to the application of the Council for the powers of a Parish Council under section 6 (1) (a) and 17 (8) of the Act. lam therefore directed to request that you will bring these matters before the Vestry, and forward to the Board a copy of any resolution which may be passed embodying the views of the meeting on the pro- posals of the District Council referred to in the last two preceding paragraphs of this letter. I am, gentlemen, your obedient servant, S. B. PROVO, assistant secre- tarv." The copies of the application of the Urban Counci referred to, were as follows :—Under date 9th Ju1y,1895 Mr. E. Marshall, secretary to the Runcorn Urban Dis- trict Council, wrote : " I beg to inform your lordships that at a meeting of the Runcorn Urban District Council held on the 4th July, 1895, the following resolution was unanimously adopted That application be made to the Local Government Board under section 33 of the Local Government Act, 1894, for an order conferring on the Council all the following matters :-1, the appointment of overseers and the revocation of appointment of assist- ant overseers ; 2, the powers, duties, or liabilities of a Parish Council, particularly those under section 6 (1) (a and b) ; section 8 (1) (b, e and k) ; section 9, and sec- tion 14 of the Local Government Act, 1894. The com- mittee consider the power to appoint assistant overseers of great importance, as in this parish the election of assistant overseer is in the vestry with power for anyone to demand a poll. Such a method is most unsuitable that could be devised for the election of an official. The powers of the vestry are needed, as the Council having taken over the Burial Board under section 62 should have power to appoint salaries of cemetery officials without appealing to the vestry, as required by the Burials' Act, 1852, section 15. The power to accept gifts under sec- tion 8 (1) (to') appears desirable in view of Sir J. T. Brunner's proposal to transfer the Guild Hall to the Council upon trust." In a further communicationdated 31st Ju1y,1895. Mr. Marshall States: "Adverting to your letter of the 25th inst., I am directed to state in reply that there being no Parish Council or meeting within the district of the Runcorn Urban District, my council con- sider that all powers conferred on Parish Councils or meetings and not already vested in the Urban District Council should be conferred upon the Urban Council. The items specially mentioned in the resolution of the Council are those wtich appeared to be of the most pressing importance. My Council were of opinion that second to those come the provisions of section 6 (1) c (I and III.) and d; section 6 (4) ; section 10, section 13, and section 17, sub-sections (8) and (9), which they ask I may, with the necessary qualifications,be vested in them. I beg to enclose forms containing information as to Poor 'Law Parishes comprised in our district, and as to the appointment of overseers, assistant overseers,and collec- tors of poor rates therein. Mr. E. Imison moved the following resolution : "That this vestry meeting of the township of Runcorn having considered the letter of the Local Goveonment Board to the overseers of Runcorn,dated 21st December, 1895 intimiating the intention of the Board to issue an order under section 33 of the Local Government Act, 1894, conferring the powers named in the said letter upon the Urban District Council of Runcorn and asking for the observations of the vestry, thereupon, approves of the course proposed to be taken by the Local Govern- ment Board." He said that so far as the overseers were concerned they felt that the present method of appoint- ment was very unsatisfactory. He understood that so far as the alteration went with regard to the assistant overseer. Mr. Sutton would remain to continue the duties at the same remuneration he received at present, but his successor would be appointed by the Council.— Or. Gastaldi seconded, and the resolution was carried unanimously. The Chairman moved a second resolution " That this meeting approves of and concurs with the applica- tion by the Runcorn Urban District Council to the Local Government Board for the powers of a Parish Council under section 6 (1), and section 17 (8) of the Local Government Act, 1894." He said he was induced to attend that meeting as it would be the last, or probably the last,of the vestry of Runcorn. So long as the present assistant overseer filled his office properly the vestry would have nothing to do ; if he did not do so they would have duties to fulfil, but all the other powers would be transferred elsewhere. The vestry was a very ancient body. It was no doubt originally an ecclesias- tical meeting, but it was found convenient to endow thei same body with a good many civil powers. They could look back with interest to the work the vestry had done. It seemed to have now almost become a dead body, and it was desirable that the whole of its civil work should be transferred' to more modern bodies which were being developed at the present time. The vestry was the parent of local ad- ministration, and long before people thought of parish councils, urban councils or rural councils, the vestry had done interesting and useful work.—Mr. Handley, in seconding the resolution,said it seemed to be the natural outcome of the Local Government Act that they ahould meet together and put their council in possession of tbe same powers as those enjoyed by the parish council. He had been lookiag over the sections of the Act for the purpcse of seeing what powers the vestry was parting with, and what the Council were seeking to obtain. The vestry meeting was nothing more nor less than a meeting of inhabitants to talk over or settle matters connected with Church and State. It was a very ancient institu- tion, dating be thought from the days of King Alfred. They were now asked to part with those powers, and if they were asked what they were it would be difficult to define them. The great bulk of them had been trans- ferred by statute, but there were a number of powers the vestry had by custom. He thought it was a fact, that although powers had been transferred there had never been any statute passed for taking away the powers of the old vestry. They had been left intact for what they were worth. Therefore, custom gave them power to refuse what the District Council passed. He thought it was a very proper thing that in these days the District Council of any town should be entrusted with full government and responsibility for the good government of the community, with no other bodies to look after such things. Referring to the custody of the registers of baptisms, marriages and burials,he said they were to be kept by the superintendent registrar. Books and documents relating to the affairs of the church or the ecclesiastical charities would be left in the hands of he church. Any ot her books or documents would have to be handed over to the care of the District Council who would be responsible for their safe custody until each time as the County Council might decide. There was however, a saving clause that the incumbent, vicar, or churchwardens who had kept them hitherto,should have the power of inspecting them at any reasonable times. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Lake said the vestry powers were of great impor- tance to the town. The Council had taken over the work of time Burial Board and unless they had the powers of the vestry they could not fix a salary under the Burial's Act without bringing it before the vestry. They also could not borrow or pay off old loans, and thus re- duce the rate of interest. He thought it was very de- sirable that those powers should be vested in the District Council.

The re,solution was unanimously passed. Mr. Imison said as that was the last meeting of the vestry, might he take the opportunity as °De of the last overseers, of thanking the Chairman for presidine over that meeting, and also be allowed to add that they hoped that the journey they heard he was going to undertake would result in his returning in improved health. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Baudley seconded the proposition, which was carried.—The Chairman having responded, the meeting terminated.

div.head: HA.LTON.
div.p: HA.LTON.
RE-OPENINO OF SCHOOLS.—The Sunday Schools and Day Schools have been re-opened this week, after being cloFed for five weeks on account of the recent epidemic of scarlet fever.

THE WESLEY GUlLD.—Monday evening was devoted to learning new tunes from Dr. Stephenson's Hymnary, which has been adopted for use at the guild's meetings. The Rev. C. de P. Gliddon drew the attention of the members to the "Penny Poets" and "Penny Novels," which are being published by Mr. W. T. Stead, and strongly advised them to read them. It was resolved to start a Boys' Brigade in connection with the guild. The attendance was as follows :—Thirty members, 8 companions, and 9 friends. At the close of the meeting one person joined as a companion. ACCIDENT AT ASTMOOR TANNERY.—OH Saturday morn- ing, a man named James Allman met with an accident, as he was entering the tannery of Messrs. F. ;W. Rey- nolds and Son, at Astmoor. It was dark, and in stepp- ing aside to avoid a place were some buckets are kept, he fell into a tanpit full of liquor, fracturing two of his ribs by contact with the boards which divide the pit from the one next to it. He managed to get out of the pit, and to walk home to Halton, where he was attended to by Dr. Carruthers. Be is now making satisfactory progress towards recovery. PRESENTATION OF BIBLES AT THE WESLEYAN CHURCH. —A special service was held on Sunday afternoon, when 83 beautiful roan, gilt-edged copies of the revised bible were presented to those officers, teachers, and members of the adult classes, who have been connected with the Sunday school more than three years. In future, when scholars are moved up from the lower into the adult classes, they will, if they have been attending the school three years, receive a Bible similar to the above. This is a revival, in a different form, of the custom of givimg bibles to scholars who were leaving the school. The bibles were distributed hy the Rev. C. de Putron Gild- don, who, in a brief historical sketch of the school, des- cribed some of its old customs, and read several quaint rules now obsolete. That day, he said, was the 85th birthday of the only person living who was a teacher in the school when it was first opened on Ist February, 1824, viz., Mr. Henry Tipping, who now resides at Bromborough. For 70 years the school had been mak- ing progress. Children who had passed through it,were spread all over the world; and it was certain that these had not all lost the inspiration of the teaching they had received. He hoped that the t:,,ys and girls now in the school would learn of the Lord Jesus Christ so deeply, sincerely, and practically that their lives would be made noble and pure; that they would rule their lives by the bible, and so be happy and useful in the world in which God had placed them.—Mr. R. Posnett, of Run- corn, also delivered an appropriate address advising all present to put a high value on the Bible, on the Sabbath, and on family prayer. It was thought a fitting occasion on which to send a word of greeting to Mr. Tipping ; and , the Secretary was instructed to do so. MOTHERS' MEETING TEA AT THE MISSION Roo3l.—On Thursday week, at the Mission Room, Halton-rcad,Mrs. IVray entertained the memt2rs of her Mothers' Meeting at a tea, of which about 30 persons partook. Miss Brere ton and Miss L. Wright kindly assistei at the tables- The vicar was present, and delivered an appropriate address. After tea Mr. H. Thomason presided at a mis- cellaneous entertainment. Songs were contributed by the followinn. gentlemen : Messrs. G. H. Walton, T. Haddock, G. Walker, A. Povey, and T. Houghton. The choir boys from the Parish Church, rendered a sketch. entitled, " Ten little nigger boys." Mrs. Wray and Miss Jeacock acted as accompanists.

div.head: RUNCORN FREE LIBPARY LECTURES.
div.p: RUNCORN FREE LIBPARY LECTURES.

On Friday evening in the Runcorn Technical Institute, the Rev. J. S. Simpson delivered a lecture on " The Wizard of the North." Dr. McDougall occupied the chair, and there were also on the platform Messrs. William Handley (chairman of the Free Library Committee), J. W. Cunningham, and J. D. Jones (librarian). In the course of his lecture Mr. Simpson remarked that it had been said that Sir Walter Scott's works had become classic. He was sorry if that was the case because they found that the term classic had become synonymous with neglect. Many men of letters had been able to gain a beautiful style by constantly reading Sir Walter Scott's writings. After alluding to Scott's birth in 1771,and the times in which he lived, the lecturer said Sir Walter Scott's nature unfitted him from taking part in the great movements of his day. He lived in the past and he reproduced the past which had a great fascination for him. Referring to the poet's first composition "The Lay of the Last Minstrel," which was written at the request of Lady Dalkeith, he said it was received with little applause and great abuse. Jeffrey's criticisms, however, brought Scott into prominence, and his other poems were received with acclamation, not only by the Scotch, but the English people as well. Scott was essen- tially an artist aid could paint a picture in words. His sentences were full of life and simplicity. But the people wanted a poet who could voice the intense desires of their heart at this time, and Bcott showed his generosity in making way for a man—Lord Byron—whom he knew to be a better poet than himself,and devoted his abilities to novel writing. The Waverley novels were marked by the same charac- teristics as the poems; there was the same simplicity, directness of expression, and faithfulness of description. He wrote with an ease which they did not find in any other writer. He made the past live; his characters being historic were written' faithfully according to his- tory. They were no mere puppets going before us on the stage pulled by a string by the writer. They were full of truth and throbbing with life. He was very happy in his portraiture of women characters, the finest being that of Jeanie Jeans the heroine of "The Heart of Mid-Lothian." In that character he seemed to have put the best he knew of woman. She was a homely woman, born in humble circumstances, a gentle sister, a loving daughter, affectionate lover, and one who would give her life in :.elf sacrifice for the good of her own sister. She was but the type of Scotch women, she had the characteristics of the peasantry ; she was no new woman with a taste for manly sport and passions, anl yet she fascinated and interested us. Mr. Sampson pro- ceeded to speak of the nobility of Scott's character, and the richness of Scotland in good men and women, and in 'conclusion said Scott died in harness, with a name un- tarnished. In the thousands of leaves he had written, there was not one sentence which he could have wished had never been written. (Applause.) The lecturer was thanked for his services on the motion of Mr. Cunningham,seconded by Mr. Jones. The Chairman's services were also acknowledged on the Motion of Mr. Handley, seconded by Mr. E. Marshall.

Commander Mllardy, Chief Constable of Lanarkshire, committed suicide by drowning himself in the Clyde on Thursday afternoon. He had announced his intention of doing so,and weighted his pockets with dumbells. A child named Eastwood died at Bradford Infirmary on Thursday from the effects of injuries received by the fall of a chimney' stack through the roof of an infant school at Lowmoor on Wednesday, this being the second death. In the case of another child recovery is considerd to be very doubtful. Some of the other cases of injuries are serious.

BOOK FOR MARRIED WOMEN.

The information contained in this book ougkt to be known by every married woman, aud it will not harm the unmarried to read. The book is conveniently divided into 12 chapters. The first chapter treats of the changes at puberty,or when a girl becomes a woman. The second chapter treats of marriage from a doctor's standpoint ; points out the best age tor marriage, and who should have children and who not, and furnishes useful in- formation that one can ordinarily get only from an in- telligent doctor. The third chipter treats of the marriage of blood relations; and condemns such marriages as a rule. Chapter four tretts of the signs of pregnancy. The fifth chapter tells how a woman should live during the pregnant state. The sixt`a cha,ter treats of mishaps and how to avoid them. The seventh chapter treats cf maternal impressions and shows that birthmarks are not due tolongings on the part of the mother, bat rather to her poor health. The eighth chapter teaches how to have easy confinements. Certain people believe that women should bring forth in pain and trouble, but the • hygienic physician says that confinements can 1. • made comparatively easy if certain rules are obeyed ; these rules are given. The ninth chapter treats of the proper management of confinement until the baby is born, use tenth chapter tells how to treat the mother till she is up and about again. The eleventh ohapter treats of sterility ; gives the main causes of it, how these may be overcome and children result The last chapter treats of the " change," a most important article for all women over forty. The book is full of useful information and no book is written which goes so thoroughly into matters relating to married women. Some may think too much is told ; such can scarcely be the case. for knowledge is power and the means ot attaining hapnlness. The book can be had from Dr. T• R. div.head: TAKING COLD.
div.p: TAKING COLD.

A" Cold "is not necessarily the result of a high or ow temperature. A person may go from a hot bath directly into a cold one, or into snow even, and not take cold. lie may remain out in the coldest atmosphere until chilled through, and still not take cold. On the contrary,he may take cold by pouring a couple of table- spoonfuls of water upon some parts of his dress, or by standing in a door, or before a stove, or by sitting near a window or other opening, where one part of the body is colder than another part. Let it be kept in mind that uniformity of temperature over the whole body is the great thing to be looked after. It is the unequal heat upon oinerent parts of the body that produces Colds, by disturbing the uniform circulation of the blood, which in turn induces congestion of some Dart. Beep the feet always dry and warm, avoid draughts of air, keep the system braced up by plenty of sleep. and good food, and by a powerful Tonic, and you will be proof against a Cold and its results. div.head: BEFORE TUE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE TUE MAGISTRATES.

AN UNNATURAL MOTHER.—THIYMPING A BABY'S FACE. •At the Warrington Borough Court on Monday, Mary Mahon, 15, Platt-st., a young married woman, was charged with having on the 4th January. assaulted and beaten Thomas Mahon, a child of 11 months.—P.C. Newey said that at 20 minutes to 7 o'clock on the day in question he received a complaint from a shopkeeper in Buttermarket-st., about defendant thrashing the child and in consequence ht, followed her and saw her strike the child in the face with her shut fiat and also in the middle of its back. She also shook it. Her husband who was with her tried to pacify it but could not. Both of them were drunk. When brought to the police station the child's face was swollen and it was crying. —The Chief Constable stated that he saw the woman brought in under the influence of drink. The child was shrieking in a fearful manner, and its face was battered as if it had been knocked against a wall. It was evi- dently suffering great pain.—Defendant denied the offence and said she only struck the child on the hand. It was crying because it had a burn ma the arm.—Mrs. Williamson, a neighbour, said defendant was a kind mether.—Defendant's husband also said that she was kind to the child as it was their first baby.—The magis- trates imposed a penalty of 10s. and costs (21 23.), or in default 14 days hard labour. AN OLD POACHER CAUGHT. Before Messrs. the Mayor, Alderman Harrison and Mr. J. W.Hayward.at the Borough Court on Monday,George Sephton, 8, pack Stamford-street, an elderly man, was charged with having been searched on the sth January and found in possession of inapliments for killing game— to wit, pegs, a net. and bag.—P.C. Barlow stated that at a quarter to four on the afternoon of Sunday. the sth of this month, he was in company with P.C. Clough at Friar's Green end. on the Arpley road, when they saw the defendant coming from the direction of Arpley fields. Noticing he appeared rather bulky, witness stopped him and making a search found the net wound round his waist, and the pegs in his pocket. He gave the excuse that he had been trying to sell them. There was no game upon him.—ln answer to a query from the bench as to defendant's trade, Barlow said : Poaching, he does nothing else.—Defendant denied that he was going for game and added that he had a right to have the-instru- ments with him in daytime.—The Chief Constable pointed out that the implements were concealed and that It was not likely that he would carry them about on a Sunday for pride. Defendant was a notorious poacher and had been before magistrates 21 times for similar offences.—The magistrates fined defendant 10s. and costs or 14 days hard labour, and forfeited the nets,etc. THEFT OF A PURSE OF GOLD A SUDDEN TEBIPTA- . TION." Thomas lenningS, a yeti!, Veslding at Sankey, aged 18 years, was brought before Mr. John Fairclough, and Mr. R. Garnett, at the Warrington Borough Court on Wednesday morning, on the charge of stealing on Mon- day a purse. containing £22 103., the property of Thos. Higham,Priestley-st.—Mr. Talbot said that Mr. Higham carried on business as a pork butcher, at 2,Priestley-st., Bank Quay. At about five o'clock on Monday after- noon his wife had occasion to place in the cash drawer of the shop, a corduroy purse containing £22 10s. or £a3 in gold. The shop was left without anybody in it for some considerable period. At six o'clock, Mrs. Hig- ham missed the purse containing the cash, and the same evening information was given to the police. It then transpired that the prisoner vi.ited the shop shortly be- fore six o'clock in company with a young man named King, who delivered milk for Mr. Grange, at -Sankey. King went into the back part of the premises through the shop, leaving the prisoner by himself in the shop. King was sometime in the house watching some black- puddings being made, and when he returned into the shop he found prisoner behind the counter in close proxi- mity to the drawer. Prisoner was very flurried and confused and said " Make haste, come en." They then left the shop. In the course of the evening, the prisoner changed half a sovereign to get some tobacco. He also made an extraordinary speech to King the same evening. He said "If you and I were to steal a purse, and a policeman were to come for us, do you know what I should do." King replied that he did not know. " Why," said prisoner, " I would cut my throat." In the course of the next day his apprehensions were realised, and a policeman (Monaghan) did come for him, and brought him to the police station,on the suspicion of stealing the money. Be, at first, stoutly denied any knowledge of the money or the possession of it. After some hours' detention, however, he (Mr. Talbot) visited the cells,and prisoner asked to speak to him. He then made a voluntary statement, and accompanied Detective Inspector Spinks. and Detective Sergeant Monaghan to a field in Sankey and showed them two places where the money had been buried. £22 7s. had been found and thus only a few shillings had been spent. He then admitted the offence, and said he was sorry,and the reason he had taken it was that it was a sudden temptation. In prisoner's favour it could be said that that was his first offence, and he had assisted the police ia the recovery of the money which was almost intact. The purse was also found in Liverpool- read.—Mrs. Jennings, the mother of the prisoner, said that her son "had a different bringing up than he had come to." Be dared not bring anything home which did not belong to him. He went to St. Mary's Sunday school at Sankey,and had passed the sixth standard at the day school.—Mr. Garnett (to prisoner) : What in- diced you to do it.—Prisoner : It was on the floor.— Mrs. Higham however denied that it was on the floor, and prisoner then said that it was on a bench.—Mr. Talbot: It's getting a little higher.—After considerable consultation, Mr. Fairclough, addressing the prisoner, said that he had not been there before, and the bench did not wish to make a gaol bird of him. However, if he were brought before them again, he would be dealt severely with. They would be lenient with him that morning considering his age and previous good charac- ter, and sentenced him to one day's imprisonmeat.

Shortly after the start good passing ensued between Evans, Barber and Broady, but the latter was-collared before he could become dangerous. Hassell and Micialeburgh drove the homesters back and Smethurst make a aood reply to a kick by Forster, play rested in dangerous quarters for the homesters. Frice gave relief with a good kick. Mlckle- i burgh took a pass at the 25 flag and running well got over and grounded near the corner, the kick at goal proving futile. Higginbottom dribbled well down the touch and picking up and passing to Monks the latter was floored near the line. Wall kicked to half way where good passing took place between Price and Bar- ber, Broady missed catching Barber's pass and in trying to recover possession,injured nis foot which necessitated his removal from the field of play. Lawless was drafted in his place at threequarter. Spruce cleared a rush in excellent style, hut the visitors again became agvessive and a minor resulted. Lawless made a good run down the open and kicking, the forwards followed up well, rushed the ball over the line Bailey equalizing while Evans converted and gave the homesters a lead of two points. Mickleburgh came away to the Warrington 25 where a serimuvige took place. Higginbottom stole away and ran to half-way, where he passed to Barber who rounded his opponents in fine style and grounded near the posts, Evans again doing the needful. Halftime Warrington 2 goals, Broughton 1 try. Oa resuming play settled in midfield. Forster made a good attempt to get through I but was pushed into touch, while a minute later Barber ; was almost over. Warrington kept up a severe pressure I; and good, play by Price, Higginbottom, Barber, Evans. ard Lawless resulted in the latter being pushed into touch on the line. Savage got over from time line out but the ball was ruled back. The visitors now had a turn of pressine- but the defence of Spruce was of first class order. Final score ‘Varrington 2 goals Broughton Rangers I 1 try

WARRINGTON ST.M&RY.S V.ST.HELEss"A."—This match was played on the ground of the former on Saturday. Tne Saints won the toss,and the gime had not been long in progress when Dakin dribbled the hail over the line and scored, the goal kick failing. The visitors invaded the home quarters at the restart, but found Rou,ghley safe,and the home team ag,..in pressed,some nice passing by the backs ending in G. Roughley scoring,the kick at goal again failing.. from the kick off the visi ors were again penned in their own quarteis, and from a sciirn- mage Mason got nicely away and scored underneath the posts, Roughley conv,rting. St. Helens pressed at the re-start, and some passing by the forwards gave an opening for one of the backs, who scored. Half time score—St. Mary's, one goal, two tries ; St. Helens " A," one try. The second half of the game was of a one sided description,the Saints having matters all their own way, and tries were scored by Hampson (three) and Siddall (one), Mason converting one of the tries,the final score being—St. Mary's,two goals, five tries (25 points) ; St. Heiens "A," one try.

{•.••• A NOTED RUNCORN CHARACVER.—Ann Corcoran, Mersey- et., was summoned for being drunk and disorderly in Mer- sey-at.. on January 4th. —P.C. Gregory proved the case.— Inspector Hicks stated that the defendant was nearly burnt to death a short time ago through being drunk. She was only just improving, and now that she wad able to hobble about a little she was as bad as ever in getting drunk.—The magistrates committed her to prison for 14 daTs. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Louisa Mills, Poole-lane, was fined ss. including costs for being drunk and disorderly in Poole-laae.—The case was stated by P.O Ridgway. A WARRINGTON HAWKER IN TROUBLE.—ThOrnag Leigh. a Warrington hawker with one of Mr. Stewart's carts,Warring- ton. was charged with having .in use a cart without having the name cf the owner painted thereon.—P.C. Juett stated that when he stopped the defendant he gave him a wrong name and addiess. aad he had great difficulty in tracing him. —A fine of 2s. 6d. and 12s. Bd. costs was imposed. DRUNICENNESS.—For this offence. David Sumner, Hades- town, was fined. 55. and costs; Patrick Hussey, Winwick, 2s. 6d.; Richard Unsworth, 2s. 6d.; Patrick Conway. Golborne, 2s. 6d. THEATRICAL LICENCE.—Mr. Mather was granted a license to hold theatrical entertainments in Winwick and Padgate schools for one month. BOUND OVER.— Joseph Cook and Henry Houghton were bound over for three months for fighting in Newton on January 7th. SnocEDG ASSAULT ON A WlFE.—Daniel Reece, Gelborne, was charged with assaulting and beating, his wife Elizabeth Reece, on January 6h.—Mr. Stuart, who prosecuted, said that Ref:s,e and his wife had been married for eight years, and resided at Legh-street, Golborne. For six years, the plaint,ff instructed him, she had suffered from the hands of her husband who was constantly assaulting her. They kept a chip shlp in Golborne, and for some reason, the husband was jealous of his wife. On the day in question, Mrs. Reece was washing the clothes, when the husband came in, and put her on the floor where he committed a most outrageous assault upon her. She sustained such injuries that she had been under the doctor ever since. The wi e was anxious for a separation order, and he therefore applied for one under the new act which came into force on January Ist of the present year.—Mrs Reece was then called and gave evid-nce of the assault which her husband had committed upon her, and said that it was not the first time he had attempted a similar thing. He had also made some dreadful threats to her. She was determined to live with him no longer.—Ralph Miller corroborated the compla,nant's statement with regard to threats made to her by the defendant.—Dr. Part. of Golborne said thst he bad examined the complainant and found her suffering fr m injuries which must have been caused by violence. The prisoner denied that he had committted the injwries he was charged with, but the magistrates after having retired to consider their decision, said th tt they found that the prisoner was guilty of the offence with whilh he was charged, Mr. Stone said that during his experience as a magistrate, this was one of the most brutal cases that had ever been brought before him, or that he had ever heard in any court. He only wished they could deal with him more severely. He would be sent to goal for, three months' hard labour.—Mr. Stuart then applied for a separation order, and prisoner w-is served formally with a summons charging him with being found guilty of an aggravated assault, and requir- ing him to show cause why a separation order should not be made upon him for a judicial separation from his wife. The magistrates thereupon granted the order,and ordered prisoner to pay 10s. per week towards his wife's maintenance. The The prisoner was ordered to pay the doctor's fee.

div.head: VACCINATION -IN RA.MSGATE.
div.p: VACCINATION -IN RA.MSGATE.

A mother living in Addington Street states :—" My baby was healthy and strong and free from disease until vaccinated,when a large tbscess formed under the arm and sores formed all over the bedy and head. Its suffering for weeks was intense. Being in good circum- stances, we were able to obtain first-class medical advice but it was of no avail. Nothing could be done to allevi- ate the agony of the poor little sufferer, and at last he succumbed to convulsions." Another mother, living on East Cliffe, writes :—" My child was clear from all signs, but the vaccination has poisoned his arm. It has a large abscess beneath the arm, as large as an hen's egg, causing great suffering night and day for some weeks. It is now three months since vaccinated, and one of the wounds still continues to discharge. The blood and matter coming from the child has been dreadful to see." Another mother, in St. Lawrence, had a fine healthy boy, not a blemish on him until vaccinated, but since then the poor little fellow has endured fearful suffering. small, painful blisters coming out nearly all over his body. So long as vaccination continues, so long will we hear such stories as these. The best doctors could not save the child. All doctors admit they have not yet found either a preventive or a cure for these diseases of vaccin- ation. That is why there is so much suffering, so much disease. and so many deaths. By its antiseptic action, which is harmless to the child, it kills the myriads of germs as soon as they enter the blond from the vaccinator's knife. Thus it acts as a preventive if taken in time, and also acts equally well as a cure, though not so rapidly, if taken after the diseases have entered the system through the blood. As this remedy is a perfectly new discovery, it cannot be prepared by anyone but the Vaccination Virus Vanquisher Company, Limited,of 31,Snow Hill, London, who possess the only prescription of the doctor who made the great discovery.
