INDEPENDENT ORDER OF _ODDFELLOWS
WARRINGTON DISTRICT.

The quarterly meeting of the above district was held at the club's headquarter& 11, Academy-st., under the presidency of Prov. G.M. A Boyle. The accounts bore a favourable aspect and with the auditors' report were unanimously passed. Dele- gates were appointed to attend at the county con- ference, to be held at Sad dleworth, and it was also decided to send representatives to the A.M.C. to be held at. Bristol. Prov. D.G.M. F. J. Whittle was elected l'rov. Grand Master for the next twelve months. The newly-elected G.M. was duly installed by the retiring G.M.. and on taking his seat he had a hearty reception. He hpoke at considerable length on various ,übjects, and his remarks respecting the Children Burial Society, the Widows' and Orphans' Fund, and the general work of the society were received with universal approval. Bro. Whittle also made reference to the less the society had ens- tined by the death of P.P.G.M. Charles Horrabin. P.G. Samuel Ryan was elected Deputy G.M.

div.head: ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ASSOCIATION.

RUNCORN ASSOCIATION V. ORFORD BARRACKS.—The above teams played off their first league fixture on Sat- urday at Runcorn, in grand weather, and before a good crowd. The players filed up as follows :—Runcorn : Goal, Rough ; full backs, Carter and Bloor ; half backs; Pie, Paton and Jones; forwards, Burrows, Walker, Bailie, Walker, Peacock. Orford Barracks : Goal,Brown ; full backs, Harling and Hughes ; half backs, Mather, Lierman and Coy ; forwards, Pixton, Baker, Surrig wood, Fox, Cross, and punctually at 2.45 the leather was set a going, and before very long Bailie opened the score with a good shot. The game was keeely contested up to half time, but the visiting forwards were a long way below concert pitch, and failed to shoot in the right direction. Peacock added another before the interval, and the homesters turned round with a lead of two goals. The soldiers now went off with a dash, and Bloor was called upon but relieved. The home forwards were now irresistible, and passed accurately and prettily. Goals were thickly registered by Peacock (2), W. Walker (2), S. Walker (4), and Bailie (1). There was not the dispar- ity between the teams that the score would indicate,but the home forwards could for once do nothing vvrong,and thi. Blues' half backs were checking every attempt of the visitors' front rank. The visitors, of course, are scarcely ever able to play the same team twice in suc- cession, their players being constantly on the move, and therefore combination can scarcely be expected from them. Final result—Runcorn, 11 goals ;Orford Barracks, nil FOLTCE v.Towx HALL.—On Saturday afternoon the first match of the season in connection with the Police club was played between a team selected frcm themselves and the Corpoiation employes on the police ground behind Fairfield schools. The Chief Constable kicked off, and play was very even throughout. At half-time the score was Town Hall one goal, Police nil. The second half was still very exciting, although no score was made on either side, the result being as shown above, a victory for the visitors.

div.head: NORTHERN RIMBY UNION.
div.p: THE NORTHERN RIMBY UNION.

A special meeting of the committee of the Northern Rugby Football Union was held on Tuesday, at the Spread Eagle Hotel, in Manchester, under the chairman- ship of Mr. H. H. Waller (Brighouse). The members present were Messrs. J. Nicholl (Halifax), J. Smith (Widnes), W. Carroll (Runcorn), H. Hutchinson (Wake- field Trinity), A. Brewer (Hull), T. Wright (Hunslet),H. Sewell (Leeds). A. Fattorini (Manningham), J.E.Warren (Warrington), E. Gresty (Broughton Rangers), J. Platt (Oldham), F. Dennett (St. Helens). J. Underwood (Wigan), J. M. Mills (Stockport), H. Rowson (Tylesley). The first business before the meeting was the decision of the grounds on which the county matches should be played and the dates on which they should take place. After some discussion it was decided, on the motion of Mr. Smith (Widnes). seconded by Mr. Fattorini (Man- ningham), that the matches Lancashire v. Cheshire and Yorkshire v. Cheshire should be played on off days. It was further decided, on the motion of Mr. Warren (Warrington), who found a seconder in Mr. Platt (Oldham), that the Lancashire v. Cheshire match should be played on the ground of the Broughton Rangers on Wednesday, ' January 29. Mr. Smith (Widnes), then moved, and Mr. Brewer (Hull), seconded, that the Yorkshire v. Cheshire match should be played at Runcorn on February 12. When the ground and date of the Lancashire v. York- shire match came up for settlement an animated discus- sion arose as to the towns in Yorkshire best suited for the fixture. A letter was read from the Huddersfield Club urging that the match should take place on their ground, and the representatives on the Committee of Hull, Manningham, and Halifax also put in claims for their respective grounds. It was generally conceded that the main motive of the Committee in their selection would be the securing of the best possible " gate." A vote by ballot resulted as follows :—Huddersfield ten, Halifax, two, and Hull one. Huddersfield was, therefore, the 'ground selected. Mr. Nicholl (Halifax) moved, and Mr. Warren (Warrington) seconded, that February 29 snoula be the date of this match—Lancashire v. Yorkshire. This was carried unanimously. It was decided that the arrangements for the matches should be left in the hands of the home county in each case. For the Lancashire v. Cheshire match Mr. H. Hutchinson (Wakefield frinity) was appointed referee, and Mr. Smith (Widnes) for the Yorkshire v. Cheshire fixture. Mr. W. Jones (Runcorn) was selected as referee for the Lancashire v. Yorkshire match. The next business before the meeting was the consideration of the conduct of the St. Helens Club in an alleged breach of (competition) rule 22. It ap- peared that the club had played in their team a man named Jacques,who was ineligible under this rule. The St. Helens Club applied to Hull for the transfer of this player but were met with a refusal. Jacques was "white- washed" by the Rugby Union, and under the circum- stances St. Helens argued that he needed no transfer, and they played him against Oldham. The captain of the St. Helens Club was called in and gave an explana- tion of the circumstance,but it proved unsatisfactory to the Committee, and on the motion of Mr. Nicholl, seconded by Mr. Wright, it was decided to penalise the club by deducting two points from its score in the North- ern Union League table, this decision not to apply to its position in the table of the Lancashire section.

NORTHERN RUGBY UNION. WARRINGTON v. LIVERSEDGE.

The Warrington first team fulfilled another •of their Yorkshire engagements on Saturday, when they jour- need to Liversedge to play their first match with the club there. Liversedge is a small town of about 12,000 inhabitant', between Huddersfield and Bradford. It is a colliery b elage, with very little that is attractive either in or about it. To get there in time the Warring- ton team had to leave Warrington at ten o'clock in the morning, goine from Bank Station through Manchester and Huddersfield. The company had provided a saloon carriage for the accernmodation of the team, and not- withstanding the feet that the journey in itself is most uninteresting , the players managed to while away the three and a half hours they were on the way in a inure or legs agreeable fashion. On arrival at Liversedge ,s found that there was a waggonette, to wineo were attaelied three horses, waiting to convey the Learn to the club's head-quarters. A capital start was made, but after the first hundred yards had been travelled, the horses enowed a decided disinclination to proceed furthcr up the hill, and com- menced to "back." This extraordinary procedure on the part of the horses caused no small alarm amongst the occupants of the waggonette, many of them leaving it more hurriedly tnan gracefully. Ultimately the back of the waggonette caught against a good rail fence. which divided two roads, and the vehicle remained there until the horses were induced to go forward. This they commenced to do as suddenly as they had previously stopped and "backed," with the result that several cel the visitors were left to climb a rather steep hill, at the top of which they managed to get into the waggon- ette again. The Liversedge club have heaclq .arters of their own, with dressing rooms, a reading room, and billiard room. The building overlooke the ground,which is a good one and well provided wi;.h stand accoinmeda- Von. As a precaution in case of frost,the ground had been covered with straw. The kick off took place promptly at 2.45,the teams being as follows :—Warring, ton : Heeeom, full bark; Carey,Scott, Cross and Lewle3s„ threequarters • Clark, end Foclen, half-backs ; Nevins, Burrows, Barrett, Andrews, Swift, Wilcock, Fairhurst, and Tnonrton,forwards. Liversedge : Lister, full back ; Fearnlev, Sharp, Jenkinson, and Woinersley, three- quarters; Barker and Wood, half-hacks; Parkin, Hutch- inson, G. Smith, Ford, Sykes, L. Smith, Howard and Priestley, forwards. Of the players selected, Burton at three-quarters and Foden at half were absent from the Warrington team, their places being taken by Scott and O'Brien. Barber, the Warrington captain, was also im able to go with the team, which was captained in his ebsence by Nevins. The home team only underwent one I change, Hutchinson taking the place of Steele in the forwards. The gate was a very small one, rather below the average it was said. If there were a thousand spec- tators on the field that would be all. It was explained that owing to two or three recent defeats, the gates had fallen off. The game' was a very interesting one to watch, bat there was very little about it to describe. In the first half, the visitors had undoubtedly the best of matterseeressing Liversedge time after time.but they were only able to score once, when Hill succeeded in kicking a penelty goal. One or two attempts were made to place goals from free kicks, but they failed. Scott, Cross and Carey were conspicuous for a splendid passing movement, Carey finally trying a drop at goal which failed. He would perhaps have (lane better had he tried to run. The Warrington forwards in this half really played a magnificent game, being points ahead of their opponents, while the backs also played well, very few mistakes being made. Half-time had almost arrived and all were expecting the whistle to blow when Liversedge managed to get the ball well into Warrineton quarters, kicking into teuch near the corner. Following the line out there was a scrimmage, Barber got possession and some passing resulted in VVomersley getting over, the place kick proving abortive. The whistle now blew, leaving the score equal, three points each. In the second half, the home team had a slight advantage. The visit- ing forwards especially towards the close seemed to get " fagged." and Liversedge frequently pressed. War- rington, however, played on very pluckily and right to the last minute it seemed as though the game would enp in a draw. Again when time was almost up,Liversedge got to the Warrington line. There was a scrimmage opposite the goal, and the ball getting loose was kicked by Barker across to Womersley, who managed to rush over nearly at the corner. Sharpe, by a good kick,con- verted the point into a goal. On two or three occasions Warrington had hard lines. A splendid dribble down the field by Lawless,Foden and Scott looked as though it would end in scoring, but Lister saved in time. As the _ _ . _ .

_ result of some smart'. play by Nevins, Lawless shortly afterwards had a clear ran in, when the ball was ruled back on the ground that it had been knocked on. War- rington were by no means overplayed.. Taking the two halves together, the teams were evenly matched, but Liversedge had away otkicking into touch,which saved their forvrards,while Warrington generally kicked down the field, the forwards each time following up,by a con • tinned repetition of this process they got more or less expended towards the close. The game ended in a win for Liversedge by one goal and one try to Warrington a penalty goal.

div.head: WIDNES v. STOCKPORT.
div.p: WIDNES v. STOCKPORT.

At Widnes en Saturday afternoon, before 2,500 persons. The ground was in good condition, but there was a slight wind. Barber started for Widnes, who pressed, and after Peters had got in a good run, Jones scored amid loud applause, The place kick was taken by Johnson but it failed. Stockport then took up the pressure,and a big punt by Saville gave Sands an oppor- tunity, which he utilized, the home defence showing up poorly. Play was fast and exciting, and H. Peters made another good run, and this time was successful, but the place kick was abortive. The home team continued to press, Saville having all his work cut out. Barber did a smart piece of work, but it was ineffective, and Motters- head passing to Sands the latter player secured a good ' try, Saville converting. Roused by this reverse the home 'forwards indulged in a round of smart passing, H. Peters being cheered for breaking away. Barber got the ball and making sure got a try, the place kick failing. Half-time—Stockport, two goals (ten points) ; Widnes, three tries (nine). Mottershead restarted, and for a moment the visitors became dangerous. Nevin, who had gone threequarter, got in a good kick, and Widnes returned the pressure. They literally bombarded the Cestrians' goal, and bad hard lines on several occasions. Finally Widnes secured another try, and Nevitt con- verted. There was no more scoring, the result being, Widnes one goal, three tries (14 points) ; Stockport, two goals (ten points).

div.head: RUNCORN v. BRADFORD.
div.p: RUNCORN v. BRADFORD.

Runcorn were sadly handicapped on Saturday in hav- ing to face the powerful Bradford team with an attenu- ated team, for added to those already injured, Warder, Walker, Reece, and Williams were unable to make the journey, and little hopes were expected in Runcorn that the team doing duty would be able to bring back a couple of points. There were several alterations on the Bradford side. Pollard, Toothill,and W. Sugden did not turn out, their places being taken by Barstow,Robinson, and Ramsden,whilst on the Runcorn side West, Stutbs, and Darlington played. There was as usual, whenever the Cestrians visit that historic ground,a big crowd,some 8,000 people lining the en3lesure when the teams en- tered the arena. Sugden commenced the game for Bradford, play settling near the half way. A combined dribble by the Bradfordians transferred play to Runcorn quarters. The visitors came away beautifully, in which the twis Faulkners were prominent,and put Bradford on the defensive. A kick by Cooper relieved to the centre. Robertson, Firth, Sugden, with the ball at their toes, made a bold bid for the visitors' line, but Butterworth repulsed their efforts. Bradford quickly renewed the pressure, Bairstow, Dobson, and Cooper playing splen- didly together. The visitors by spirited play took opera- tions into the home territory, where Faulkner had a fetile shot at goal from a free catch. Runcorn played a remarkably good game, which kept Bradford on the de- fence, though they failed to score anything tangible up to half time. On re-starting the visitors had their work set in keeping Bradford from scoring, but they offered a stubborn defence, Butterworth proving very safe as a custodian. Still Bradford were having all the best of the argument until Wood commenced a bit of passing,which pinned the home team on their line. Robertson, Firth, and Bairtow relieved, and midfield was the scene of fast and open play. A line piece of footwork, headed by Robertson. once more put Bradford on the attack, but Myers,Faulkner, and Butterworth cleared in remarkable style,and prevented a score,the game ending in a draw, nothing having been scored.

div.head: SINGULAR NULLITY OF MARRIAGE
div.p: SINGULAR NULLITY OF MARRIAGE
CASE. ENOCH ARDEN UP TO DATE.

A singular nullity ef marriage case came before Mr. Justice dames on Tuesday. The petitioner, Mr. Wilkins, went through a ceremony of marriage with the respon- dent in 1865 at Plymouth. She had been previously married to George Rickard, and it was taken for granted that he was dead. Some time ago she petitioned for judicial separation, and, on the question then being raised, the jury found that her first husband, Mr. George Rickard, was dead. Since then, however, Mr. Rickard has reappeared, after living for thirty-five years in America. Wilkins, therefore, sought to have his marri- age with the respondent declared null and void.—Mr. Inderwick, Q.C., wno appeared for the petitioner, said that Rickard nad been examined by an order of the Court, and was now ready to give evidence.—Mr. Jus- tice Barnes After the verdict of the jury, I suppose WO respondent's counsel will contend that I am bound to find that he is dead, although he is now here in court? —(Laughter,)—Mr. Bayford, Q.C. : that is so.—Mr. Inderwick said he had been looking for a precedent in regard to this matter, and had come across one. There was the case of Sir Charks Napier, who was reported to have been killed at the battle of Corunna. His family proceeied to prove his will, and distributed his estate. Sir Charles afterwards came to this country, and made a personal application that he might have the probate of his own will revoked. (Laughter.)—Mr. George Rickard was then called. From his depositions it appeared that he was a carpenter, and had lived in America for thirty-five years. He was born at Devon- port. In 1854 he married the respondent at Plymouth. Afterwards he lived with her at Tor Point. In 1857 he sailed in the Indus to the West Indies, and afterwards wont to the United States, returning to this country in 1858. He landed at Bristol, and wrote to his wife, she staving with him for one day. He then returned to the United States, she refusing to accompany him—Mr. Bayford said that the respondent did not recognise Rickard as her former husband, but she was not pre- pared to deny on oath that he was the man.—A number of Rickard's relatives were then called,and gave evidence as to his identity.—Mr. Inderwick : If your Lordship is satisfied as to the identity of the man,it is clear that a mistake occurred at the former trial, although possibly the verdict was right on the evidenc,, as it then stood.— Mr. Justice Barnes : How can I get over the decree of the court and the verdict of the jury ? Is not the pro- per course for you to move for a new trial in the Court of Appeal P—l have no doubt as to these people being married, but the question of estoppel is a serious one. The fact not being in dispute,it seems a pity that coun- sel cannot meet each other in some way so as to reduce the eypenso of going to the Court of Appeal.—Eventually his Lordship said he would adjourn the case until he heard what course had been adopted.

div.head: WHIT REALLY HAPPENED.
div.p: WHIT REALLY HAPPENED.

The stomach is too often blamed for the inability of the system to assimilate nourishment. For instance, Dyspepsia is frequently one of the ill effects of Congump. tion. So are night sweats ; but it is poor logic to sup- pose that by treating night sweats you can cure Con- sumption. People are often prone to think that, if they lose flesh or show other signs of failing health, their stomachs are out of order.

It would be well if we could trace disease to the stomach, and treat that organ, for this would resolve the practice of medicine down to a very simple basis. But we must look further than the stornach for the cause of imperfect nutrition. We must look to the blood, the means of carrying nourishment to all parts of the body. The blood must be supplied with substances that make flesh and increase our vital force. This is the secret of curing Consumption, Scrofula, Anemia, Rickets,Maras- mus, and other wasting diseases.

I know of quite a remarkable ease of a British subject living in South Africa. whose friends thought he was going to be a victim o! Consumption. I had a letter from him which he says you can read : "ST. GEORGE'S HOTEL, CAPE Tows,

"Messrs. FCOTT & BOWER, Ltd., London. "DEAR SlRS,—Three years ago I went into the interior of Africa. I was then in perfect health, weighing nearly thirteen stone. While there I caught a fever which hung about me for many months. After about four months of this fever I began to feel pains in my lungs. I did not pay very much attention to these pains at first,until they grew more trcublesome and I began to cough. My coughing became intense ;it wrenched and .trained my lungs, and soon I was raising quantities of blood. The pains in my lungs continued to grow worse, and I became so emaciated in weight that my friends thought I could not possibly live. "In February last, when I was in Smithfield, in the Orange Free State, a friend advised me to try Scott's Emulsion. He said he believed it would do me a great deal of good. I had beard of the Emulsion in England, and to think of getting it down here in Africa was, in- deed, like greeting an old friend. When one is far from the land of his birth, early associations are,indeed,raore tender than they are at home.

"I began to take the Emulsion as directed, and felt relief at once. My cough became easier from the outset. I did not wrench and strain as I had been doing, and it did rot hurt my lungs so much, and I found also that the pain in my lungs was relieved. I could not believe that any remedy would have such quick and satcsfactory results. I kept raising less and less quantities of blood, until I did not raise any at all, and at the same time I began to feel stronger and better in every way. I rested more quietly at night, and steadily gained in weight. It seems most extraordinary, but nevertheless it is a fact that during February. March, and April, the time that I took your Emulsion, I gained three stone in weight and completely recovered my health. I am now as well as I ever was, thanks to your excellent Emulsion and I cannot say too much in its favour. Everybody who suffers with affections of the lungs, as I did, knows what the coughing and raising of blood means. In Scott's Emulsion I found ft relief that I did not think .z should ever have,a.nd the very fact of my having regained my strength and health by taking Scott's Emulsion con- vinced ms that it is a wonderful remedy for Consumption and all of its kindred ailments.
"Thanking you most cordially for the good Scott's Emulsion has done me, and hoping others will profit by my experience,
"I remain, Yours very truly, "GEORGE REINHARD."

No better proof of the nourishing powers of Scott's Emulsion could be offered thin is given in Mr. Reinhard's letter. He has described his case much better than I could,and 1 commend his letter to your consideration. (4)

div.head: OPPORTUNITIES FOR ENGINEERS IN
div.p: OPPORTUNITIES FOR ENGINEERS IN
JAPAN

The new number of the quarte r "Japanese Journal" contains a letter from the special correspondent of that paper in Japan, in which he says :—" It is perhaps not to much to say that for engineers of almost every class, no country at the present time offers such opportunities as Japan. Especially does this apply to manufacturers of railway materials, bridges, and structural ironwork generally, textile machinery of every kind, engines of all types, machine tools of every description, and machinery for practically every kind of industry." "I have received," he adds, "information of numerous pro- jects which are to be carried out here, some of them immediately, and all of them within a. comparatively short space of time. These include .quite a number of new railways or extensions to existing ones. Many of them are of short distances, varying from ten to fifty miles, while one or two will be nearly one hundred miles in length." The same correspondent observes that an important feature for manufacturers of machiners in- tended for Japan to consider is the stature of the Japanese. The average height of Japanese being less that that of home operative.s, it is sometinses found that machinery made on the same model as that in use i,r.l England is somewhat difficult for the Japanese to mani- pulate.

TRAP ACCIDENT AT NEWTON. On Monday afternoon Mr and Mrs. J. Cald Golborne, had a miraculous escape from serious ac- cident when driving through Newton. It appears they were proceeding to Earlestown to attend the i funeral of the late Mr. IL Walton, n a conveyance owned and driven by Mr. Dalton, of Golborne, and when going along High-st., Newton, one of the wheels came off, and the trap swerving the other wheel came in contact with one of the tree protec- tions on the side of the road. The horse became alarmed, and breaking the traces it dashed away at full speed along Ashton-lane, but was fortunately stopped without injury. The occupants of the trap were pitched out, but besides being shaken, they suffered little injury.

div.head: RETIREMENT OF A WARRINGTON
div.p: RETIREMENT OF A WARRINGTON
STATION MASTER.

-- Mr. W. H. Rigbey.stationinaster at the Central Statim (Cheshire Lines), Warrington, is about to retire from that position. Mr. Rigbey has served the long term of forty-five years on different railways, thirty of which have been under the Cheshire Lines Committee. His first appointment was stationmaster at Kington, the terminus of the Leominster and Kington Railway, a portion of the Shrewsbury and Hereford Railways, a line which gave the late Sir George Finlay, of the London and North-Western Railway, his first appointment as a railway manager. Subsequently. Mr. Rigbey became a goods manager at Welshpool on the ' Cambrian Railway, under the late Sir Georg 3 Finlay. Before coming to Warrington, Mr. Rigbey held the im- portant position of cashier and accountant at the Bruns- wick Goods Department when the Cheshire Lines was comparatively in its infancy, and when passengers were conveyed in omnibuses between the Brunswick Dock Station and the central offices of the company, which were then in Alexandra Buildings, James-st., and when the late Mr. William English was manager of the com- pany. The Cheshire Lines Railway had at that time only a line of their own between Bruns- wick Dock and Garston, from which latter station they had running powers over the London and North Weston low level system through Arpley Station, Warrington, on to Broadheath, whence via Cheadle and Baguley they extended to Stockport. Mr. Rigbey's connection withlWarrington commenced with the opening of the Cheshire Lines Railway at Warring- ton, for he was appointed stationmaster when the Central Station was opened. The line was opened at Warrington for goods traffic in June, 1873, and for passenger traffic between Liverpool and Manchester in July, 1873,since whieh air. Rigbey had held the appoint- ment. He now retires on superannuation.

div.head: 3IARRIAGE OF MR. JAMES STRANGE
div.p: 3IARRIAGE OF MR. JAMES STRANGE
AND MISS ARNOLD.

Stockton Heath was all en fete on Thursday,week on the occasion of the marriage of Mr..lames Strange, Latchford, to Miss Gertude Arnold, second daugh- ter of Mr. William Arnold, of Stockton Heath. A long time before the ceremony took place, the chapel at Hill Cliffe was crowded with friends and well-wishers of the bride and bridegroom. The officiating minister was the Rev. J. S. Hughes. The bride looked exceedingly well, being attired in a pale creme oatmeal dress trimmed with merveilleux silk and Brussolls lace, and white velvet hat with ostrich feathers. She also carried a bouquet com- posed of lilies of the valley, and camellias, and wore a diamond brooch, the gift of the bridegroom. The bridesmaids were four in number, Miss Annie Arnold and Miss Martha Strange being dressed in pink crepon and white hats with ostrich feathers, and Miss Evelyn Arnold and Miss Edith Strange, who were at- tired in biscuit Bengaline cloth, trimmed with primrose. Upon the entrance of the wedding party, the choir Eang the hymm, " The voice that breathed o'er Eden," and at the close, Mr. Peter Harrison played Mendelssohn's Wedding March. After the completion of the ceremony the party proceeded to the Co-operative Hall,Sankey-st., Warrington, where a sumptuous repast was partaken of. After the healths of the Queen,the bride and bride- groom, the host and hostess, had been drunk, the rest of the evening was spent in songs, games, etc., which were continued until an early hour in the morning. The presents were very numerous and valuable, and included the following :—Bedrootn suit and kitchen furniture, Mr. and Mrs. James Strange,Summerhill ; tea service, Miss Fenn; Strange ; eider down quilt, Mr. John Strange ; table cloth, Masters James and Percy Strange; /Air of decanters,Mr. William Strange ; Yankee rocking chair, Mr. and Mrs. A. Richardson ; set of carvers, Mr. Harry Richardson ; silver biscuit barrel,Miss Richardson; handsome marble clock, Mr. F. R. and E. Whitlow, High Legh ; pair of blankets, Mrs. Whitlow ; set ef carvers, Miss Whitlow ; coalbox, Mr. B. Whitlow ; pair of orna- ments and copper kettle, Mr. T. Rigby ; cheese dish,Mr. Harry Hartley; set of jugs, Mr. J. Unsworth ; brass fire irons, Mr. W. Whittle ; linen, Mrs. Arnold ; cushion, Miss A. Arnold ; tea cosy, Mrs.Houghton ; cheese dish, Mrs. E. 1/41low ; chenille table cloth, Mr. William Arnold; table cloth, Miss Lily Wilding and Miss Hobson; two dozen knives and forks, Mrs. Breakall, Liverpool; dinner cruet, Mr. and Mrs. Dodd; silver teapot, Mr. J. and Mr. B. Bradford; pair of ornamental jugs, Mr. Bradford; set of jugs, Mr. W. Bradford ; trinket set, Mr. Critchley; water bottle, three glasses of preserve dishes, and towels, Mr. and Mrs. Ashley: set of curtains, Mr. and Mrs. J. Monks; trinket set and six tumblers, Mr. J. Monks and Miss Ashley ; cushion, Mr. A. Ashley; gipsy table and stools, Miss M. and Miss E. GENIUS IN GLASS.

A ramble through the Patent Offices of the world assures one of the genius man has for inventing things. So numerous are his devices in this direction that to at- tempt to chronicle them all would be a labour of Hercu- lean proportious, and we shall therefore confine our re- marks to some ingenius and novel contrivances in which glass plays thectnef part. Among these is a glass coffin, which is guaranteed proof against decay and rats. Sp long as no deliberate attempt is made to smash it, it ought to last for ever. Another contrivance is a stair- case made wholly of glass, steps, landings and newel post being all of that material. Yet another is a glass barrel. But, perhaps,the most remarkable invention of the glass man is a billiard table of glass. The day may yet arrive when people will live in glass houses. A patent has been secured by another inventor for glass bricks of a peculiar pattern. The material of which they are composed being a first rate non-conduc- tor, these bricks will keep the cold out of a dwelling built of them, while admitting the light. It is claimed they will exclude noise,being hollow. Furthermore,the inmates of a glass house need not be afraid of being ander too close observation by neighbours, inasmuch as it is not requisite that the bricks shall be transparent. They may be of opaque ground glass or of any colour that may be suitable tor decorative effect. Thus,before many years have passed,it may be considered the height of luxury to occupy a dwelling of glass. Glass bricks, of course,are expensive. People who live in glass houses will be able to afford to wear clothes of glass. That sounds like nonsense,but the fact is that beautiful and most delicate fabrics are made out of spun glass. Nearly twenty years ago there was shown at a foreign exhibi- tion a bonnet composed entirely of glass. The flowers on it were glass, and so were the ribbons, which looked like the finest satin. The patentee of this process de- scribes it as suitable for the manufucture of neckties, shawls, table covers, Sze. In fabrics of this kind very fine quality of glass is used. It is spun in threads of ex- ceeding delicacy, and of these several colours may be produced at the same time. They are woven in a loom of ordinary pattern. Anybody may observe that a thin sheet of glass is somewhat elastic. The threads em- ployed in weaving are of such fineness as to be perfectly pliable and not at all brittle. With a gown of glass would naturally go a pair of glass slippers. One genius has invented a process for making glass slippers in moulds. They would do very well for danc-1 jug. There is no reason why a glass gown should not be woven of irridescent glass so that the wearer would look like an animated rainbow on a ball room floor—one] dazzling shimmer of ever-changing hues. Until recently , the manufacture of irridescent glass was set down in the list of the lost arts. But in 1878 it was re-discovered. ' and now it is a common commercial article. it is made by exposing the melted glass to the vapours of salts of sodium. Great numbers of bottles, plates and other articles of glass which were made and used long before the Christian era have been dug up in Cyprus and else- where. Many of them have a beautiful irridescence,bu it is the result of decay. Glass will rot like anything thins else, and decay has split the structure ot this ancient glass into laminre, or flakes, which interrupt the light so as toproduce brilliant red, green, purple, and other rainbow colours. The window blinds ot the glass house of the future will be glass, of course. That is another patent, and the inventor suggests that such blinds may be made of whatever colours are desired. Baby in the nursery,perhaps, will play with glass build- ing bricks and at a suitable age he will receive a Christ- mastgift of a pair of roller skates with glass rollers. Both of these ideas have been patented. When he is old enough to go fishing, he will not dig worms in the gar- den, but will be provided with artificial bait in the shape of a hollow minnow of glass, coated on the inside partly with a solution of gold or silver and partly with a luminous paint. Glass bedsteads may be proof against lightning and insects, but it is hardly to be ex- pected that glass houses should be free from mice. The inmates could hardly do better than employ glass traps for the capture of such vermin. The great advantage of the glass mousetrap,according to the statement of the inventor, is that " if one mouse enters the trap he may be seen by others who chance to go that way, and they will be ieclined to join the one inside, especially when they observe that he is nibbling a choice morsel." Up to date the glass mousetrap has not made itself popular, notwithstanding the important arguments in its favour, and of most of the other devices described it is unfortu- nately true that they have not proved profitable to the person who contrived them. This remark, huwever, by no means applies to the glass lemon-squeezer, which is already a familiar how.ehold utensil. The inventor of it is said to have sold his rights for £lO,OOO. One of the most remarkable inventions in glass, by the way,was that of a Venetian named Joquin, in 1656. He noticed that the scaler of a fish called the tolea.k gave a milky hue to the water,and that glass beads dipped into such water looked like pearls when dry. Subsequently the idea was conceived of making hollow beads of glass and lining them with the peculiar substance froen the scales of the fish, and it is in this way that the so-called Rom4n rearis are now manufactured. It is to this sub- stance that the irridescence of ther scales of many specie of fishes is due.—" Seience Siftings."
Charles Cox, manager of a working man's club. a Higham Ferrers, was on Monday fined in sums amou t- in g in all to £B5 for having on tour occasions sold drink without a license.

div.head: MARRIAGE OF MRS. VANDERBILT.
div.p: MARRIAGE OF MRS. VANDERBILT.

Mrs. Alva Vanderbilt, fermerly the wife of Mr. William K. Vanderuilt (from whem she obtained a di- vorce a little more than a year ago), and mother of the young Duchess of Marlborough, was married in New York on Saturday to Mr. Oliver Belmont, the brother of the banker,who was instrumental in placing upon the market the last United States Government loan. The marriage was a civil one,the ceremony being performed at the private residence of the bride by Mr. Strong, Mayor of New York.
The fourteen millions of silk hats manufactured in the United Kingdom last year are calculated to have been worth nearly four millions pounds.
THE EXAMINER, SA110111) XY, JANITARY 18, 1896.
