div.p: Letter 0 to the etlitor.
PROPOSED CRICKET LEAGUE.

Sir,—As the cricket season is now fast approaching, I think it is quite time something definite was done with regard to forming a "Cricket Lague" ih the town. I believe the wish is pretty general that such a league should be formed, and lam sure it would greatly en- courage local clubs, especially if the senior club could be persuaded to take the matter in hand. Will some club secretary call a meeting of local secretaries and then we shall soon arrive at the feeling of the local clubs in res- pect to the movement.—Yours truly, A LOCAL SECRETARY. Warrington, January 14th, 1896.

ANOTHER REPLY TO MR. PEERS. Sir,—Just a word,and my last, about Mr. John Peers' "Tale of the tub." My friend suspects my sex. He seems perplexed, .for visions of feminine beauty float before his perturoed mertal optics. The new woman upsets his balance—an improper female, as his friend Carlyle would say—so excites him. Grant Allen,'Thomas Hardy, and" The woman who did" xere enough to ap- pal any with poor nerves—with their cyclist gambols, their bloomer costumes, their divided skirts, and their other absurdities and abnormll Niagara shootings—and after ! No my friend John, I don't want to picture the new woman in your scientific pabulums and environ- ment. 'Tis a spectacle for the gods! But the young men shall see visions,and the old men shall dream dreams and you and I shall ask for the old paths, and walk accordingly ! Pardon my getting, into Exodus before we had done with Genesis. Therefore let me say with re- gard to your dictum anent the Bible saying not a word about slavery—Jesus Christ says, " Our Father" is the common Parent of all, and the Fatherhood of God is the doctrine of the Bible. " All ye are brethren " is the cardinal thought (or at least one of them) of the New Testament. None are s,) blind as those who will not see ! Further and once more I ask Confucius, or Christ ? I say Christ ? The Christ of the Ages, the Anointed, the Christ of God ! I cannot argue about your negatives, your ifs and buts. I shall meet you ere long at Phillipi. —and just you think of Huxley's words in " Contem- porary Review," December 1870, pp. 14, 15. "By the study of what other book could children be so much humanised and made to feel that each figure in that vast historical procession fills, like themselves, but a momen- tary space in the interval between two eternities." I note with pleasure Mr. John Peers' sober and sedate language, and thank him for it. —Yours respectfully, AMOS WRITE. January 10th, 1896.

div.head: MR. JOHN PEERS AND HIS BIBLICAL CRIIICISAI.
div.p: MR. JOHN PEERS AND HIS BIBLICAL CRIIICISAI.

Sir,—Ycur fluent but inaccurate correspondent, Mr. Peers, devotes much time and energy to sneering at the superstitions and denouncing the errors of Christians. His reproofs would carry weight if he himself were con- sistent and trustworthy ; but when one who poses as a champion of truth and reason is so often incorrect and illogical, Christians may be excused if they ignore his attacks. In your last Issue he asserts that the title Christ " is the outcome of Greek mysticism and genius for fabling" and gives`wbat he appears to regard as its Greek equiva- lent,Kristos. The Greek equivalent is of course Coristos, but the sublime self-confidence which enables Mr. Peers to correct (?) the received spelling is equally evident in bis statement about Greek mysticism. Messiah, Christ, Anointel,.are three forms of the same title ; and nothing can be more certain than that the idea of a Christ or Anointed one, far from being " the outcome of Greek mysticism" is an essentially Jewish conception. The earliest .traces of it occur in the writings of the great prophets of the Bth century B.C. where the Messiah is foreshadowed as a royal and military leader; towards the close of the Exile the idea of a suffering Messiah,who should be a religious teacher and leader, was embodied in the writings of the Babylonian Isaiah; and in varying degrees one or both of these conceptions influenced the later development of the Messianic idea. Mr. Peers' further on, asserts that " Calvinism is the most logical and Biblical form of sectarian Christianity," a statement whose truth or falsehood depends on the meanings attached to "Calvinism " and " sectarian Christianity." I shall be glad if Mr. Peers can find time to define these terms and to set forth the evidence on which his assertion is based. To me, Calvinism has always seemed a distortion of Christianity. Between the two Johns Calvin and Peers, there is much in common. Except that one defended a particular set of dogmas which the other as uncompromisingly attacks, there is little difference between them. In both we find the hon- est bigotry of zealous ignorance conspicuously displayed and both show the same irrational contempt for all who presume to differ from them. If Mr. Peers would dlvote a little of his leisure to the etudy of the origins of Christianity, and strive to ascer- tain what its Founder really taught, he would, I appre- bend, soon see the folly of writing of its " dour and immoral reality."—Yours truly,
LAYMAN.

R. JOHN PEERS AND "A TALE OF A TUB.' Sir, —I have read, in your issue of the 4th inn, a letter over the name of John Pcers,with the peculiar heading, " A Tale of a Tub.' After readin,„.. it twiee I have come to the conclusion that the " tub " mentioned is a mysterious one, and is, without doubt, two-handed. I may also add that the quantity it holds is,conaparatively speaking, a little and yet a lot. Before going further, will you allow me to say that I have not the honour of knowing Mr. John Peers; and, further, I don't wish, in any way, to attack his name. My only reason for writing is, seeing that I am not "steeped to the lips in religious subjects," to learn from him what I am sure he will most readily give, I mean, information. In doing so he will greatly benefit.not only myself, but others who arc desirous of learning more on such a serious subject. To make myself clear in the matter I must refer, and quote, from his last letter in the" Examieer." He says "No such person as • Jesus Christ ' ever lived upon this earth." Is this true? Have we been deceived so long? Is the Bible after all a nursery story ? written like a large number of the present day Fairy stories ' with a one special aim,and that,for a pecuniary benefit. If so, what a myth the Bible is. But wait a moment. What proof has Mr. John Peers for this assertion ? Further, "Jesus of Nazareth was a Jew, and most certainly (the italics are mine) would not have answered to the Greek appellaticn." Not quite so quick, Mr. Peers. I must, certainly, add a query to that remark. Seeing that I was not living at the time I must, like my friend, refer to what other writers have said ,and I find,in doing so, that the word Jesus is the Latin form of the Greek _resoles, a name which corresponds to the Hebrew Yehoshu'a, contracted to Yeshu'a, or Joshua. meaning "help to Jehovah." It was, I understand, a common name among the Jews, and in its Hebrew and Greek forms it occurs several times in both Testaments. The word Christ was originally a title meaning in the Greek "anointed," but in the New Testament It is used as equivalent to the Hebrew term " Messiah," the pre- eminently anointed one,the long-expected'deliverer of the nation. In the gospels,where it occurs about forty times, it is usually given as a title, "the Christ " ; but in other parts of the New Testament, where it occurs over 200 times, we find it is generally used as a proper name,and this usage has ever since been retained. I dare not tread further at present, as I feel that I have already trespassed, but I do hope that Mr. John Peers will answer my letter candidly,—l know he will not sneer at it—seeing that I am young and quite willing to hear both sides of the question—and fight the battle fairly. The odds, certainly, are sadly against my arguing with effect, against Mr. John Peers. Ido not write purposely for argument,—for mere sake of sound —but truth after all, sh-add conquer, and, I trust, that the time is nigh when yeung men will be privileged to speak out and feel not afraid.—Yours truly, VIVIAN GREY.

MR. JOIN PEERS AND HIS METtIODS. Sir,—Your correspondent, "Amos White," need not consider himself taken aback by the effrontery of Mr. John Peers. It is the common style of this profuse scribbler when he has nothing in the shape of argument to offer to revile those whose reasonings he is unable to meet. It would at times seem as if he were conscious of the miserable cause he has espoused, and to make up for its want of weight or character, to assail with fanatical virulence those who may happen to differ from him. This feature of his- style has been often remarked in past discussions. But of late the public seems to have got wearied of his utterances ; and the silent con- tempt with which he has been treated so long appears to have touched him so keenly that he is determined to play the clown, a",l make the folk grin—as "Amos White" very aptly puts it—if he cannot, at least, con- vince them.

It is the old trick from the time of the pagan Lucre- tius to the volatile French buffoon of the last century, and from Tom Pain down to Robert Inc,rolsby and John Peers. This latter personage would do well however to consider whether reckless assumptions,blind prejudibes, and crass ignorance, zuch as many of his letters display are at all likely to effect the purpose—whatever that may be—which he may have in view. What can we think of a man, who, if he knows aught of the results of the great missionary movements of the century now near its close, can only compare the work itself to "carrying religious frying pans and blankets to Timbuctoo ?" Is either his intelligence cr capacity of judgment worth more than what we might find among the natives of that dark region? Re knows, or at least

BABIES ON FIRE, BABIES BURNING UP, with itch- ing and burning eczemas, and other torturing, disfigur- ing skin anp scalp diseases. Nne but mothers realise how these little ones suffer when their tender skins are literally on fire. To known that a warm bath with CUTI- CUBA SOAP and a single application of CUTICURA (oint- ment), the great skin cure, will in the majority of cases afford instant relief, permit rest and sleep and point to a speedy cure, and not to use them without a moment's delay is to fail in our duty. Think of the years of suffer- ing entailed by such neglect, years not only of physical but of mental suffering by reason of personal disfigure- ment, added to a bodily torture. Cures made in infancy #34 Childhood are speedy, permanent, and economical.

assumes to know something about China —he has heard of the great Confucian maxim "do unto others as you would they should do to you ; " and one would imagine that this is all he ever did hear, for he seems to know nothing of the work of Morrison, of Milne, of Medhurst, and a whole band of Christian men and pioneers, of whom even Charles Darwin and men of his class have spoken in terms of .unbounded admiration, but of whom and all such your Penketh luminary can only describe as haying gone on an errand of "teaching your grand- mother to suck eggs ! " I need not refer to the great moral transformation affected in the South Sea Islands, in great parts of Africa, India, and other vast.portions of the glote by the missionary labours of this 19th century, and by means of that very gospel of Christ, which an ignorant sceptic seems at a loss to find words to vilify. Enough however of this subject. I have only time for a word of reference to another item of Mr. Peer's contri- butions to your epistolary columns. He would fain pose as a Biblical critic. I wonder that he has no conception of the grotesqueness of his assumption. Let me tell him plainly that he has about as much of acquirements or faculty for such a role, as a native of Timbuctoo. A man who can talk of Jesus Christ as a mere myth, and could affirm seriously that no such person as He ever lived on this earth, is a fitting subject for the nearest lunatic asylum. When he talks of myths I wonder if he knows what a myth is, and what are the conditions under which a myth may be assumed. He has perhaps heard the phrase" mythical theory "and does not seem to be aware that it is one of the exploded follies of a foolish school dating back to the earlier years of this century. It will perhaps be information for him that sceptical writers eyen,with any regard for their position and credit have abandoned the absurd and untenable theory of a mythical Christ, and are only too ready now to seek other and saner justification for their scepticism. Mr. Peers would do well to make himself better acquainted with the subjects he presumes to write upon. It is clear that he knows little or nothing of t he evidences of Christianity, and has no practical acquaintance with New Testament truths.llHe is utterly incompetent to talk about such themes and he would do better to look ahead when haply he may discover the forces in the Gospel of Christ which are destined to sweep his, and every other "refuge of lies "to deserved oblivion.—Yours truly, ZAMIN ER. 9, January, 1896.

div.head: PRESENTATION TO COUNCILLOR WILLIAM PIERPOD.TT,
div.p: PRESENTATION TO COUN- CILLOR WILLIAM PIERPOD.TT,
MEETING AT THE LIBERAL CLUB.

As we announced last week, the Liberals of Warrington have subscribed for a handsome testi- monial for presentation to Councillor William Pier- point, J.P., the chairman of the Liberal Executive, in recognition of his long and unwavering support of the cause of progress in Warrington and the dis- trict. The presentation consisted of a sterling silver tea and coffee service and massive silver salver. The inscription on the salver runs as follows :—" Pre- sented with other pieces of plate to William Pier- point, Esq., J.P., Chairman of th e Executive Com- mittee, by the members of the Warrington Liberal Association, in grateful recognition of his long and invaluable services to the cause of progress in this town and neighbourhood. December, 1895." On Wednesday evening,the testimonial was presented to Councillor Pierpoint at a meeting at the Liberal Club, and previous to the meeting a tea was partaken of in the newsroom of the club, at which a large number sat down. The catering was in the capable hands of Mr. Mitchell, the manager. At the subsequent proceedings the chair was occupied by Mr. T. Morris,F.Ci.S., and he was supported by a large number of the leading Libe- rals of the town.

div.head: LETTERS OF APOLOGY.
div.p: LETTERS OF APOLOGY.

The toast to the Queen was duly honoured ,after which Councillor Roberts read the letters and telegrams from those who were unable to be present. He said that in the first place Mr. John Rylands, the President of the Association, whose delicate state of health, and whose age prevented his being present there that night,sent his heartiest and kindest greetings and joined with them in good wishes to the Chairman of the Executive. He was with them in spirit,if he was not personally. Dr.Gornall was unable to be present, as also were Councillor Dun- can, who unfortunately was not well, and Mr. Din- widdie. _ _ _

Mr. ROBERTS then read the following telegram from Mr. Scott's sister :—" H. Roberts, Esq., Arplev-street, Warrington. You will, I know, regret to hear that my brother, who was just recovering from his attack of pleurisy caught cold on his return from Blackpool,where he went for change of air, and has for the past ten days been laid up with a severe attack of bronchitis. He wishes me to say how much he regrets he will be unable to be present at the presentation to Mr. William Pierpoint to-night. He is unable to write Mr. Pierpoint himself, but he wishes me to ask you to convey to him his warmest regards, together with the hope that he may long be spared to occupy the position he has so ably filled for many years past to the Liberal party in Warrington. Kindest regaris to all from Mr. Scott, Mrs. Brown." (Applause.) Mr. Scott had also sent the following telegram to Mr. Pierpoint " William Pierpoint, Esq., J.P., Liberal Club,—l deeply regret, owing to illness being unable to join. otheesin doing hon- our to you to-night. I am sure I am expressing the sentiments of all Liberals in Warrington, and my own, when I say that to-night's presentation is only a very small token of the high regard and esteem which they, like myself feel for you. I trust that for many years you may be spared in health, strength and prosperity to guide the helm of Liberalism in the borough of Warring- ton. Accept my warmest regards, sincerely yours, PERCIVAL B. Scow." (Applause.) Before proceeding any further, Councillor ROBERTS said that he proposed that the following telegram be sent to Mr. Scott in reply : " Warrington Liberals assembled to honour Pierpoint, thank you for kind message, and wish you speedy recovery." This was carried with acclamation. Councillor ROBERTS then read the following letter from Mr. Ziba Armitage, J.P.—" Dear Mr. Roberts,—l regret that I am quite unable to be present at the presentation to Mr. Pierpoint on Wednesday evening, having been confined to the house for the past fortnight. Hoping that you may have a pleasant gathering in acknowledg- ment of the services which Mr. Pierpoint has so ably rendered to the Liberal party, I. am, yours truly, ZIBA ARMITAGE." Mr. Edwin J.Guest J.P. ,wrote :—"Dear Mr.Roberts,— In consequence of a previous engagement,' regret that I shall be unable to be present at the tea on Wednesday. I should have been very glad to join with you in doing honour to our tried friend and champion, William Pier- point. I trust that the presentation to be made to him on Wednesday, will inspire him with fresh enthusiam for the cause that at the moment is thrust aside by forces tending to support monopolies and to resist the progress of society. Mr. Pierpoint has proved himself a valiant leader of the Liberal party in Warrington in a time of depressing defeat. I trust that his reward will not end in having the confidence of friends merely, but that it will be consummated in the rout of the enemy. (Ap- plause.) With hest wishes for the success of your gathering on Wednesday." Mr. FBANY A. ROBERTS wrote: "Dear sir,—l much regret that it will be impossible to be present next 'Wed- nesday evening at the • presentation to Mr. Pierpoint, much as I should have liked to have been. He well de- serves the warmest thanks of the Liberal party in the borough, and I sincerely trust that his efforts for its suc- cess may soon be rewarded in the way that he would appreciate most, by changing the parliamentary repre- sentation. Such a triumph as the November elections certainly points that this is well within the power of the party if united and vigorous." (Hear, hear and ap- plause.) Mr. ARTHUR BROWNE wrote: " Dear sir,—l am much obliged for your invitation to be present at tlee Liberal club this evening, on the occasion of the presentation to Mr. William Pierpoint. lam sorry,however,to say that I cannot be present owing to an engagement I have in the theatrical world at Nantwich Town Hall, but I hope you will have a pleasant evening, and that Mr. Pierpoint will accept the gift in the spirit in which it was meant. Kindly excuse my absence to Mr. Pierpoint." (Ap- plause.) Mr. SAMUEL DUNBOBBIN sent the following letter: " Sir, I regret that cannot be present, to partake of tea with you to-morrow night, as I am engaged at the Druids' Hall up to 10.30 p.m. I hope you may have a pleasant evening and that Mr. Pierpoint will live many years to enjoy his testimonial." (Applause.) The CHAIRMAN said that they had met that night to do honour to one to whom honour was due—(hear, hear)—and he thought that the honour they were put- ting upon their friend Mr. Pierpoint that night was what they owed to him. (Applause.) There was not very much question that at one time in the history of the Liberal party in Warrington, only a few years back, if Mr. Pierpoint had not come to the rescue, in being not only treasurer but chairman of the Association they would have "been in a hole." He was one of those who held to the patty at a time of gloom. (Flear,hear.) That night, he was reminded very strongly of the time when they had supporting the cause of Liberalism Gordon McMinnies, and Samuel Rigby, men who almost worked themselves to death in the cause. To-day, they had passed out of those gloomy times, but Mr. Pierpoint had during that time been ever ready with his money and his time. (Applause.) He was sure that all of them were pleased to give that moment° to Mr. Pierpoint. (Applause.) And he was glad that they had not to ask anybody twice to give once. (Applause. )Those who could not afford it were not asked—they only asked those who could afford it and those were only too willing to sub- scribe. (Applause.) The present would be welcome to Mr. Pierpoint as it was an expression of the kindly feel- ings felt towards him by the members of the party. He would ask them all to drink his health.
This was done with musical honours, the member of the meeting singing "For he's a jolly good feliovr."
The death is announced from Killarney of Sir Maurice O'Connell, Bart., a nephew of the Liberator.

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, JANUARY 18, 1896.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, JANUARY 18, 1896.
EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
VIADUCT INSTITUTE, EARLESTOWN.

It will be seen from an advertisement that the Rev. G. Talahin Newton, will lecture in the large reading room of the Viaduct Institute on Tuesday evening, January 28th, taking for his subject " Elijah : the National Reformer." Mr. Newton is a powerful orator, and an intellectual treat is guar- anteed for those who can be present. BAPTIST MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.

On Thursday evening the ordinary meeting of this Society was declared an open night, and a lec- ture was given by the Rev, (e. E. Miller, before a fair audience, entitled " The history of the struggle for religious liberty/ The lecture was illustrated with lime light views, the lantern being worked by Mr. Lawson.

div.head: PROPERTY SALE A.T EARLESTOWN
div.p: PROPERTY SALE A.T EARLESTOWN

At the New Market Inn, Earlestown, on Monday evening, Messrs. Walton and Wood, auctioneers, brought under the hammer, two lots of property. There was a fair attendance of intending pur- chasers, but the bidding cannot be said to have been btisk. The first lot put was shop and dwell- mg-house, 36 Queen-street, now occupied by Mr.W Littler. This was disposed of for £361 to Mr. Gleave, St. Helens. The other lot consisting of four dwelling-houses in Athol-street, Earlestown, was withdrawn.

div.head: 1.0.G.T.
div.p: The usual weekly session of the Earlestown Ebenezer Lpdge was held in the Co-operative Hall, on Tuesday. Bro. W. Hatton, c.T., presided, and there was a fair attendance of members and friends. An invitation from the Tyldesley Lodge was read and arrangements made to visit the same. The pro- gramme for the evening was "Surprise Night,"' single members being responsible. 11,1r.George Dring gave an exhibition of magic lantern views, which was of an excellent character and also instructive. Thanks were accorded to Mr.Dring for his excellent services. _

div.head: EARLESTOWN PRIMITIVE METHODISTS.
div.p: EARLESTOWN PRIMITIVE METHODISTS.

On Thursday evening under the auspices of the Primitive Methodists branch of the Christian En- deavour Society, a concert and elocutionary enter- tainment was given in the Primitive Methodist Schoolroom. There was only a very sparse audience, but an excellent programme was submitted. Prof. F. Morgan, of Manchester, an elocutionist of some reputation had been engaged, and gave some capi- tal expBsitions of well-know pieces,including Mark Twain's" The tightest place I ever was in,"" How Bill Adams won the battle of Waterloo,"" Tantler's Sister," "A Modern Hero," &c. Several selections were interspersed, the artistes being Messrs. A. Baxter, and W. Limond, Misses Roberts and R. Corlett, each of whom acquitted themselves admir- ably. Mr. :ii. Leyland accompanied.

div.head: GOOD TEMP-LARS.
div.p: GOOD TEMP-LARS.

The weekly session of the Hope of Earlestown lodge of Good Templars was held in the Co-opera- tive Hall, Earlestown, on Monday evening. Bro. James Hatton presided, and there was a very large attendance of members and visitors. One candidate was initiated and several others were proposed. Bro. Newman, gave a report of the No. 1 Convention held at St, Helens on Saturday, which was adopteo. Arrangements were made for the juvenile New Year's party to be held at St. Helens next Saturday, after which a social meeting will be held. A report was given of the New Year adult soiree, which was a financial success, there being a balance in hand. Arrangements were made for the next session to be an open one, when there would be a visit from one of the principal lodges of Liver- pool, and an address would be given by the Rev. J. A. Lee of Liverpool. Sisters Warburton and Ord were responsible for the evenings programme, a number of games being indulged in, fruit and refreshments being handed round at intervals. SONS OF TEMPERANCE.

The Samuel Morley Section of Cadets of Temper- ance met on Wednesday in the Co.operative Hall, Earlestown. Bro. J. Judson, W.F., presided. After opening one new member was initiated. The elec- tion of officers for the current quarter resulted as follows :—W.A., Sister Louisa Barrett; V.A., Bro. Joseph Worrall ;. secretary, Bro. Arthur Porter; watchman, Bro. Lewis Jones; G., Bro. Ellenor Bar- rett. The section was visited by Bros. .Burrows, Hewitt, and Anders of St. Helens, and Bro. Chal- mers of Haydock• •The cadets were each presented with an otange on leaving by the worthy patron. The Britains Need Division met at eight o'clock in the same room. The meeting was called to order by Bro. Burrows, G.W.P., and the installation was proceeded with by the G.W.P. Two new members were initiated, and one reported as having violated rule 2 and a committee formed to investigate the same. One was proposed fJr membership and ar- rangements for her admission to the order was made. The visiting Brothers, Burrows, Anderton, Hewitt, and Chalmers were thanked for their cervices.

div.head: DEATH OF AN OLD EARLESTOWN RESIDENT.
div.p: DEATH OF AN OLD EARLESTOWN RESIDENT.

We have this we3k to chronicle the death of Mr. Joseph Mulreay, one of Earlestown's oldest resi- dents, which took place at the residence of his grand-daughter. in Bing-st., on Wednesday morn- ing, at the advanced age of 78 years. Mr. Mulreay came to Earlestown upwards of 40 years ago, and for many years was employed as a blacksmith at the Viaduct Works. Some years ago, however, he retired on a competency, and up to the time of his death appeared to enjoy good health, being, with the exception of a slight deafness, in full possession of all his faculties. His death supervened on a very brief illness. WEEK OF UNITED PRAYER.

During the past week, concluding on Sunday last united and universal prayer, has been held in the various places of worship in Earlestown. The first meeting was held Qn Sunday week at the Co-opera- tive Hall, and was conducted by Mr. Thomas Clarke the subject being "Humiliation and thanksgiving." On Monday at the Baptist church by the Rev. James Allatt, subject " Personal Consecration ;" Tuesday, Primitive Methodist church, Mr. J. Dring, "Nations and their rulers ;" Wednesday, Wesleyan church, Rev. F. E. Miller, "Families and schools? Thursday,Cochzregational church, Rev. E. R. Davies " Tbe Church Universal and Jesus ;" Friday, Salva- tion Army Barracks, Rev. J. Bartley," Home and Foreign Missions ;" Saturday Wesleyan Lecture Hall, "Praise meeting," conducted by Captain Thomas. On Sunday night there was an exchange of pulpits, the Rev. James Allatt (Congregational) occupying the Wesleyan pulpit; Rev. J. Bartley, (Wesleyan), the Primitive Methodist; Rev, E. R. Davies (Primitive), the Baptist ; Rev. F. E. Miller (Baptist), the Congregational ; Mr. G. Dring (Town Mission), Salvation Army; and Captain Thomas the Co-operative Hall Mission. After the services, all the ministers were present at a united Sacramental service held in the Wesleyan church, and conducted by the Rev. James Allatt. The services all through were well attended, and it is anticipated they have been productive of some good.

div.head: SALT TRADE IN 1895.
div.p: THE SALT TRADE IN 1895.

The annual official returns Nf the salt trade just issued show that on the whole 1895 was a normal year. Tbe total shipments of white salt came to 642,556 tons and of rock salt 62,932, tons, making a total of 705,498 tons. The average for the ten years of Viite salt is 713,501 tons and of rock salt 71,429 tons. In white salt there have been increases in ten markets amounting to 71,082 tons,against decreases in seven markets of 58,487 tons. The rock salt returns show an increase on white and rock salt on the year of 18,542 tons. The shipments to the United States, owing to the removal of the duty on salt, have been the largest -since 1888, the total quan- tity sent to the Northern States being 64,064 tons, and to the Southern States 81,338 tons. The shipments to British North America have been slightly in excess of those of 1894, while those to the West Indies and Central America have been practically the same. The South American market has shown the largest relative increase of any, more than 50 per cent. of an increase c,n the shipments of 1894 having been made. There has been a slight improvement in the African market, not- withstanding that Germany is troubling the English manufacturers bere,as in many other places. The East Indian market shows the largest absolute decrease of the year, amounting to no less than 47,368 tons, or over 80 per cent, of the total decrease. In the rock salt depart- ment Cheshire holds its own with great difficulty,owing to the unusually severe competition with Germany in the Continental markets and Fleetwood and Carrickfer- gus at home. Fleetwood has shipped of white and rock salt in 1895 over 94,000 tons, as against 60,000 in 1894. The exports from Middlesborough district have been less than in 1894, both coastwise arid foreign. The salt trade on the Manchester Snip Canal has not increased very much.

A shocking murder has been perpetrated near Clones, County Monaghan, the victim being a servant girl, who struck on the head by her master with a wooden " beetle." death resulting almost immediately. Mail advises from Tokio, state that the new Japanese Budget has been increased by 20,000,000 yen in respect of the Army estimates, and by 24,000,000 yen in respect Navy. It is proposed to increase the effective strength of the Army by 100 per cent. within ten years, and the Navy by 200 per cent. within the same period.

div.head: WARRINGTON DEBATING SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON DEBATING SOCIETY.
"THE SOUTH AFRICAN CRISIS."

A well-attended meeting of this society was held in the Masonic Hall, Bold-street, on Tuesday even- ing. Mr. T. Morris, F.G.S., presided, and the sub- ject of debate was " The South African Crisis," introduced by Mr. F. R. Roberts, M.A., L.L.B. The CHAIRMAN said with regard to the subject be must con less that his knowledge of it consisted of reading only, and reading without thinking was like a lame man without a crutch—not much good. He must therefore confess his ignorance but before he left the room he felt sure be would know more than he did and he depended upon the speakers for enlightenment. From what he had seen it seemed to him that the Chartered Coin- pany's policy was one of greed—of a few men with a lot of money who wanted more, and it looked as if they meant taking it if they could from some- body else, and he was not displeased that they were caught in their own net. If he had been ad- judicator he did not think he would have been so kind to some of them as the president had been. (Hear, hear.) Mr. ROBERTS, in opening the debate, said he thought the word " crisis " had been most rightly used for per- haps in the whole history of our foreign relations it wonlci be difficult to find such a combination of circum- stances which might more properly and fairly be de- scribed as a state of crisis in our national affairs, and this they called" The South African Crisis." Perhaps for the right understanding of their subject it would be wise if they traced historically the growth of what was known as the Transvaal Republie,and also the Chartered Company of South Africa. The speaker then related the settling of the Dutch Boers and the English in South Afrita. how they formed a joint colony, and how, in consequence of the Boers finding the conditions of Government not altogether suited to their mode of life, they " trekked " into that portion of South Africa im• mediately north ot the British Colonies and across the Vaal river, and in course of time two Dutch republics were established. The one across the Vaal became known as the Transvaal. Gradually the Btitish had asserted a kind of protectorate over this also, but their rule was again found intolerable, and led up to the insurrection of the Boers. which ultimately resulted in the ignomini- ous defeat of the British troops. Mr. Gladstone, on being brought into closer acquaintance with the facts, did what was, perhaps, the most righteous thing ever done by any statesman. Be recognised the superior claims of the Boers, and brought the war to a close by admitting their right to independence. Subsequently, isolated parties of Englishmen found their way into the Transvaal in search of gold, and gradually Johannes- burg, arose. It grew rapidly when it was known that paying gold was to be found there, and ultimately a difficult position occurred. Resident there was a body of 17,000 Boers, who possessed tne Government ; and a " foreign," or unfranehised body of 60,00 Johannes- burghers. Mr. Roberts referred to the character of the Boers and remarked on their deep 'religious spirit, force of character, and possession of a certain amount of mental enlightenment and culture. The Chartered Company was the first disturbing element. It was the creation of Mr. Cecil Rhodes, and it grew to such im- portance that the governing powers at home gave it a charter, conferring Imperial powers upon what was nothing more nor less than a trading company. Mas- honaland was conquered, primarily to hunt for gold,but this not being found as plentiful as expected, Matabele- land became the object of envy by the company. A quarrel was picked with Lobengula as in the case of Mashonaland, and then followed the tragic events of the Matabele War, the death of Lobengula, and the parcel- ling out of the land amongst the company's nominees. Here again, the company had been misled, and in its desire to create another boom in its shares it began to cast longing eyes upon the Transvaal, where, of course, gold was very abundant, and where it would be neces- sary to oust the Boer Government and to establish the government of the Chartered Company in its place. It was therefore necessary to bring the discontent of the Johanneshurgers to a heat so as to create a state of things calling for the intervention of the farces of the company. Hoping that success would justify their efforts they send their filibusters across the border to—death and humiliation. (Applause.) Com- ing to the raid, Mr. Roberts ridiculed the idea that the men of Johannesburg were willing to fight for their lives throught not having a vote. Their invitation to Jameson was a put-up plan of Rhodes and the Company. He thought Presidsnt Kruger had set this country an example of statesmanship which it would be well to follow, and he was also not ashamed to-day to call him- self once more a follower of Mr. Chamberlain. (Applause.) The Conservative Government, to its hon- our, had also risen to the height of the occasion. In Mr. Roberts' opinion nothing but the most frank and unqualified disavowal of the proceedings of the company and the unlawful conduct of Dr. Jameson could re-estab- lish England in her position as a justice-loving nation. If the complicity of the heads of the Chartered Company was established they should be rigorously punished, and the company should be compelled to pay whatever indemnity was decided as being due to the Boer Govern- ment, and if necessary the charter to be forfeited. Con- cluding, Mr. Roberts said it was not by actions such as those of the company that the gloss? of England had been up-built; and the permanence of her power could only be assured by the continuance of the course of fair and honest dealing. Councillor BENNETT congratulated Mr. Roberts upon the able speech which he had made but not in the able case he had put before them. Although he had dis- agreed with him in some things they were proud of a secretary who could give them a speech so capable and so eloquent. He had noticed that Mr. Roberts and others of his party had a sort of disposition to look at every- thing through unsEnglish spectacles and blame their own countrymen. He said in the first place that after the Zulu war the Transvaal was annexed because we were under the impression that a large number of Boers desired it. When the Boers rose we were ill-advised in coming to terms. It was clearly Mr. Gladstone's duty to cancel tht annexation and revert to the status quo but having expressed in the eyes of all the world his determination to stand by the annexation it was an act of the grossest folly to abandon it under the circum- stances we did abandon it. We should have kept the Transvaal in the interest of the 700,000 natives who pre- ferred our rule to that of the Boers. Mr. Roberts was bitter against the Chartered Co. Personally,the speaker believed the Company had acted foolishly but we must not forget that our flag flew over the greater part of South Africa through the pluck, enterprise and skill of these men. To regard the policy of Mr. Rhodes and the Co. as one of greed was a small and petty view to take of their action. We could not forget that after all the detractos of Mr. Rhodes had hurled their epithets at him,we owed the great part of our Empire there to him. He believed Mr. Rhodes' dominating idea had been to create a United Empire in Africa. It was Mr. Bennett's opinion that the objection to paying taxes and the wish to have a voice in the government of the country that caused the Johannesburgers to ask Jameson to their assistance. Mr. Jour; GANDY disagreed with Mr. Roberts as to the character of the Boers whom he stigmatised as the biggest thieves of the lot, and he was afraid from what he had learnt there was a good deal of the cowboy and ruffian about them. The Uitlanders greatly outnumbered the Boers and he supposed that practically Johannes- burg belonged to them by act of purchase. He therefore strongly questioned the right of the Boers to deny them the rights of citizenship. While by no means sympathis- ing with Dr. Jameson he thought there was a good deal to be said for all those men, and he was not prepared to

put all the blame upon then until they learnt more about it. He was glad the Government had shown a strong hand and its action was admired by all. German interest appeared to be threatened and the Kaiser imme- diately attempted to stick his finger in the pie. England was disposed to mete out justice to those who were not prepared to mete it out themselves. (Applause.) In his opinion we should have less in the future of those taunts to England in this matter. He concluded by ex- pressing the wish that out of all this evil, good might result. Mr. J. GRACE in a speech denunciatory of the Boers applied to them the term of a "hypocritical, salmsing- ing lot of humbugs," who worked the negroes to death and lived upon the products of their labour, and for which they were never paid. Johannesburg, ho said, ought to be styled Judasburg, and be asserted that the nature of the fight outside the town proved that British valour was by no means oil the wane. Mr. J. C. DALToN after supporting Mr. Roberts' argu- ments in a forcible manner and stating that he did not think it surprising that other nations looked upon Eng- land's declaimer with suspicion, wandered a little from the subject and criticised this county's action towards Ireland. Mr. KILOALLON, like Mr. Dalton, said that the Uit- landers were being treated to-day as England had treated Ireland. He admired the courage of Dr. Jameson and his followers, but condemned in strong terms the heads of the Chartered Company. Mr. E. J. HALL referred in uncomplimentary terms to the Boma and contended that they were doing us a great injustice by not admitting us to a share of government, seeing that by our enterprise, skill,and industry we had transformed a comparatively poor country into a wealthy and flourishing one. They were in the minority both in population and as regarded ownership of land. They had invited us to the place, and had asked Mr. Cecil Rhodes actually—the man whom they now reviled—to develops the resources of the country. Yet notwith- standing the immense amount of capital, skilled labour, Szc., which the English, Germans, and the French had poured into the place,they were not given the right of citizenship. The time for Dr. Jameson's action was not ripe ; it was possibly ten years too soon ; but the time would come when justice would have to be done in the Uitlanders. The CHAIRMAN in conclusion said it was most unjusti- fiable for any Englishman to take the law into his own , hands and commit depredations before he had righteous
't,;«iv&igkV,

cause for doing so. The Chartered Co. he believed, had gone to Africa for gold, and if they could not get it in one place they meant to have it in another. Referring to Germany he said he hoped Emperor would have more sense and discretion before long, and use it before giving expression to words which wounded where they should not, and made enemies where they ought not. In conclusion he referred in eulogistic terms to the firm position taken up by Mr. Chamberlain in the matter,and proposed that a resolution should go from that meeting to Mr. Chamberlain appreciating his conduct. (Ap- plause. ) Mr.BOBEIITS seconded, and in replying to the speakers of the evening, said there seemed to be a consensus of opinion that a mistake had been Fnade,and some of their friends seemed to think that the Boers did not come to court with clean hands. England had the right of inter- ference and not the company. (Applause.) It yids a manufactured crime, but we should not hang the men without hearing them. If the Efitlanders were suffer- ing from a lo,s of franchise could they believe that they would cry to God of this injustice ? Would a British artisan without his vote? No. All the Boers received from the Englishmen was a royalty on every ounce of gold recovered from the reefs. The debate then closed.

div.head: WARRINGTON.
div.p: WARRINGTON.
THE WORKINGMEN'S GOSPEL TEMPERANCE MISSION.

On Saturday night another "free and easy:" meeting was held. Mr. A. Horrocks presided. Mr. R. Drury amused the audience with Lancashire readings, "The Co-op." and "A trip to Yorkland." Mr. H. Heald recited an original piece, "A bit about Warrington Town," and both wete applauded for their.efforts. Songs, &c., were also given and refreshments served.—A gospel temperance meeting was held on Sunday night, Mr. W. Nightingale making an excellent chairman. M. J. J. Caldicott, of Manchester, formerly of Warriugton, gave an in- teresting address on "The Evolution of Society." He held that society was evolving out of its ori- ginal selfishness. Christ's teachings were lifting society upward and Godward. Mr. J. W. Tanner and Mr.J. Drury also gave earnest addresses on the blessings of temperance. The meeting was well attended.—On Tuesday night a well attended Band of Hope meeting was held conducted by the Presi- dent, Mr. A. Horrocks. STOVES.—Iron Merchant, GARLAND, Bridge-street BAND OF HOPE MEETING.

On Monday evening last the feurth of a series of Band of Hope meetings was held in the Ebenezer Church, Buttermarket-st. Mr. J.L. Robins occupied the chair. The meeting was opened by the singing of the well known hymn, "'Yield not to tempta- tion," after which God's blessing was invoked by short but earnest prayer. The Chairman in the course of his remarks showed the advantages of total abstinence, strongly advising all present to become abstainers. During the evening several re- citations were said by the children,including a long and beautiful piece given by Miss Plinston. Several solos and duets were given by Mr. J. Cotterell, Mr. J. Critchley, Miss Bibby, and Miss Tomkinson. Messrs. Richardson and Taylor gave two solos and a duet on the cornet and euphonium. The meeting was also enlivened with a piece by the ckoir an 4 a selection from "Gabaur" on string and reed instru- ments accompanied by the pian3. The closing piece was a very enjoyable dialogue given by a few Buckley-st. friends, who had kindly offered their services for the night. The meeting through- out was well sustained and thoroughly appreciated by a large audience. At half-past nine the pro- ceedings were brought to a close by the singing of the doxology and prayer. hum NATIONAL CLUB AND REGISTRATION :SOCIETY.

The weekly meeting of the Irish Club was held in the club room on Sunday, the chair being taken by Mr. Patrick Lane. The annual election of officers for the club took place, with the following results: President, Mr. J. C. Dalton: vice-presidents. Messrs, John Mullins, P. Lane, Malone, McGarty, P. Kenny. and D. Donnellan ; hon. secretary, Lieutenant McGarty; hon. treasurer, Mr. Patrick Lane, 4, Town- hill. The following gentlemen were appointed the Committee of Management: Messrs. McDermott, Noon, McCormack, Logan, Flanaghan, Belly, P. Walshe, John Mather, James O'Toole, Brian, O'Donnell, P. O'Boyle, E. G. Kenny, P. Toohey, Crowe, William Malone, T Kilgallon. T. Hughes, M. Flannery, J. Tynan, P. Hughes, J. Gannon. B. McCoy, and T. McGlynn; auditors, Messrs. Mather and Logan. The President addressed the meeting, and after thanking the members for electing him to the position of president of the club, he said in the course of a lengthy speech, that Irishmen located in Warrington had a right to be represented on the Council, the Board of Guardians, and on the Bench. Practically, the Irish people living in Warrington were without direct representation. The means they intended to adopt in order to bring about the desirable ends they had in view were as follows :—They would enlist a large number of volunteers to go out every Sunday to take an in- ventory of the Irishiposition in regard to the regis- ter. They would have debates, history classes,sing- ing classes, a literary society, and from time to time public demonstrations. (Applause.) Com- parisons were odious, but what other political bodies had to pay men to do for their cause the Irish club would get from Irishmen out of pure love and devotion—gratis! He concluded by urging all Irishmen to rally round the green flag, and help them on to victory. (Applause.) The meeting was also addressed by Messrs. Lane and McGarty. The membership totals up to 100.

div.head: FRODSHAIt.
div.p: FRODSHAIt.

"A VISIT TO Romx."—At the weekly meeting of the Werleyan Mutual Improvement Class, held on Thursday evening last, Mr. F. J. Norman. J.P., of Runcorn, delivered a lecture on " A Visit to Rome." The lecturer ably described many incidents in the life and work of St. Paul, as contained in the many legends which were in existence. Mr. Crosby,by the manipulation of the lime- light lantern, was enabled to make the lecture still more attractive by showing numerous views of the beauties of the city. At the close a vote of thanks was passed to the lecturer.

div.head: MR. RHODES SAILS FOR ENGLAND.
div.p: MR. RHODES SAILS FOR ENGLAND.
The Press Association is informed by the British South Africa Company that Mr. Rhodes.after consultation with the Board of Directors, decided t•-) sail yesterday for Eng- land.

div.head: MORE SHIPS FOR THE NAVY.
div.p: MORE SHIPS FOR THE NAVY.

The Admiralty have (says the "Times ") invited the principal private shipbuilding firms in the country to tender for the construction and immediate commence- ment of ten additional cruisers. These new vessels will be of similar design to the Pelorus, third-class cruiser, about to be launched at Sheerness. They will be 300 feet long, and of about 3,000 tons displacement, with engines of 7,000 i.h.p., which are estimated to give them a speed of 20 knots. The boilers are to be on the water- tube principle, and the proposed armament, which is heauy for their size, will be wholly composed of quick. firing guns. The contracts for these vessels will be divided amongst the fire successful firms tendering, in groups of two ships to each firm. It is anticipated that all ten vessels will be completed for service in a little over twelve months. The Admiralty have also requested all firms having Government contracts in hand to give precedence to that work over orders from private owners.

div.head: JIM TRANSVAAL RAID.
div.p: JIM TRANSVAAL RAID.
JAMESON TO COME TO ENGLAND.

Pretoria, Tuesday, 6 p.m.—A final agreement was arrived at this afternoon between Sir Hercules Robinson and the Transvaal Government. According to the terms of the arrangement, Dr. Jameson and his officers will be conveyed as prisoners to England, to be arraigned there. The rank and file of Jameson's force are handed over to Her Majesty's Government, to be conducted without demonstration to England or elsewhere' and to be dealt with as the British Govesnment shall deem fit. The High Commissioner has instructed the Governor of Natal to make the necessary arrangements on the Natal border for taking over the prisoners. The rank and file have already arrived at Volksrust. STRONG ALLEGATIONS AGAINST THE CHARTERED

div.head: COMPANY.
div.p: COMPANY.

The High Commissioner has informed the Colonial Office that between fifty and sixty members of Johannes- burg Reform Committee are to be tried] at Pretoria on the charge of armed rebellion against the Government. It is alleged, Sir Hercules Robinson adds, that the Government have evidence of a widespread conspiracy to seize upon the government and make use:of the wealth of the country to rehabilitate the finances of the Char- tered Company. The accused are well treated. The Colonial Office will be represented by counsel at the trial, who will watch over the interests of the American, Bri- tish, and Belgian citizens among the ptisoners. The British force at Delagoa Bay has been strengthened.
Biddulph Grange, Stoke-on-Trent, has been practically destroyed by fire, the damage being estimated at £30,000.
EARLESTOWN MUSICAL SOCIETY.
ANNUAL CONCERT.

This society,which has been in existence a couple of years, under the conductorship of Mr.E.Leyland, gave on Tuesday evening in the Town Hall, Earles- town, a representation of Handes oratorio "The Messiah." Considering this is the second occasion within about twelve months on which the society has submitted this iratorio before the Eariestown public, there was a very fair audience,who heartily applauded the various items which merited appre- ciation. The chorus and orchestra numbered about 100 and, judging from the manner in which the choruses were submitted, the vocalists must have been subjected to very careful training. The band was a mixture of players drawn from various sources, and perhaps this to some extent will ac- count for the only moderate display which they made. Mr. R. H. Pearson (Warrington), was leader of the band, Mr. J. Prescott presided at the organ, and Miss Sudworth at the piano. To assist in the production the following principals had been en- gaged :—Miss Young (soprano, Manchester) ; Mrs. Shaw (contralto), Mr. H. Berry (tenor, St. Helens) ; and Mr. N. Johnson, bass. It is not our intention to go through the various recitatives and choruses seriatim, but we may state that Mr. Berry satisfac- torily acquitted himself in the items he submitted, his rendering of "Comfort ye," and "But Thou didst not leave," being exceptionally fine. Not a whit behind was Mr. N. Johnson, who possesses a voice of very fair range, and he efficiently treated the numbers allotted to him. Mrs. Shaw, a good con- tralto, although perhaps a trifle weak, was not altogether happy in the recitative "Thus saith the Lord," and air "But who may abide,' but she was more successful in the air "The people that walked," and she was deservedly applauded. Miss Young handled her parts very cleverly,and on each occasion was well received. Of some of the choruses we cannot speak too highly,and taken all round the choir shows distinct signs of improvement. It is only to be expected, however, that in sue,h a choir there should be flaws, but it is gratifying to state, and creditable to the conductor, that errors were very few indeed. One thing noticeable was the fact that the bass was far too heavy, and on seve- ral occasions the trebles and tenors could not be heard, more especially was this noticed in the chorus "For unto us a Child is born." On the whole, however, the choir gave very little cause for complaint, the parts being smartly picked up, and excellent time kept. "Behold the Lamb," " All we like sheep." and " Since by man came death," de- serve special mention for the excellent manner in which they were rendered; but " Lift up your heads," certainly gave room for improvement. Mr. E. Leyland wielded the baton in a very efficient style, and to this no doubt was due the excellent time which was kept in rendering the choruses. It would be as well, however, in the event of any future production of a similar character.if the band could undergo a .course of training with the choir, so that all may be in complete accord.

div.head: EARLESTOWN WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL PRIZE DISTRIBUTION.
div.p: EARLESTOWN WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL PRIZE DISTRIBUTION.

On Sunday afternoon in the Earlestown Wesleyan Chapel, the prizes gained by the scholars attending the above school who are included in the round 0 class which embraces those who have not been absent or late on a single occasion during the past year, were distri- buted by the Rev. J. Bartley. The proceedings were presided over by Mr. Bartley and he was supported by the Rev. W. G. Bowden of St. Helens, Messrs. W. Clare, J. H. Profit and P. Parr (secretary). After the meeting had been formally opened with singing and prayer, a sacred solo, " I live for those who love me," was sung by Miss Maggie Davies. Mr. Peter Parr (secretary) afterwards read the report for the past year,in which be said the school was divided into three sections, viz.,senior,junior and infants. These were further divided into 32 classes. Teachers and officers on the books 74, of whom 34 were required in the mornings and 39 in the , afternoon. Scholars on the books 465, last year 475, decrease 10. Average attendance : teachers, morning 24, afternoon 33, scholars, morning 160, afternoon 210 Teachers meeting in society classes 53, increase 13, scholars meeting in society classes kincluding juniors) 102, increase 16. The health and vigour of the juvenile Missionary Society was a course of great encouragement and spoke well for the energy and tact of its secretary. Last year their results were a wonder but they were a much greater wonder this year. The 60 collectors had gathered together in pence and halfpence the right noble sum of £75, one third of which went to the foreign mis- sions, one third to the general home mission fund, and one third to home mission work in their own circuit. They would be lacking in gratefulness if they did not mention their high appreciation of Mrs. George Warbur- ton's services as secretary of that branch, and also their very deep regret that she had been compelled to resign the position. They earnestly hoped that her mantle might fall upon her successor, Miss Birchall,and thatshe might be as successful in her work. The library after being closed for a long period was reopened last June. and was going on very successfully. It had 57 readers; 710 volumes had been issued since its opening, being a, little over 30 per issue. The only drawback to its com- plete success was a lack of books and want of funds, two great obstacles, but they had every confidence that the energy of their librarian would surmount even these. The Band of Hope Society had been very active during the year and promised a still greater activity in the near future. The prizes to be presented that afternoon showed the interest that was still taken in the round 0 class, the recipients having regularly attended school morning and afternoon and early each time throughout the year. The finances showed receipts, including a balance of £l4 103. 4d. from the previous year, to be £66 103. Bd. and the ex- penditure £63 183.-1.1 d., leaving a balance of £2 Ils. 103. During the year the various branches of the school had had their special day, when efforts were put forth to gather in fruit, each being attended with good results. They would take that opportunity of tendering to the parents and friends of those teachers and scholars who had been taken from them by death, their deepest sym- pathy and assurance of their prayers. In conclusion they asked for the school and its workers a continuance of generous support and earnest prayers. (Applause.) Miss 0. Roberts then sang in good taste " My father, lead thou me."

The Rev. J. Bartley afterwards gave a short address, pointing out that the children did not gain the prizes by their own unaided efforts, but by a system of co-opera- tion, showing the industriousness of the mothers. Miss Lily Barr sang "Jesus, gentle Jesus," and Miss 0. Clare in a pleasing manner sang "I will his me down to yonder bank." The Rev. W. G. Bowden next addressed the children on the building of character, drawing distinctions be- tween a man's reputation and his character. Miss Ethel Collinge sang "Wonderful love." The Rev. J. Bartley then distributed about 120 books as awards. and after singing the doxology the gathering terminated.

WEEKLY REPORT ON THE HEA.LTH OF WARRINGTON. Week ending 4th January, 1806. During the week, which was the Ist of the current year, the following births and deaths were registered : Births. Deaths Warrington 55 2 1 Latchford 5 2 Total 6O 23 The excess of births over deaths was 37. The death rate from all causes was equal to 20 5 per 1,000, against 16.8 the average of the previous four weeks, and against 15.4 the corresponding week of last year. The death rate from the seven chief zytnotic diseases was equal to 4.5 per 1,000, against 4•5 the average rate of the four previous weeks, and against 0.8 the corresponding week of 1895. The ages of mortality were- 0— 1 1-5 5-15 15-25 25-65 65 up. 7 6 1 1 7 1 23 23 The deaths included-4 from measles, 1 from diphtheria, 2 from rickets, 2 from phthisis, 1 from old age, 2 from brain disease, 3 from heart disease, 1 from lung disease, 1 from burns. The following cases of infectious disease have been reported during the week :—Membraneous croup, 1 case, scarlet fever 5 cases, enteric fever 1 case. Total number of patients in hospital on Jan. 4th-42. METEOROLOGY.—The mean temperature was 46.1 Fah., and therefore 12.7 degrees higher than the preceding week. The maximum temperature 55 F., was recorded on the 3rd inst., and the rnimimum temperature 30 F., on the 29th inst. The Rainfall measured .44 inch. The general direc- tion of the wind was S.E. The reading of the Anemo- meter denoting 855 miles. JOHN H. GORNALL, Medical Officer of Health.
